#5481. Fisher Island Penthouse Sells After $12.2 Million Price Cut—Becoming the Private Island’s Second-Priciest Sale Ever

A stunning seven-bedroom penthouse at Palazzo Della Luna on Fisher Island, which originally hit the market in Miami Beach for $50 million in June 2025, sold on Oct. 28, 2026, for $37.8 million.

Even with a discount of $12.2 million, or about 24%, off its original asking price, the sale is the ultra-exclusive island’s second-highest residential sale ever. The island's top record-breaking sale was a five-bedroom condo that sold for $40 million in 2021.

The seller was represented by Sam Gaita of The Corcoran Group, and the buyer was represented by Andrew Holtz of Compass.

According to The South Florida Business Journal, the seller was “ALJ Properties USA LLC, managed by Alicia L. Jarrett and Camilo Miguel Jr. with the same address in Miami as Mast Capital, where Miguel is founder and CEO.” The penthouse last changed hands for $23.75 million in 2021.

Built in 2019, the sophisticated 9,852-square-foot home has luxurious finishes, including gallery-style walls, wide-oak flooring, and a Boffi kitchen with double Miele and Sub-Zero appliances. The sale works out to $3,837 per square foot.

Floor-to-ceiling windows surround the unit, and retractable glass walls open to 4,500 square feet of outdoor terraces with panoramic views of the Atlantic Ocean, Biscayne Bay, and the Miami skyline.

The lavish primary suite has a fireplace, lounge area, dual walk-in closets, and a fluted marble bath with sweeping 180-degree views.

The condo also has a 2,500-square-foot rooftop terrace for entertaining, with an outdoor kitchen and its own private pool.

“Without question, the private rooftop terrace with a swimming pool is the most impressive feature,” Gaita said. “This is the only ‘lower’ penthouse on Fisher Island offering a private rooftop with a pool, which is an extremely rare feature throughout all of Miami.”

There are also separate staff quarters and garage parking for two cars.

“Fisher Island is an ultra-exclusive, private country club island accessible only by boat or helicopter,” he noted. “This 216-acre private island offers a private beach club, yacht club, multiple dining venues, tennis, pickleball, padel, spa and more, reserved for members and their guests only.”

Gaita said what ultimately drove the record sale was “attracting the buyer who best aligned with and appreciated the one-of-a-kind features the property has to offer.”

He also noted that its exclusive location “on a private island comparable to a country club, isn’t something that can be easily replicated and serious buyers understand that value."

#5480. Just 3 Major U.S. Metros Are Seller’s Markets–the Fewest Since the Pandemic Freeze

Just three of the 50 most populous U.S. metro areas were seller’s markets in October. That’s tied for the fewest in records dating back to 2016, matching April 2020, when the pandemic froze the housing market.

Nassau County, NY was the number-one seller’s market, with 24.7% fewer sellers than buyers. The other seller’s markets were Newark, NJ (-14.3%) and Montgomery County, PA (-12.1%).

All three seller’s markets became less strong seller’s markets in October. In Nassau County, there were 28.3% fewer sellers than buyers in September, a bigger gap than October’s 24.7%. Newark’s gap shrunk from 17.6% to 14.3%, and Montgomery County’s shrunk from 20.1% to 12.1%. Milwaukee, which was a seller’s market in September, is now balanced, meaning it doesn’t favor sellers or buyers.

The seller’s markets are places where limited homebuilding has kept housing supply tight. In the greater New York City area, combine that with strong demand for homes near a major job center, and buyers are competing for homes. Home-sale prices rose an average of 3.3% year over year across the three seller’s markets in October. That’s compared with a 0.3% uptick across all of the buyer’s markets, a sign that in seller’s markets, competition among buyers is pushing up home prices.

“Buyers looking in these pockets of the Northeast should be prepared for a very different experience than buyers elsewhere in the country,” said Redfin Senior Economist Asad Khan. “They may have less room to negotiate, especially on desirable, move-in-ready homes, and could face multiple-offer situations. If you’re shopping in one of these markets, it’s especially important to know your budget, be ready to act when the right home comes along and avoid getting swept up in a bidding war.”

Seller’s markets are the exception to a national picture that heavily favors buyers.

Nationwide, homebuyers have more negotiating power than at any point in Redfin’s records. There were an estimated 70.5% more home sellers than buyers in the U.S. housing market in October, the biggest gap in records dating back to 2013.

That marks the sixth record-breaking month in a row, and the margin is up from 65.6% in September. The Sun Belt is driving the extreme buyer’s market nationwide, led by huge seller surpluses in Miami, Nashville, TN and Las Vegas.

When sellers outnumber buyers, buyers typically have more negotiating power because they have options. That’s why a market with a lot more sellers than buyers is considered a buyer’s market. We define a market where there are over 10% more sellers than buyers as a buyer’s market and a market where there are over 10% fewer sellers than buyers as a seller’s market. A market where the gap is plus or minus 10% is considered a balanced market.

We estimated the number of buyers using proprietary Redfin data on the typical time from a buyer’s first tour to close of purchase, and MLS data on active listings and pending sales. The estimated number of sellers in the market is simply the number of active listings in the MLS. These estimates are seasonally adjusted and subject to revision. See a more detailed methodology here and view an interactive dashboard here.

It’s only a buyer’s market for people who can afford to buy. High housing costs and economic jitters have pushed many would-be homebuyers to back off in recent years, creating the imbalance between buyers and sellers we see today.

“A buyer-friendly market can help make homeownership a little more attainable, even if it doesn’t solve the affordability challenges that have kept many people on the sidelines,” Khan said. “Sellers are increasingly competing for buyers’ attention, which can translate into price reductions, concessions and other savings. First-time buyers don’t have equity from a previous home to put toward a purchase, which makes saving for a down payment a big hurdle–but they also don’t have to sell a home before they can buy or give up a low mortgage rate.  With a historic buyer’s market and home prices that are finally ticking down after three years of increases, first-time buyers who have been waiting–and can afford today’s costs–may have an opportunity to make a move.”

The gap between buyers and sellers widened in October because would-be buyers retreated, while sellers continued listing their homes, albeit at a sluggish pace.

There were an estimated 895,752 homebuyers in the market nationwide in October, the lowest level in records dating back to 2013. That’s down 2% from a month earlier, the sixth straight monthly decline. Mortgage rates averaged 7.33% in October, up from 6.86% in September, which priced out more would-be buyers.

On the flip side, there were an estimated 1,526,984 home sellers in the market, the most since March 2020. That’s up 0.9% month over month.

The number of homes on the market is piling up because many homes are lingering on the market for months without going under contract. Each month, more new listings are adding to the big pool of supply.

Some homeowners keep listing their houses despite falling demand because many have given up on waiting for lower rates. They may want to sell now because they’re worried prices could decline, and some need to move for a new job, a growing family, or another life change. But many homeowners who don’t need to move have substantial equity and little pressure to sell, so they may hold off on listing.

Over 80% of U.S. metro areas, 41 of the 50 Redfin analyzed, are buyer’s markets. That matches September’s record.

For the third month in a row, Miami and Nashville have the biggest surpluses of sellers over buyers. Miami had 195.8% more sellers than buyers in October, and Nashville had 159.5% more. Las Vegas (149.9%) was third on the list. In the top 13 buyer’s markets, there were more than twice as many sellers as buyers in October. Nearly all are in the Sun Belt; four are in Texas and four are in Florida.

The Sun Belt, particularly Texas and Florida, is home to some of the nation’s biggest buyer’s markets, partly because of robust homebuilding. Builders are continuing to add new homes even as demand cools, swelling inventory and giving buyers more options and negotiating power.

Demand has cooled largely because rising mortgage rates and stubbornly high home prices are pricing buyers out. In Florida, rising HOA and homeowners insurance costs are exacerbating the affordability squeeze.

Six metros were “balanced” in October, neither buyer’s nor seller’s markets: Chicago (8.1% more sellers than buyers), Boston (7.5%), Providence, RI (7.5%), New Brunswick, NJ (5.6%), Milwaukee (0.6% fewer sellers than buyers) and San Francisco (6.9% fewer).

The surplus of home sellers over buyers grew month over month in 34 of the 41 buyer’s markets in October.

The surplus increased most in Miami, which also has the biggest surplus of sellers over buyers; there were 195.8% more sellers than buyers in October, up from 160.5% the month before. The next-biggest monthly increases were in Las Vegas, where there were 149.9% more sellers than buyers, up from 122.8%, and Nashville (159.5%, up from 134.3%).

House hunters lost negotiating power in seven buyer’s markets. The surplus of sellers over buyers fell from September to October in Fort Worth, TX (91.6%, down from 100%), St. Louis (23.1%, down from 27.1%), Austin (124.8%, down from 128.2%), Dallas (118.6%, down from 120.5%), Jacksonville, FL, Pittsburgh and Los Angeles. All of them remain buyer’s markets.

#5478. Bill Cosby Knocks $2 Million Off Original Listing Price of Manhattan Townhouse in Latest Attempt To Sell

Bill Cosby has been looking to offload his longtime New York City townhouse since early 2025, and he's slashed the price once again.

The six-bedroom, 4.5-bathroom dwelling now boasts an asking price of $4,999,000, with the listing touting it as a "rare Treadwell Farm townhouse opportunity under $5 million."

The disgraced star first listed the home in April 2025, shortly after news broke that he was facing foreclosure on this property and a much pricier Manhattan townhome he owned at the time.

The more expensive abode was sold for $28 million, while this particular home had a complicated journey.

In July 2025, the asking price was dropped to $6.75 million. Then in December, the listing was removed.

At the time, listing agent Adam Schneider of Corcoran Westside Columbus told Realtor.com® that Cosby and his wife, Camille, chose to delist the home to carry out a series of updates after they resolved the financial issues clouding the property.

"All issues with the lender have been resolved," Schneider said in a December 2025 email. "The property is now being renovated and we plan to list it in the New Year."

The home returned to the market in January 2026 for $6.75 million. At the end of April, the price dipped to $5.99 million.

The townhouse would go on to be listed and removed twice more in 2026—reappearing in August at the same $5.99 million asking, and again in September at a reduced $5.49 million.

The listing directly speaks to the price reduction: "At this reduced price point, the opportunity is clear: there is very little in the 20-foot Upper East Side townhouse market that is this substantial, this flexible, and this well-positioned."

While the listing does not explicitly mention the aforementioned renovation, it does suggest there is still room for change.

"The next owner can preserve what works, improve what matters, and invest directly into a home that reflects their own taste, lifestyle, and long-term vision," it reads.

Spanning 5,000 square feet across a basement and four levels, the property has an open floor plan and includes elevator access and private outdoor space.

"Its flexible floor plan allows for bedroom and bathroom realignment, giving the next owner the option to refresh for the 2020s, personalize, or more fully reimagine the home over time," the listing reads.

The home has a handful of original features, including the red oak banisters, exposed brick, and mahogany and mosaic hardwood flooring.

Crown moldings, high ceilings, and period fireplaces also add character throughout.

A large eat-in kitchen anchors the garden level, and it has been equipped with stainless-steel appliances, including a restaurant-grade Montague Grizzly stove.

A formal dining room includes a wood-burning fireplace, as well as French doors that lead to an enclosed sunroom and a landscaped backyard.

Two generously sized living rooms round out the second level, while the third foor has two large bedrooms and a shared sitting or dressing area.

The primary suite is located on the fourth level and includes a fireplace and two additional spaces that could be used as bedrooms, offices, or other purposes.

The basement includes laundry facilities and storage space, while the rooftop has "meaningful potential for future customization and expansion."

Previous reports indicated that the property had primarily been used by Cosby's son, Ennis, who was murdered in Los Angeles in 1997. It is not clear whether the actor continued to use it regularly, as it is understood that Cosby and his wife—who remained by his side throughout his sexual assault scandal—have been living primarily at their home in a suburb of Philadelphia.

The couple purchased the townhouse in 1980 for $1.19 million.

#5477. Applied Materials posts impressive 53% jump in revenue as it beats expectations again

Semiconductor industry giant Applied Materials Inc. chalked up another strong quarter as it continued to cash in on the artificial intelligence boom, delivering fourth-quarter results that surpassed Wall Street’s expectations on earnings and revenue.

The company reported adjusted earnings of $4.16 per share on revenue of $10.41 billion, up by an impressive 53% from a year earlier. The results were impressive, with analysts modeling earnings of just $4.06 per share on sales of $10.3 billion. Net income rose to $2.71 billion, up from $1.89 billion in the same period one year ago.

Applied Materials is the world’s biggest supplier of the equipment used by semiconductor manufacturers such as Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. Ltd., Samsung Electronics Co. Ltd. and Micron Technology Inc., so its results are widely seen as a bellwether for the broader chipmaking industry. If Applied is growing, it means chipmakers are investing in their factories and presumably expecting to churn out more chips, driving growth in the industry. The company manufactures all sorts of machines to support different semiconductor manufacturing processes, catering to the most advanced silicon for AI workloads.

Chief Executive Gary Dickerson (pictured) said the company delivered record-breaking results in fiscal 2026, with full-year sales rising 21% from the prior year, to $34.31 billion. He also said the semiconductor systems business unit is on track to grow more than 40% in calendar 2026. “AI continues to fuel strong incremental demand for semiconductors and Applied has the most-enabling portfolio to advance the AI computing roadmap, putting us in a great position for multiyear revenue and profit growth,” he added.

Applied’s stock was under pressure earlier in the day following the news of Nvidia Corp. CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation, which came after he admitted to having an affair with a woman who is believed to be working for China’s intelligence services. Some investors worry that instability at Nvidia, which is the world’s most dominant AI chip supplier, could have a knock-on effect on the broader chipmaking industry.

However, the strong results brought Applied’s daytime slide to a halt, and the stock gained more than 2.5% in late trading. In the year to date, its stock is up 48%.

Applied’s main business, the semiconductor systems unit, saw revenue jump from $4.88 billion in the year-ago period to $7.99 billion. Meanwhile, sales from the smaller applied global services segment rose from $1.5 billion a year earlier, to $1.89 billion.

For the current quarter, Applied said it’s looking for earnings of $4.35 per share at the midpoint of its guidance range, with revenue coming to $11.1 billion. Those numbers were better than expected too, with the Street modeling first quarter earnings of just $4.24 per share on sales of $10.85 billion.

During the quarter, Applied made a big splash when it said it’s going to invest $5 billion in a new chip research and development facility located in Silicon Valley. It’s called the EPIC Center, and it will act as a shared R&D center for chipmakers to collaborate on new process manufacturing technologies.

Initial partners include Intel Corp., which is working with Applied and other companies on the development of next-generation transistors, interconnects and advanced packaging technologies. Other founding partners include Kioxia Corp., BE Semiconductor Industries N.V. and the UCLA Samueli School of Engineering.

#5476. The Generational Housing Divide: Millennials Had It Better Than Baby Boomers–Until the Pandemic Changed the Math

If millennials hadn’t spent so much money on avocado toast, they’d all own their dream home by now–right? Wrong. Just over half of millennials own their home. For the rest, housing costs have soared so much in recent years that skipping the avocado toast in their 20s wouldn’t have made a dent.

The story isn’t about constant struggle, though–it’s about timing. Elder millennials who bought a home in their early 30s had it better than baby boomers did at the same age: Historically low mortgage rates and higher household incomes meant those millennials spent about 27% of their income on housing at age 30, compared with 36% for boomers. Then the pandemic changed the math. Mortgage rates jumped from around 3% to nearly 7%, and home prices surged. Since rates rose above 6% in 2022, elder millennials have spent up to 35% of their income on monthly mortgage payments, compared with roughly 25% for boomers at the same age–even though millennials earn more, adjusted for inflation.

Boomers might point out that mortgage rates were much higher in their day. They’d be right: Rates peaked at over 16% in 1981 and stayed in double digits for much of the decade. But prices were lower. In the 1980s, when many boomers were in their 30s, the typical U.S. home sold for about $235,000 to $265,000 in today’s dollars. When elder millennials reached the same age–prime homebuying age–in the 2010s and 2020s, typical prices ranged from about $275,000 to $455,000.

Key takeaway: Buying at the wrong time was painful for both generations, but boomers had a better chance to recover. Falling rates throughout the late 1980s, 1990s and early 2000s gave them many opportunities to refinance into lower payments. Millennials who bought before 2022 secured historically low mortgages; those who bought later—or never managed to buy—face a much less forgiving market. Of course, it’s possible the market could become more forgiving for millennials over time; rates may eventually fall significantly enough that many millennials have the opportunity to refinance into lower payments.

This is based on an analysis of Redfin and U.S. Census data. A few notes to help contextualize the numbers: All dollar figures are adjusted for inflation. Much of the data illustrates each generation’s typical experience at a given age, combining everyone in that generation who has reached that age, whenever that happened for them. Because millennials are still aging into their 40s, for example, our 40-to-44 figures only capture the oldest millennials, who hit those ages between 2021 and 2025. All boomers have been through that age range, so their figures include the whole generation. Please see the end of this report for a detailed methodology.

In their early 30s, elder millennials who bought a home spent a smaller share of their income on housing than boomers did at the same age, despite much higher home prices. Imagine a median-earning millennial born in 1984 who bought a home at age 30. They would have spent around 27% of their income to purchase the typical home, within the “don’t spend more than 30% of your income on housing costs” rule of thumb.

Two factors helped: cheap borrowing and higher household incomes. Millennials benefited from roughly a decade of historically low mortgage rates; they fell below 3% in 2021. Millennials also tend to have higher household incomes than boomers did at the same age. At age 37, the typical elder millennial household earned an average of $100,000, compared with $88,000 when boomers were that age. The discrepancy is partly because two-income households are more common today. About 78% of women participate in the U.S. workforce, up from roughly 60% in 1980. It’s also worth noting that millennials typically work similar hours for more money than baby boomers at the same life stage.

The millennial advantage didn’t last. Mortgage rates jumped from around 3% in late 2021 to nearly 7% in late 2022, after home prices had surged about 40% nationwide during the pandemic homebuying frenzy. Rising rates often cool prices, but this time, prices didn’t fall. That mix of high prices and mortgage rates that had doubled from their pandemic-era low meant Americans had to spend a much higher share of their income to buy a home. Imagine that same millennial, born in 1984: If they bought a home at age 40 instead of 30, their housing costs shot up to about 35% of their income.

Rising prices and rates also priced many Americans completely out of the housing market, which is why elder millennials have a lower homeownership rate than baby boomers at the same age.

“For millennials who haven’t yet bought a home, affordability is a challenge. But it’s important to remember that you’re not trying to climb Mount Everest, you’re just trying to get back to 2018 or 2019, which was the last time the average homebuyer was spending just about 30% of their income on housing,” said Chen Zhao, Redfin’s head of economic research. “Before the pandemic, younger generations actually had it easier than the ones before them. But then home prices surged during the pandemic homebuying frenzy and mortgage rates shot up, while incomes kept growing at a normal pace–and the advantage flipped. If you bought in 2020 or 2021, you’re coming out ahead, but those years were the exception, not the rule. One piece of hope for younger Americans who haven’t yet bought a home: Home prices are already falling in parts of the U.S. and they’re softening in others, which means we could be headed back to 2018 or 2019 levels sooner rather than later.”

Millennials are also contending with other major expenses; childcare costs are squeezing them particularly hard. A recent Redfin analysis found that housing and childcare consume more than half of the typical American’s household income. Student loans are another big expense; millennials have significantly more student loan debt than boomers did at the same age.

Adult Gen Zers, who are in their twenties, are tracking behind millennials at the same stage of life. Gen Zers have spent anywhere from 40% of 60% of their income to buy the typical home since they’ve reached homebuying age. That’s partly because they’re still young enough that they haven’t yet hit their earnings peak, so their current income is lower than older generations, and partly because housing costs are higher than in the past. But as Gen Zers move through their careers, their earnings are likely to grow substantially, as they have for every generation before them. Combined with a gradual normalization in housing costs, homeownership should become increasingly attainable over time.

Baby boomers faced their own affordability crisis when they were young, in the 1980s. In their early 20s, the typical boomer household who bought a home would have spent more than 60% of its income on housing costs, reflecting the era’s runaway inflation and double-digit mortgage rates.

But their housing burden fell quickly as they aged, dropping to around 40% of income by their late 20s and 26% by their late 30s. Baby boomers’ homeownership rate steadily rose from about half in 1985 to over 70% by the late 1990s, and it kept climbing after that. By their 40s and 50s, the share of homebuyers’ income spent on housing had settled into the low-to-mid 20% range, lower than millennials at the same point in their life.

Much of that relief came from the same force that had hurt them initially—mortgage rates—as rates gradually declined through the 1980s and 1990s, letting many boomers refinance into far more manageable payments even as home prices kept climbing.

Millennials haven’t had the same opportunity. Those who bought before 2022 locked in historically low rates, while those who bought later faced a costly combination of high prices and climbing rates. Would-be buyers who couldn’t afford that combination were left out altogether.

“The housing market has historically been better for baby boomers than younger generations because lower home prices and higher rates are preferable to higher home prices and lower rates,” Zhao said. “You can refinance your rate into a lower housing payment, and that’s exactly what boomers did: They refinanced for up to 40 years as rates kept falling. Then home prices soared, which is why a lot of boomers are rich in real estate.”

That dynamic shows up clearly when you ask people directly. In a recent Redfin survey, more than three-quarters (76%) of baby boomers homeowners said they can easily afford their payment, while the rest struggle. Roughly half (53%) of millennial homeowners can easily afford their payment, and the other half struggle.

The same generational squeeze shows up in the reasons people are staying put in their current home. Among people unlikely to move soon, 43% of millennials cited high home prices as a reason, compared with 31% of boomers. Three in 10 (30%) millennials pointed to high mortgage rates, versus just 18% of boomers, likely because many baby boomers have paid off their mortgage and built up substantial equity. This is from a Redfin survey conducted by Ipsos in May 2026, fielded to 4,000 U.S. residents.

Consider two hypothetical couples. Alex and Jordan are millennials born in 1984 and live on two incomes, a common setup for millennial households. Pat and Chris are baby boomers born in 1956 and got by on one, more typical for their generation. The numbers below show what it would have cost each couple to buy a home to buy a home in their early 30s and their late 30s.

This analysis uses income data from 1976 to 2025 from the U.S. Census Bureau’s Current Population Survey Annual Social and Economic Supplement (CPS ASEC), accessed through IPUMS. The sample includes household heads aged 19 and older, and results are weighted using CPS household weights.

Each household is assigned to a generation based on the age of the household head in the survey year.

Home prices. We start with the 2025 median sale price of U.S. single-family homes from Redfin data ($456,409). Prices for earlier years are estimated by scaling that 2025 price back using the S&P Cotality Case-Shiller U.S. National Home Price Index from 1987 onward and the FHFA All-Transactions House Price Index for years before 1987. Both indexes are averaged by year.

Monthly housing payment. For each year, we calculate the monthly payment to buy a median-priced home. It covers principal, interest, property taxes and homeowners insurance. We assume:

Income and inflation. Household income is total household income as reported in the CPS ASEC. All income and payment figures are converted to 2025 dollars using the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U).

Share of income spent on housing. For each generation and age, we calculate the median monthly housing payment and the median household income, and divide the payment by one-twelfth of the income.

How to read the results by age.  Much of the data in this report shows each generation’s typical experience at a given age. Because a generation spans many birth years, people born at the start of that generation turn, say, 40 in a different calendar year than people born at the end of it. For this analysis, each age point combines averages for everyone from that generation who has reached that age, in whatever year that actually was for them. For instance, millennials (born 1981 to 1996) have only had the oldest members of their generation—those born in the early-to-mid 1980s—reach their 40s so far. So when we show what the typical 40-to-44-year-old millennial paid for housing, we’re only capturing people who hit that age between 2021 and 2025. Younger millennials haven’t gotten there yet. Baby boomers (born 1946 to 1964) are fully through that age range, their 40-to-44 data point include averages from all boomers.

As a data journalist at Redfin, Dana Anderson writes about the numbers behind real estate trends. #5475. October Existing-Home Sales Sink to 16-Year Low; Rates Only Partly to Blame

The National Association of Realtors®’ (NAR) Existing-Home Sales report for October came in on a somewhat dismal note: Existing-home sales decreased 5.5% month-over-month to a rate of 3.75 million.

That marks the lowest level since August 2010’s 3.68 million, according to Realtor.com®  Chief Economist Danielle Hale.

Year-over-year home sales were down 8.8% compared to October 2025, which recorded a sales pace of 4.11 million.

Month-over-month sales declined in the Midwest, South and West, but held steady in the relatively “inventory-constrained” and “competitive” Northeast market, Hale noted. Year-over-year sales, however, declined for all four regions.

NAR Chief Economist Lawrence Yun blamed mortgage rates. “Homebuying is difficult when mortgage rates have climbed to their highest levels since 2000, aside from a single month in 2023. As a result, home sales fell to their lowest level since August 2010,” he said.

As the housing market enters its slowest season, rates that have held above 7%—a huge leap from before the Iran War, when they touched 6%—have depressed demand and discouraged many buyers, who already face longer-term issues with housing affordability.

Hale concurred with Yun’s diagnosis. According to her, climbing mortgage rates in September (the time when many October closed sales would have been in contract) “were the highest rates of 2026 at the time…and they likely derailed some homebuying plans.”

If mortgage rates “derailed” home-buying plans in October, could the recent ease in mortgage rates signal a gentler turn in the market in the coming months?

Hale thinks the story is not so simple. In her words, the October market “reflect(ed) a perfect storm of an abrupt shift in the financial environment and large uncertainties in the pre-election period for both policy and the economy just as the housing market usually slows for the season.”

She added that “several factors are likely to put a floor under how low rates can go, including a strong economy and jobs market, persistent inflation, and an expected need for tighter monetary policy in the near term combined with sizable demand for capital from both governments and private companies, largely to finance AI-related investments.”

Overall, Hale said she “expect(s) to see more homebuyers come back into the market as we move away from recent mortgage rate highs, but the upside will be limited.”

Sean Fergus, VP of Economic Research at builder-focused data and analytics firms NewHomeSource and Zonda, largely came to the same conclusion as Hale.

“Rates have since eased,” he said, “but buyers need to trust that relief will last before they come back in force.”

Yun had a more positive outlook, predicated on whether mortgage rates continue to decline. In NAR’s press release, he said that “(b)ased on the current underwhelming home sales pace at a time of consistent job growth, there could be sizable pent-up demand if mortgage rates decline.”

Yun also commented on the relatively good financial position of homeowners currently, saying that they “are largely in a comfortable financial position due to sizable housing wealth accumulation.”

As evidence for this claim, he pointed to the “historically low” number of distressed property sales, which “remains…at only 2% of all transactions.”

As a final sort of snapshot on the real estate ecosystem, total unsold inventory ticked up 1.3% to 1.59 million units, or the equivalent of 5.1 months’ supply. September 2026 recorded 4.7 months’ worth of unsold inventory, still higher than 4.4 months’ unsold inventory in October 2025, from which 1.59 million units represents a 4.6% yearly  increase.

Median existing-home sale prices increased more modestly, only crawling up 0.4% year-over-year to $416,700. The same median price was $414,900 last October. Even so, this is the 40th consecutive month of year-over-year price increases.

Audrey Jiang is an editorial intern for RISMedia.

#5474. Rates Come Down Again but Remain Over 7%

wood block of percentage change to UP and Down arrow. Interest rate, GDP, stocks market, financial, deflation and Inflation, ranking, mortgage, debt, Loan and Economic Recession concept

Mortgage rates eased again for the fourth-straight week but remain almost a full percentage point over last year at this time, a key reason buyers continue to hold back and why the market remains sluggish.

The latest Freddie Mac Primary Mortgage Market Survey® released Thursday shows the average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage rate at 7.11%, down seven bases points from  7.18% last week. The 30-year FRM is still up year-over-year from 6.24% last year. The 15-year FRM averaged 6.45%, down from 6.57%. A year ago at this time, the 15-year FRM averaged 5.49%.

At presstime, the average rate was back up to 7.42% Thursday afternoon, according to Mortgage News Daily.

Bright MLS Chief Economist Lisa Sturtevant said that while rates are at their lowest level since late September, borrowing costs are still nearly a full percentage point higher than they were last year at this time.

“While rates have declined for three weeks in a row, homebuyers are still holding back,” Sturtevant said in a statement. “Higher rates, along with on-going economic uncertainty, are key reasons why housing market activity is so sluggish this fall.

She also said there is little reason to expect rates to come down further this year, and that, given this week’s inflation report, it’s more likely for rates to increase instead.

“So far, we haven’t seen higher rates lead to widespread price declines,” she said. “In fact, home prices are still rising in many local markets. Inventory is rising but higher rates are causing sellers to pause along with buyers. Because both sides of the supply-demand equation are slowing, it’s not likely for home prices to drop significantly even if rates move higher.”

Sturtevant noted that data on pending home sales suggest that sales are going to continue to be anemic in the fourth quarter. “It is very likely we will end 2026 with a total of fewer than 4 million existing home sales for the first time since the 1990s.”

Realtor.com Senior Economist Jiayi Xu added that the recent downtrend trend with rates could potentially reverse next week as the 10-year yield returns to 5%.

“The strong October jobs report showed the labor market holding up well, clearing the way for the Fed’s next rate hike,” Xu said in a statement. “On Tuesday morning, before the CPI release, Fed Governor Christopher Waller said a larger 50-basis-point move should be considered in December’s meeting if inflation came in hot. Shortly afterward, the October CPI report came in hotter than forecast, pushing the 10-year Treasury yield toward 5%. A December hike is now essentially priced in. The debate is no longer if the Fed hikes, but how far and how fast.”

Xu also said today’s homebuyers are being squeezed by both high mortgage rates and high inflation, with inflation being the bigger long-term problem.

“High rates raise monthly payments and shrink the loan a buyer can qualify for, and the recent pullback in pending sales shows how sensitive buyers are,” she said. “But persistent high inflation is what keeps the Fed hiking and rates elevated. Inflation also leaves households with less to put toward a home, especially when wages lag prices. First-time buyers feel it most. With no equity to lean on, they must save a down payment from budgets already stretched thin. Even if rates ease, living costs rising faster than pay will keep weighing on demand for years.”

#5473. Sellers Are Cutting Home Prices the Most in These Markets—Led by One ‘Weirdly Nice’ City

As the market slowed in October due to seasonal trends and elevated mortgage rates, more than 1 in 5 listings throughout the country saw a price reduction, the highest October level since 2022.

For a few major metros, the share of price-reduced homes has pulled significantly ahead of the national share of listings with price reductions, which stood at 20.5%.

Price reductions were most common in Salt Lake City, where a whopping 31.8% of listings had price cuts as of October. The median listing price in October was $559,000 in Salt Lake City, a 3.5% decrease from October 2025, according to the Realtor.com economic research team’s monthly housing trends report.

The share of price-reduced homes in Salt Lake City increased 1.6 percentage points over last October.

Salt Lake City is followed closely by Indianapolis, where 31.7% of homes have had a price reduction, and Denver, with 30.9%.

Of the 50 largest metro areas in the U.S., these 10 had the largest share of price reductions in October:

Of these top 10 cities for price reductions, eight also topped the list in October 2025, confirming these are mostly longstanding softer markets, according to Realtor.com senior economist Jake Krimmel.

Raleigh and front-runner Salt Lake City are the latest to join the top 10 cities where price cuts are most frequent.

For Salt Lake City, Indianapolis, Portland, and Denver, price cuts can be common as the weather grows colder and the market has less movement, says Krimmel.

“These markets in particular compared to the rest of the list, which is mostly Sun Belt, can be very unfavorable to sellers when the weather gets cold and buyers stay away until spring,” the economist says.

The reason for widespread price decreases in Salt Lake City may go a step further, showcasing a unique aspect of the city’s market: Buyers are “weirdly nice,” according to Joel Carson, who has been a real estate agent in the area for over 30 years.

“Utah is very unique in that people don’t lowball offers. They don’t want to offend the seller, so they’ll wait for that price reduction before they offer,” Carson tells Realtor.com. “Sellers are always asking, ‘Why wouldn’t they just offer me less?’ And the reason is that we have weirdly nice people here, and they don’t want to be offensive.”

For Carson and fellow agents in the area, the understanding of this politeness helps them properly advise sellers.

When the market is slow, like it has been this fall, he tends to take homes he’s listing off the market for 30 days to let them rest. They can then be relisted with fresh days on the market and a significant price reduction.

When buyers are hesitating, pricing ahead of the market is key to staying competitive. By pricing 5% to 8% under current value, listings attract buyers who may be wary of asking for price concessions, according to Carson.

Uncertainty surrounding the midterm elections, elevated mortgage rates, and concerns about affordability slowed October down, with pending sales down 10.5% and contract signings down 17% year over year.

Still, the right price reduction can result in multiple bites from buyers, Carson says.

“Just this last week, we were at $345,000 on a house and we went to $320,000 and got an offer, so we’re under contract. We actually got two offers,” says Carson. “Once you know what your seller’s bandwidth is, I try to do a large price reduction versus these tiny little ones, and it’s very effective.”

Of the 50 largest metros, 12 saw price cuts on a quarter or more of listings, and 34 are running above their cut rate last year.

Metros where price cuts were the least common in October were New York City at 12.6%; Buffalo, NY, at 13%; and Hartford, CT, at 14.2%.

#5471. Five thoughts from Cisco’s first quarter of fiscal 2027

GUEST COLUMN by Zeus Kerravala

Cisco Systems Inc. opened fiscal 2027 with a quarter that should put any question about whether artificial intelligence will act as a massive tailwind for it to rest. Revenue and earnings hit records, growth rates were the best Cisco has posted in more than 15 years, and management raised its full-year outlook and AI infrastructure revenue target.

While Cisco has delivered a string of solid quarters, some investors are concerned about the durability of the growth. After listening to the analyst call, I maintain that accelerated growth is what Cisco watchers should expect, as AI will act as a catalyst for several years. Here are my five thoughts, plus the one metric I think investors should care about most:

Asked why this isn’t simply the top of a hyperscaler spending cycle, Chief Executive Chuck Robbins (pictured) cited five growth drivers: hyperscale AI, the campus refresh, the “post-Mythos” security upgrade cycle, sovereign infrastructure and enterprise hybrid data centers. “All five of these are multiyear, multibillion,” he said. “And they’re all in relatively early stages.” In particular, the enterprise opportunity is in its infancy. Using the baseball analogy for “what inning” we’re in, the pitchers are still warming up, and enterprise is what Cisco does best.

Though hyperscalers have been driving AI growth across the industry, only one of the five trends Robbins highlighted was related to that group of companies. Chief Financial Officer Mark Patterson reinforced the point by breaking down the guidance raise, noting that a large share came from Cisco’s core, non-hyperscale business. “It’s not just campus,” he said. “It’s broad-based, and the core continues to do quite well.”

The market still views the enterprise as a slow-refresh business. The call made a strong case that it’s about to become the bigger part of Cisco’s AI story.

During the investor Q&A, a data point was worth highlighting. Robbins said that of the campus switching Cisco sold this quarter, “only 9% was really coming from the new portfolio.” Despite multiple quarters of strong campus growth, the installed base has barely moved to the next generation.

Two forces will push this base to accelerate an upgrade. One is agentic AI, which Robbins said is driving “modernization for bandwidth reasons” because agents generate traffic that campus networks were never designed to handle. The other is the security fallout from frontier models such as Anthropic’s Claude Mythos — the Mythos moment. “We’re beginning to hear from customers who are attributing orders to early Mythos implications,” Robbins said, noting that European service providers are upgrading managed customer premises equipment.

Robbins added that customers “got to get the architecture exactly right.” That suggests a long, deliberate redesign rather than a buying spree, which is characteristic of a multiyear cycle.

Cisco has long been criticized for building its own silicon as the industry shifted to merchant silicon. Robbins said that outside of optics, the hyperscale AI business is “100% Silicon One-based platforms.” The P200 continues to win scale-across deals, and the G300 is now in customer labs.

Asked why Cisco keeps winning those deals, Robbins kept it simple: “It’s really about performance and power. And there’s just this whole focus on diversity of silicon in the space.” The second point is the more strategic one. No hyperscaler wants a single supplier for any critical layer of its AI fabric, and Cisco is the credible second source.

The bigger long-term play is the enterprise. Silicon One is already shipping across parts of the enterprise portfolio, and Robbins said the target to convert all of it by fiscal 2029 “is still on track.” That gives Cisco a single silicon architecture from the hyperscale data center to the branch, with cost and roadmap control competitors can’t match.

The reality is that at Cisco’s volumes, it makes no sense to buy merchant silicon. Not only can it build it cheaper, but it can also optimize it specifically for its own features and capabilities.

A theme running through the call is that AI is decentralizing. “Our enterprise customers will be running AI applications in the cloud, but they’re also investing heavily in private data centers,” Robbins said. “They want to run open-weight and open-source models in their own data centers. They want to train on their own data in their own data centers.”

Sovereignty is driving in the same direction, with Cisco extending its Sovereign Critical Infrastructure portfolio from Europe to Canada and preannouncing India. Robbins noted that Cisco is “one of the few companies that has maintained a robust on-premises portfolio.” For years, analysts treated that on-premises focus as a liability. In a world where countries and regulated industries want operational control, it has become an advantage.

Equally important is what Cisco isn’t chasing. Robbins called neocloud exposure “relatively immaterial,” adding that “we’ve been very conservative relative to the credit situations.” That’s a disciplined choice. Cisco is growing into the safest parts of the AI build-out rather than financing its riskiest buyers.

Given the number of neoclouds, one could look at them as a massive pot of gold, but they often required vendor financing. If the neocloud isn’t successful, it’s the financing organization left holding the bag. This was the case with CLECs in the Internet days. Cisco was conservative then and will continue to be.

Security has been the weak spot in Cisco’s story, so this quarter’s progress matters. Robbins said core security orders, excluding Splunk, were “the best it’s been in three years,” with firewalls, Zero Trust secure access, and AI Defense all gaining customers. Patterson said Cisco is “a little bit above the expectations that we set out” and feels “good about turning the corner.”

The refresh cycle drives near-term numbers, but the strategic prize is trust for AI agents. Robbins said enterprise conversations now center on “agentic security, agentic identity, agentic observability, as well as the new security architecture needed for the AI era.” The network is where agent traffic flows, making it the natural enforcement point. Cisco owns more of that network than anyone.

Investor concerns received clear answers. On margins, Patterson said, “gross margins are pretty much right on target,” and on supply, “we’re seeing not a lot of issues at all.” Robbins added that Cisco is growing revenue “with less headcount than we had at the beginning” two years ago.

The number I’d watch most closely isn’t AI revenue, campus orders, or gross margin. It’s the growth of Cisco Cloud Control. Robbins mentioned it almost in passing, noting thousands of sign-ups and integrations with AI Canvas, Cisco IQ and Cisco Model Foundry. Most people will think of Cloud Control as a network management tool, but that badly understates its potential.

Cloud Control is now Cisco’s core product. The best analogy is VMware vCenter, the data center’s control point that turned a collection of products into a sticky platform. Cheaper, sometimes free hypervisors never made a dent in VMware’s share because the operational control gained from vCenter far outweighed the few bucks saved on hypervisor licenses. Cloud Control is broader and potentially more impactful because Cisco is positioning it as the control point for enterprise AI, not just the network through the following capabilities.

Cisco’s numerous network and security competitors have their own agentic operations platforms, and many beat Cisco to market. However, Cisco played the long game. In my conversations with Chief Product Officer Jeetu Patel, he has been emphatic about how important Cloud Control is to Cisco’s vision of shifting to a platform company. It enables customers to manage the underlying infrastructure, including third parties, through a single dashboard.

If Cloud Control becomes the enterprise IT console for managing AI-era infrastructure, Cisco stops competing on boxes and starts competing on control. Hardware cycles always ebb and flow, so always being best of breed is impossible. Whether this one becomes a transformation for Cisco depends on whether customers run their environments on Cloud Control. My advice to Cisco is to start disclosing active usage, partner integrations, and attach rates for the platform.

My advice to investors is to start asking for them. That number will tell you what Cisco is worth five years from now.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

#5470. EXCLUSIVE: ’90 Day Fiancé’ Star Let Her Fiancé Live Rent-Free in Her Ghana Apartment—See What She Found When She Returned

Not every tenant leaves a rental unit in the condition they found it, so when one “90 Day Fiancé: The Other Way” cast member let her fiancé live "rent-free" in her apartment while she was away on another continent, she immediately inspected every inch of the place upon her return.

Michelle is one of seven Americans making the move abroad for love on TLC’s hit dating show, “90 Day Fiancé: The Other Way.” The popular spinoff of the “90 Day Fiancé” series applies the original premise in reverse and sees U.S. citizens moving to foreign countries for the partners they plan to marry.

Michelle, a self-described hustler who flips cars for a living, is in the process of relocating from Dallas, TX to Accra, Ghana for Felix, a bartender she met and fell for while traveling through West Africa.

“I’m moving across the world to be with Felix,” she states in a trailer for the new season that premiered Oct. 8. “I’m taking a massive, terrifying risk.”

In addition to committing to Felix, Michelle is also bound to the lease she signed for an apartment in his hometown, despite her own doubts and her family’s concerns about her relationship. Michelle has ongoing trust issues with Felix and his family, while Michelle’s adult daughter, Kiera, and her mother, Shelly, are both unconvinced Felix is The One.

In an exclusive clip shared with Realtor.com from the forthcoming episode, “Out of the Frying Pan, Into the Family,” Michelle is seen examining her place in Ghana where Felix had been living unsupervised—on her dime.

“The last time I was here, him and his daddy robbed me,” says Michelle about the state of their relationship, while explaining the financial arrangement that’s been in place during their time apart. “And since I've been gone, the whole time he's been living off the rent I paid for—rent-free. So if I even find a stain in this apartment, I'm about ready to lose my sh*t.”

After the couple pulls up to a multi-story building, and Michelle makes her into the apartment, she is pleasantly surprised.

“Oh, wow, the room is so clean,” she says. “Oh my gosh, you knew better.”

As Michelle moves through the open floor plan apartment, the living room and kitchen are revealed.

A black leather-like sofa, chair, and ottoman form a seating area that sits atop a gray area rug.

Behind that set-up, a trio of black and chrome barstools belly up to a wooden countertop with an open-shelf wine rack.

The working space of the kitchen is comprised of an L-shaped countertop, black modern cabinetry, and a stainless steel top-mount refrigerator. White paint covers most of the walls, though there’s a feature wall with a tile finish that mimics the room’s tile flooring.

Just beyond the kitchen, a honey-toned wooden door is where Michelle enters the bedroom.

“I want to put my stuff up,” she explains, before stumbling upon a romantic gesture Felix orchestrated for their reunion.

On top of a black tufted headboard bed with floral blue pillowcases and gray bedding, an arrangement of flower petals spell out the message, “Love U Mimi.”

“Oh, that's so sweet. Thank you,” Michelle responds.

Across the white-walled room, Felix declares his love.

“Everything you see, this is how I feel. It's just my feelings. This is my feelings,” he affirms.

Standing in front of a window with gray curtains and white bars, Michelle pushes back on his statements of love.

She asks, “But if that's your feelings, why are you mean to me when I'm not here?”

Felix shrugs and apologizes, which prompts Michelle to head back to the front of the apartment, where a flat-screen is mounted on one wall and a poster-sized photo of the couple hangs on another.

Behind the scenes, Felix expresses his disappointment over Michelle’s rocky arrival.

“I just picked Michelle from the airport and I was thinking we were going to be happy and then talk about our issues later, and it's not happening like that,” he says. “It's really making me feel very bad because we've been apart for too long and coming together is like a special thing for both of us, but it's very disappointing that things are not going very well right away.”

While things didn’t get off to a smooth start, perhaps being together under the same roof at the same time will be a better environment for the betrothed couple to work on their relationship’s necessary repairs.

“90 Day Fiancé: The Other Way” airs Sundays at 8 p.m. on TLC and streams the next day on HBO Max.

#5468. Google Cloud takes aim at the cost of keeping idle AI agents running on Kubernetes

Kubernetes has become the go-to platform for distributed training and inference, but what happens to the compute bill when it runs AI agents that spend most of their time waiting?

When an agent’s container or virtual machine stays provisioned, customers pay for the wait as well as the work. To help customers control those costs and make agent workloads more predictable, Google LLC has donated three projects to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation, according to Allan Naim (pictured, left), director of product management, AI infrastructure, at Google Cloud. For Kubernetes itself, the new challenge is freeing up compute between bursts of activity while letting each agent pick up where it left off.

“Act 2 is a few years back; Kubernetes became the de facto for inference and training,” Naim said. “What’s really interesting right now is we’re embarking on this Act 3 … where the typical patterns are very, very different from how Kubernetes was designed.”

Naim and Gari Singh (right), product manager at Google Cloud, spoke with theCUBE’s Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how Google Cloud is using open-source tools to cut compute costs when AI agents sit idle. (* Disclosure below.)

Cost presents a serious problem in agentic workloads, with agents sitting idle 90% to 95% of the time waiting on models, test runs or human approvals, Naim explained. Google developed Agent Substrate, an open-source runtime that hosts AI agents in isolated environments on Kubernetes. When an agent is suspended, the runtime saves a snapshot of its memory and local files and frees up its compute for other agents. When work resumes, it restores the agent from that snapshot in an available sandbox.

“It helps from an economic standpoint,” Naim said. “We’ve seen 10x reduction in cost in terms of running Agent Substrate on Kubernetes versus running these agents directly on dedicated virtual machines and containers.”

Security is another concern. In response, Google open-sourced gVisor in 2018, which sits on top of the host kernel to block or audit every system call an agent makes, according to Singh.

“Agents and agent harnesses are designed to solve a problem — and to try to solve a problem — until they can’t solve the problem,” Singh said. “They will find all kinds of clever workarounds. They know everything that’s around. You want to make sure that it didn’t go make some low-level change to [your] low-level security, didn’t make an outbound network call, didn’t try to open a file that it shouldn’t.”

Google is also working with Anyscale Inc. on KubeRay, which runs Anyscale’s Ray platform natively on Kubernetes so platform teams can offer distributed training and inference to many research groups, Singh noted. OpenRL brings that approach to reinforcement learning, which teaches post-trained models guardrails, Naim added.

“In the past, to do reinforcement learning, you needed to hire a dozen research scientists with PhDs,” Naim said. “Our goal was, ‘How can we bring reinforcement learning into the world of platform engineering so that you can run reinforcement learning on your Kubernetes environment and take advantage of it to actually do continuous improvement for your agentic workload?'”

#5465. Fed Governor Outlines Inflation Progress as ‘Disappointing,’ Sees Path to 2% Goal in the Next Year

Inflation seemed to be making good progress at the end of 2025 and start of 2026, with the Federal Reserve actually starting to cut interest rates. The start of the conflict in the Middle East in February, however, threw a wrench in that progress, as inflation turned course and began to elevate once again.

Now, after the Fed chose to raise rates at its September meeting, inflation has reached a “disappointing” state, as outlined by Federal Reserve Governor and Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman.

In a speech to the Council on Foreign Relations focusing on the current economic outlook, Bowman said that the Fed’s “progress on lowering inflation has disappointed,” but bringing down inflation does remain a “priority” for the organization.

As inflation has elevated, housing has felt the strain. Mortgage rates have been on the rise, recently returning to the 7% range. Affordability has been constrained for buyers, not just due to rate, but also due to inflation affecting their purchasing power and ability to save up for down payments.

Bowman said she remains vigilant on “monitoring expectations about AI and energy prices” and their influence on risks to lowering inflation, and she continues to “focus on interpreting the underlying trends in the economy and the evolution of financial conditions.”

“While I continue to expect that several of the factors currently boosting inflation will abate next year, currently inflation has proven to be more persistent than I had anticipated,” she continued. “It is also important to gain greater clarity on the effect of recent market volatility on financial conditions.”

Bowman said what is currently holding back progress on inflation is a “confluence of shocks,” stemming from Middle Eastern conflict, tariffs imposed from the Trump Administration and “AI-related price pressures.”

“It is important to ensure that those inflationary pressures do not intensify, further broaden, or become embedded in consumer and business expectations,” she said. “But today’s consumer price index data suggest that inflation pressures may persist for longer.”

Bowman, appointed by President Donald Trump in his first term and elevated to vice chair in 2025, said the U.S.’s conflict in the Middle East continues to exert downward pressure on the economy, but pressure is also sourcing from the AI boom and “buildout,” as she characterized it.

As for how these two issues could affect inflation in the future, Bowman said that she can see “sustained supply-chain pressures from the AI buildout greater pass-through of higher energy costs could cause inflation pressures to persist.”

However, she also said she could “envision a scenario in which the effects of the Middle East conflict and the tech investment boom wane or unwind quickly,” in which case core PCE inflation (meaning price increases excluding volatile energy fluctuations) would return toward the Fed’s 2% target in a “timelier” fashion.

In terms of the Middle East, Bowman said that as the conflict persists, energy prices could remain elevated, keeping inflation on the rise “because of increased pass-through to consumer prices of higher production and transportation costs.” Additionally, if conflict were to escalate, she said it could have “more meaningful effects on real activity because of higher uncertainty and the larger impact of energy prices on lower- and middle-income consumers.”

On the potential of a “quick resolution” to the conflict, Bowman noted that it “may take some time for energy prices to normalize” even in the aftermath.

As for AI, Bowman said she “expect(s) the AI shock to play out over some time” as plans for new data centers continue to “surge.” However, she noted that as AI investment is “increasingly being financed with external funds,” there are other potential risks it presents to the economy.

One such risk is the potential of workers being displaced. Bowman said that even though any monetary policy can’t “address that transition directly,” it can still “support a dynamic labor market that facilitates the necessary retraining and mobility of workers across jobs.”

Another risk is the financing of AI, as Bowman said that “AI revenues have been rising quickly but are not yet sufficient to pay for the expense of maintaining existing and developing new AI models and data centers.” As such, she also noted that “AI-related debt has been rising rapidly, with notable gains in corporate bonds, private credit, and project finance, and is on track to exceed $800 billion this year.”

The rapid expansion of AI has also put some “upward pressure on a number of price categories,” as Bowman noted, specifically to the prices of memory chips, semiconductors, computers and more. However, she said that she expects “production capacity to catch up to demand gradually over time.”

Bowman did point out that the risks from AI “seem to be concentrated in only a few large firms that provide AI services.”

Overall, Bowman said that if “AI-related revenues fall short of sharply rising costs, especially as public sentiment and local opposition could lead to increased regulation and delays, we could see a sharp correction in equity prices for AI firms, higher financing costs, and reduced access to credit.”

“This shock would likely slow the AI buildout and soften both economic activity and inflation,” she concluded.

Bowman said that looking ahead, her expectation is that “policies designed to boost the economic potential of the U.S. economy would continue to support productivity, growth, and business confidence.” Such policies include “pragmatic regulations, lower taxes, and more supportive policies toward businesses.”

Bowman went on to say that she does expect the labor market, which has performed resiliently through most of 2026, to “remain stable.” She also expects for inflation to “slow” as “special factors currently holding inflation elevated gradually wane or unwind next year.”

“Over time, I also expect increased AI adoption to raise productivity and put some downward pressure on inflation as lower production costs are passed through to consumer prices,” she continued.

Bowman said as these “shocks” to the economy and inflation fall back, her forecast is for “core PCE inflation to move closer to 2% next year.”

Right now, she said that the pressures persist, indicating that “there is still work to do to bring inflation closer to 2%.”

Claudia Larsen is a senior editor for RISMedia.

#5464. Agents idling while they wait on humans push Kubernetes to hand back unused resources

Agentic AI workloads are handing Kubernetes an unexpected second act. The orchestrator once dismissed as reliable but boring is now at the center of how enterprises plan to run autonomous software.

Past platform shifts, from physical servers to virtual machines and from virtual machines to containers, forced companies to wipe the slate clean and start over. This shift is different because Kubernetes was built as a platform for building platforms, according to Bobby Allen (pictured), cloud therapist at Google Cloud LLC.

“Kubernetes now, 11, 12+ years in, has this whole new life,” Allen said. “You don’t need a new platform this time. … This shift doesn’t mean that you’ve got to retool and rebuild and replatform everything, and I think that could be comforting for folks to realize that they don’t have to start from scratch.”

Allen spoke with theCUBE’s Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how Kubernetes is recovering resources spent on idle agentic AI workloads. (* Disclosure below.)

Google is putting that view into practice. The company has donated Agent Substrate, gVisor and OpenRL to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation, while engineering teams are tuning Kubernetes for agents rather than building a new stack.

“Google is doubling down on our commitment to not just open source but community-driven, collaborative, multiple-partner-involvement open source,” Allen said. “These concepts are foundational, but they’re important enough that we need to all contribute and shape these together.”

Efficiency is a big part of the motivation. Agents spend long stretches idle while they wait for human input, and the projects aim to give those resources back during the downtime, Allen explained.

“These are kind of different efforts that contribute to an open, flexible, transparent, collaborative way to make agentic workloads run better so that we can have these amazing outcomes but also be efficient with our resources,” Allen said. “We don’t want to have this sci-fi Star Trek moment where we’re stepping into the future and kill the planet.”

Bitcoin’s cycle bottom is likely already in or very close, as a Mark Zuckerberg Meta AI Bitcoin bottom prediction highlights a final low expected in the $60,000–$68,000 zone by late December 2026 or early January 2027 at the latest. As of November 11, 2026, Bitcoin trades near $73,700–$73,900, roughly 41% below its October 2025 all-time high around $126,000.

The market has been grinding lower after a failed recovery attempt into the low $80,000s, with recent sessions testing the psychologically important $73,000 level. While the short-term trend remains soft, longer-term structure and historical cycle patterns suggest the deepest part of the correction is largely complete.

Bitcoin is consolidating in a tight range after a multi-week decline. Immediate support sits at the $73,000 round number, which coincides with recent daily lows, the approximate 200-day moving average, and prior structural levels from earlier in the year.

A daily close below $73,000 would open the door to the next support cluster near $71,500 (prior swing area) and then the 50-day moving average zone around $68,500. Deeper support resides in the $62,000–$65,000 region, with the July 2026 low near $57,700–$58,000 acting as the major cycle floor.

On the upside, resistance is layered at $75,000, followed by the more significant $80,000 area. Momentum indicators such as the RSI have cooled into neutral-to-oversold territory on daily timeframes, leaving room for either a relief bounce or one final liquidity sweep lower before a more durable base forms.

Volume has been elevated on down days, consistent with distribution by short-term holders, but longer-term holder metrics and the 200-week moving average (historically a strong demand zone) continue to provide a structural floor.

Bitcoin | Net shorts just hit an ATH.The last 4 times we saw these levels, they marked a major bottom. pic.twitter.com/n9DkeYEYqy

My base-case view is that the primary cycle low was printed in July 2026 near $58,000. That level marked a roughly 54% drawdown from the prior peak, shallower than the 70–80%+ declines of previous bear markets, reflecting Bitcoin’s growing institutional base and ETF demand.

The current pullback into the low $70,000s looks more like a higher-low retest or secondary correction within a broader bottoming process rather than the start of a new leg down. If $73,000 fails, a final flush into the $62,000–$68,000 zone remains the most probable destination.

This area aligns with Fibonacci retracements of the 2025–2026 rally, prior demand zones, and the upper end of the July low region. I expect any such move to occur relatively quickly, within the next four to eight weeks, driven by residual profit-taking, macro uncertainty, or year-end positioning.

By late December 2026 or the first half of January 2027 at the latest, this process should be complete. A sustained defense of the $68,000–$70,000 area (or a higher low above $70,000) would strongly support the thesis that the bottom is in.

Conversely, a decisive break below the July low near $58,000 would invalidate the constructive view and open a path toward $50,000–$55,000, though that outcome currently carries lower probability given the maturity of the correction and the strength of long-term holder support.

In short, Bitcoin appears to be in the late stages of its post-2025 correction. The most likely final low sits in the $60,000–$68,000 range, timed for the remainder of Q4 2026 into very early 2027. Once that floor is confirmed with a higher low and a reclaim of $80,000, the stage would be set for a more meaningful recovery phase.

#5461. Las Vegas Is Running Short on $100K-a-Month Rentals as A-Listers and Athletes Drive Demand

While Las Vegas drowns in unsold homes and priced-out buyers sit on the sidelines waiting for lower mortgage rates, the luxury rental sector is booming, fueled by visiting celebrities, professional athletes, and out-of-town millionaires eyeing a permanent move.

In October, Las Vegas’ overall housing inventory reached an all-time high of nearly 11,450 units, up roughly 10% compared to a year ago, as mortgage rates topping 7% left many buyers priced out.

Yet at the very top of the local rental market, the exact opposite is happening.

Local brokers say that demand for rental mansions in Las Vegas and neighboring Henderson, NV, priced between $50,000 to $100,000 per month is severely outstripping supply.

"In the ultraluxury rental space, there's a huge shortage," Natalia Harris, global real estate adviser with Las Vegas Sotheby's International Realty, tells Realtor.com®. There are currently fewer than 10 super-luxury rentals on the market.

"We personally, day to day, feel the frustrations of the shortage of the inventory of these rentals, because we get requests and we can't even keep up with them."

Harris and her husband, fellow Sotheby's adviser Ben Harris, have been actively encouraging developers and investors to create more extravagant rental inventory to keep up with demand.

Alongside celebrity renters, the Harrises often work with out-of-town executives and entrepreneurs who are considering a relocation to Las Vegas but are not sure where exactly to put down roots.

"They're renting for a year maybe, or six months, while they're browsing and shopping for a home and figuring out where they want to be," says Natalia. This class of clients gravitates toward rentals in the $50,000- to $60,000-per-month bracket.

While in the past the biggest feeder market for high-end rentals in Vegas was California, Natalia says over the past year, momentum has shifted to Seattle. Wealthy Washington residents are increasingly eyeing tax-friendly Nevada following the recent passage of the "millionaires tax"—a 9.9% state income tax on earnings exceeding $1 million a year.

Behind this premium rental surge is the valley's rapidly rising cultural cachet.

"Vegas used to be a place where you get a cheap dinner and you gamble, maybe catch a show. But now, Vegas has become the sports and entertainment capital," says Natalia.

In recent years, Las Vegas has cemented its reputation as a top destination for world-class sports, culminating with hosting Super Bowl LVIII in 2024.

The city's jam-packed calendar includes the Formula 1 Las Vegas Grand Prix, the NASCAR Cup Series, college football and basketball tournaments, and high-stakes championship boxing. In 2028, Vegas will host the NCAA Men’s Final Four, followed the next year by Super Bowl LXIII.

Beyond headline-making marquee spectacles, Las Vegas has built a thriving local sports scene anchored by championship franchises like the Stanley Cup-winning Vegas Golden Knights and the WNBA champion Las Vegas Aces.

"Vegas has completely evolved, and the attention that we're getting from high net worth individuals ... or celebrities and athletes that are coming here for some of those events, it's just created a whole new dynamic," says Natalia.

Sports is not the city's only draw. As part of the valley's cultural evolution, the Strip has been increasingly attracting A-list entertainers at the peak of their careers, marking a major shift from decades past.

"Vegas used to be a place where artists came when they were toward the end of their career," says Natalia. "Elvis, Frank Sinatra—they would come here as they're winding down for their residencies. Now, that's not the case at all."

The city's most prestigious new venue, the Sphere, has recently featured Backstreet Boys, Metallica, and U2. Pink and John Mayer are slated for upcoming residencies.

"For us in the rental space, that's really where we're seeing our demand, because these artists aren't people that can just walk through the hotel and grab some dinner and be unnoticed and left alone," notes Natalia. "They're going to be swarmed by fans wanting photos, and they need somewhere where they can escape while they're in Vegas."

Affluent clients working with Natalia and her husband often travel with family and aides, and they seek a refuge from the frenzy of the Strip, which they can find in guard-gated golf course communities nestled in the mountains just 15 minutes outside city center.

"A lot of them don't realize there's life off the Strip," says Ben. "Once they find out about that and they stay once, they want to keep coming back."

Demand for luxury rentals in the valley predictably spikes around major events. During the Super Bowl, the Harrises secured accommodations for the families of five top starters from both the San Francisco 49ers and the Kansas City Chiefs.

Summer is a particularly busy season, drawing NBA players to town for the Summer League or off-season workouts at the elite IMPACT Basketball training facility.

These high-profile clients typically rent mansions for one to three months in ultraexclusive enclaves like MacDonald Highlands—a 1,320-acre master-planned golf community nestled in the foothills of the Black and McCullough mountains in Henderson.

The undisputed poster child for this sector of the market is 750 Dragon Ridge Drive in Henderson, which the Harrises rented out for a record-setting $100,000 per month.

The 2.2-acre property features indoor and outdoor basketball courts, a gym, a tennis court, a bowling alley, a spa, and a tour bus hookup that Ben and Natalia had installed at the request of visiting performers. It also includes a separate structure with additional bedrooms and en suite bathrooms to house a celebrity's entourage.

Beyond the square footage and high-end finishes, the most coveted amenity among most big-name Vegas renters is a panoramic view of the glittering Strip.

"Just like if you're going on a beach vacation, you want to make sure your hotel has the oceanfront views, they want to make sure they have that unobstructed Strip view so they can pull out their phone and FaceTime somebody like, 'I told you I'm doing it big in Las Vegas, look at this view of the Strip at night shining.'"

For the Harrises, witnessing their A-list clients take in that view for the first time never gets old.

"It doesn't matter how big the celebrity is, they still get so excited," says Natalia. "And it's so fun to watch that 'awe' moment when they walk into the home and just have the panoramic view of the Las Vegas Strip in front of them. That's our favorite moment."

There are some exceptions, though. Ben shared an anecdote about how, on one occasion, the aides of an unnamed Grammy winner who was staying in town insisted that all the windows be completely blacked out so he could get a good night's rest before his show the following day.

"I'm in there trying to show them the amazing views, and they're like, 'No, we can't see anything but black.' I'm like, 'Oh, just peek out for a second, please!'" he recalls with a laugh.

Once the rental agreement is signed, keeping the world-famous renters happy is the main objective.

"One of the reasons people like to rent through us is because we don't really say no," says Natalia. "If they want something, we make it work. All these homes are definitely dialed in and ready to go, but sometimes people have things that are really special to them."

Typical requests include providing a specific brand of mattress or bed, installing a cold plunge, or reconfiguring the space to create more bedrooms for staff.

Other times, the customization requests are purely for fun, such as painting an NBA team's logo on the basketball court at 750 Dragon Ridge Drive.

"You've got to make it happen at these price points," says Ben. "'No' is not an acceptable answer."

Snejana Farberov is a reporter at Realtor.com covering the U.S. housing market and the latest domestic real estate trends. She has worked as a general assignment journalist in New York City and Long Island for 16 years, writing for New York Post, Daily Mail, and News 12. Snejana earned bachelor's degrees in journalism and Italian from St. John's University, followed by a master’s degree from Columbia University School of Journalism.
