#5460. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s abrupt departure shakes AI industry’s foundations

THIS WEEK IN ENTERPRISE by Robert Hof

Honeypot or not, the Chinese executive/accused spy with whom Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted an affair this week should have been a flashing red light to him. So should fraternizing with one of your own VPs — and reportedly another employee too!

In the end, all that, and maybe more to come, was just too much for Nvidia’s board to bear despite the commanding position Huang (pictured) held not only at Nvidia but in the entire artificial intelligence industry. Indeed, the speed with which he resigned — spectacularly stupid as his behavior was — still makes me wonder if there are other shoes to drop, especially on the legal or national security fronts. Market researcher SemiAnalysis thinks it came down to pressure from the U.S. intelligence community that’s very unhappy Nvidia chips have apparently been smuggled to China.

Huang was something of an AI puppet master, providing the chips and software to power the entire industry as well as seemingly unlimited cash to fund and backstop everyone from AI leaders such as OpenAI and Anthropic to innumerable cloud compute providers worldwide. No single person inside or outside Nvidia seems likely to fill that role.

However, Nvidia really is much more than Jensen Huang. Interim CEO and CFO Colette Kress helped craft the financial arrangements that in part put Nvidia at the center of AI — though for what it’s worth, Huang himself wasn’t a fan lately. Some of his direct reports such as high-performance computing chief Ian Buck seem quite capable of carrying on, if perhaps not with Huang’s panache. One company is never one person, and shouldn’t be. I expect a less centralized Nvidia going forward, whoever’s at the top.

More than that, AI is much more than Jensen Huang, and it will continue to be going forward. It’s easy to forget that although Huang brilliantly helped create this new wave, AI and its enablers also are what made him a rock star. But that time is now over. Nvidia and certainly the AI industry shouldn’t be depending on one person to keep everything afloat anyway.

The reverberations of his sudden and shocking departure will continue to echo for a long time to come across Nvidia, its investors watching hundreds of billions of market cap evaporate, legions of Jensen fanboys and the entire artificial intelligence ecosystem. A lot of people are hoping desperately that he didn’t just pop the AI bubble (though others are thinking he did). It seems unlikely this will be the pin, but we’re dealing with a lot of unlikely things in the past week or so, for better and worse, and this shock is clearly rattling the foundations.

All that managed to overshadow what otherwise would be the big news this week: Anthropic went on the road to pitch its initial public offering. It’s hoping to raise more than $64 billion and keep the AI trade humming in Nvidia’s near-term absence. Looks like next Thursday is the big day.

And it’s not the only good news in AI — that is, if the IPO is successful. After a difficult month on the stock front, uber neocloud CoreWeave provided a pleasant AI surprise with upside earnings and guidance, lifting its shares almost 25% Wednesday. AI chipmaker Cerebras’ shares rose almost 18% in late trading Thursday on positive guidance and a Microsoft deal. Cisco Systems said demand is strong for AI infrastructure, even if investors shrugged, and chipmaking equipment supplier Applied Materials said AI boosted demand as well.

Not everyone fared so well, though. Dutch neocloud Nebius saw its shares drop almost 17% Thursday as it lowered its outlook despite close to sevenfold revenue growth in the last quarter. The stock drop no doubt was partly because of Nvidia, which is, of course, an investor. CoreWeave –yes, another Nvidia investment — lost 7% Thursday.

Couple of really big outages out there: first, Microsoft Outlook, grounding a lot of office workers, then the whole damn U.S. air traffic control system, grounding thousands of flights.

Sovereignty is on many enterprise buyers’ lips these days, the notion that enterprises need a way to assert more control over their technology estates and protect their customers’ data. TheCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante and Amit Eyal Govrin just completed the first of a series of reports on how to approach sovereignty, this one focused on the hyperscale cloud providers.

The software orchestrator Kubernetes has become boring, but as SiliconANGLE’s John Furrier said at this week’s KubeCon in Salt Lake City, that means it’s a success — with lessons for AI developers. “A lot of things that are happening in cloud-native that were involved in microservices in Kubernetes world are actually the same challenges in the AI world,” he noted.

IBM has been working hard on quantum computing for a long time now, but at its Quantum Developer Conference in Chicago this week, it showed significant progress, according to Dave Vellante. Its goal now is to show actual industry impact by 2028, a laudable goal that presents a lot of challenges, Dave wrote in his Special Breaking Analysis this week.

Next week the SC26 high-performance computing conference comes to Chicago, and theCUBE and theCUBE Research will be onsite with interviews and analysis. There’s also Microsoft Ignite in San Francisco. And earnings next week include… Nvidia! Bring the popcorn.

Here’s all of this week’s enterprise and emerging tech news, most of it not salacious, along with analysis and commentary from SiliconANGLE and beyond:

#5459. Report: Demand Surges for Single-Family Rentals

Zillow’s latest Rental Market Report shows that demand for renting single-family homes has risen, with consumers noting that they would need a $14,408 pay raise to cover the monthly costs of owning a home, even before saving for a down payment. Nationally, the typical single-family rent is $2,243 a month, compared with $2,603 a month to own a single-family home with 20% down, or $360 more each month.

“For a growing number of households, renting a house is a legitimate financial strategy,” said Kara Ng, senior economist at Zillow. “You get many of the lifestyle benefits, but it takes less income than owning and keeps more flexibility in the monthly budget. That’s the appeal for the deliberate renter.”

The size of the raise depends on the market According to Zillow, the pay raise needed to buy is now the highest since early 2025, more than double the $6,463 it took in February 2026, when mortgage rates briefly fell below 6%. The gap looks very different from market to market. It’s largest in San Jose, where the income needed to buy ($404,925) is more than double the income needed to rent ($190,561), a gap of $214,364. The next largest gap is in San Francisco ($139,353), followed by San Diego ($84,101), New York ($78,208) and Los Angeles ($78,003). The smallest annual gaps are in Pittsburgh ($2,554), Houston ($4,500) and Cincinnati ($4,774). Buffalo is the only market where buying would not require a raise.

Even with such a raise, would-be buyers still face another hurdle: saving a 20% down payment. About 30% of mortgage buyers use a gift or loan from family or friends, and 46% draw on two or more sources, including the use of down payment assistance programs, according to Zillow’s 2026 Consumer Housing Trends Report.

In addition to the monthly cost, households deciding between renting and buying should weigh the upfront costs of buying, the chance to build equity and the opportunity for renters to invest their down payment instead. Zillow’s rent vs. buy research puts the national break-even timeline—the number of years a household would need to own before buying comes out ahead—at 7.8 years with 20% down.

Rental demand keeps climbing As renting a house becomes an increasingly better value, more shoppers are turning to rentals. Rental demand is up 22.1% year over year nationwide, according to the Zillow Observed Renter Demand Index (ZORDI). Demand for single-family rentals is up 24.3%, roughly double the 12.1% rise for multifamily rentals.

Rental demand surges in the Bay Area and the Sun Belt Demand rose the most in San Jose, where ZORDI is up 78.9% from a year ago, followed by San Francisco (60.5%), Austin (59.6%), Miami (51.5%) and Jacksonville (47.9%). San Jose and San Francisco are also among the markets where buying is furthest out of reach, and where rents are rising quickly, up 8.9% and 12.2% respectively. In Austin, Miami and Jacksonville, rent growth is more moderate, at 1.1%, 2.1% and 2.6%.

Not every market is following the national trend. ZORDI is down year over year in Providence (-4.3%), Richmond (-1.9%), Baltimore (-1.7%), Hartford (-1.3%) and Washington, D.C. (-0.9%).

For more information, visit www.zillow.com.

#5458. Inside Winter’s Buzziest Getaways—Where Celebrities and Influencers Flock for an Upstate Escape

With cold weather already settling in, A-listers and influencers who call New York City home are heading north to Beacon and the Catskills—turning these upstate towns into the ultimate winter hotspots.

Celebrities and influencers have have been heading over to for an upstate New York escape in winter's hotspots—and their appeal is easy to picture as the cold weather approaches.

Between Beacon’s waterfall-side boutique hotel and the Catskills’ mountain lodges with private soaking tubs, the destinations offer plenty of reasons to leave the city behind for a few days. For some visitors, a weekend away becomes the inspiration for something more permanent.

But what does it cost to buy a place in these coveted retreats, and how much attention are they attracting from New York home shoppers?

The Catskills have drawn Hollywood actors, reality stars, and influencers for vacations, weddings, and a quieter place to call home.

Olivia Wilde and Rami Malek have both stayed at a mountain lodge in Hunter. Jennifer Grey, Ali Wentworth, Olivia Rodrigo, and George Stephanopoulos also headed to the region in 2024 to celebrate the wedding of Schuyler Fox, the daughter of Michael J. Fox and Tracy Pollan.

That same summer, YouTube star Ethan Dolan and influencer Kristina Alice chose the Catskills for their own wedding. Alice later shared photographs from the celebration on Instagram, giving followers a glimpse of their romantic setting.

The fashion crowd has embraced the area, too. Vogue editor Naomi Elizée and Anthony Blue Jr. married in a meadow in Tannersville after welcoming guests for a weekend of festivities.

For Amanda Seyfried, the Catskills offered a place to put down roots. The actress purchased a 1930s farm in 2013 while looking for a retreat from Hollywood, and the property became her main residence.

Across the Hudson, Beacon draws visitors with contemporary art, vintage shops, and an easy trip from New York City. Model and creator Bri Scalesse documented a visit that included Dia Beacon and vintage shopping—an itinerary that works for a day trip or a longer weekend.

According to Realtor.com® data, the median asking price in Beacon was $700,000 in September 2026. In Woodstock, a town included in the Catskills analysis, the median asking price was $968,750 in October.

Those figures offer snapshots of two individual markets. The broader home-search analysis covers all of Dutchess County, where Beacon is located, and five Catskills counties.

According to Realtor.com data, the Catskills accounted for 1.17% of all listing views from the New York City metro in the third quarter of 2026, up from 1.03% a year earlier.

Dutchess County’s share rose from 0.53% to 0.58%, giving the Catskills roughly twice its share of NYC-area browsing.

Both destinations gained a bigger share of a shrinking pool of views. NYC-metro views of Catskills listings fell about 28% year over year, while views of Dutchess County listings declined about 31%. NYC-area views across all listings fell more sharply, by about 37%.

New York remained the largest source of listing views for both destinations, even as shoppers elsewhere accounted for more of their audience. NYC-metro shoppers generated 37.5% of Catskills listing views, down from 42.3% a year earlier. In Dutchess County, their share slipped from 43.3% to 39.8%.

“Winter getaway buzz hasn’t translated into a winter surge in home shopping,” says Realtor.com senior economist Hannah Jones.

“Interest in the Catskills and Beacon follows normal seasonal patterns, but both places hold on to the attention of New York–area shoppers better than most markets, and they’re taking up a growing share of what those shoppers look at. At the same time, New York–area shoppers make up a smaller share of the audience for each destination than they did a year ago.”

According to Realtor.com data, NYC-metro listing views fell 21% to 25% in the Catskills and 19% to 25% in Dutchess County between the third and fourth quarters over the three years analyzed. Those declines were broadly in line with the national seasonal slowdown.

NYC-area views across all listings fell more sharply, by 30% to 37%, allowing both destinations to capture a larger share of attention heading into the holidays. In 2025, for example, the Catskills’ share of NYC-metro browsing rose from 1.03% in the third quarter to 1.23% in the fourth.

From the fourth quarter to the first, NYC-metro views fell by 2%, 8%, and 15% in the Catskills and by 6%, 5%, and 16% in Dutchess County across the three winters studied. Over those same periods, NYC-metro views across all listings rose by 2% to 10%.

For buyers picturing a winter retreat, the figures show that home browsing in these destinations slows after the holidays, even as New Yorkers’ searches pick up elsewhere.

#5457. Elon Musk Grok AI Predicts a Parabolic Stellar Lumens Rally: Can XLM Flip XRP?

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Stellar Lumens (XLM) currently trades near $0.145–$0.148 with a market capitalization around $5.2 billion, roughly one-thirteenth the size of XRP. However, Elon Musk’s Grok AI predicts that a single, highly improbable but not impossible catalyst could still ignite a parabolic advance capable of flipping XRP before January 1, 2027.

#5456. Leaving VMware starts as a cost decision, but day-two operations decide whether it works

Enterprises leaving legacy hypervisors are finding that moving virtual machines is only half the job, and that a portable data management layer often decides whether a Kubernetes migration succeeds. Rising license costs are pushing teams to run containers and VMs on one platform.

That shift is playing out at Mouser Electronics Inc., one of the world’s largest electronic components distributors. After running Red Hat Inc.’s OpenShift for containers for five to six years, the company is now building a production OpenShift Virtualization cluster to move workloads off Broadcom Inc.’s VMware, according to Ronald Waller (pictured, left), systems engineer at Mouser.

“It doesn’t matter if we’re running containers or VMs, we’re running it on the same foundation, which really works well,” Waller said. “Because we can manage those things with the same tool sets and same skill sets.”

Waller and Jon Owings (right), assistant vice president of global technical presales, cloud and data services, at Portworx by Everpure, spoke with theCUBE’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how the data management layer helps run VMs and containers on OpenShift. (* Disclosure below.)

Kubernetes already serves as a common control plane for containerized AI workloads, and pulling VMs onto it extends that standard to older applications. Everpure Inc., which rebranded from Pure Storage Inc. this year as part of a data-centric pivot, positions Portworx as the matching abstraction for storage.

“Kubernetes provides that ubiquitous control plane for all of them, and that’s what customers are asking us for,” Owings said. “The one thing that was missing was the same thing but for data.”

The learning curve for VMware administrators moving to Kubernetes is steep, and Waller has climbed it over the last year. Storage turned out to be the easy part when he built Mouser’s proof-of-concept cluster, he explained.

“I asked the storage guy what I needed from him, and he handed me a user ID and an API key. I went to Portworx Central. I configured my spec for the operator and the storage cluster, created my secret, and boom, Portworx Enterprise did everything else on the backend,” Waller said. “I didn’t even have to think about it.”

Portworx keeps building for that use case. It made data management native to OpenShift in May and unveiled new AI and VM capabilities at KubeCon. For teams following Mouser’s path, Owings sees the exit from a legacy hypervisor as a chance to rethink day-two operations on a data management layer that travels across clouds and Kubernetes distributions.

“What can we change that we didn’t like about the last 15 years? … Were we dependent on a vendor? Were we dependent on shell scripts or PowerShell?” Owings said. “We have this great opportunity to do something new, and Kubernetes has that open API that allows you to be creative.”

Here’s the complete video interview, part of SiliconANGLE’s and theCUBE’s coverage of KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA:

#5455. Inside a Secluded $3.3 Million Mediterranean Estate With a Resort-Inspired Backyard Retreat in Agoura Hills

An ultra-private estate in Agoura Hills, CA has hit the market, offering a secluded retreat in the Santa Monica Mountains for $3.295 million.

"It's tucked away into the hills and no one's around you. It's just a super private property," listing agent Michelle Meyers of The Agency tells Realtor.com®.

Set on an expansive lot that's just over an acre in the exclusive Heritage View Estates enclave, Meyers notes it's rare to find a home in the area with a yard that's this sizable and this private.

The five-bedroom, 4.5-bathroom abode spans 4,161 square feet—boasting open spaces that are defined by soaring ceilings and 10-inch-wide plank oak floors.

"It's been tailored for such effortless living," Meyers continues, noting that the sellers thoughtfully curated the 1996-built home to maximize every inch of the property, such as perfectly-organized closets in the primary suite and a "completely-custom built out" pantry in the kitchen.

Of the thoughtful upgrades, the beautifully-remodeled kitchen is surely a standout, where timeless design has been leveled-up with top-of-the-line appliances, stunning countertops, and designer lighting.

The ground floor is an excellent spot to entertain from the moment visitors step through the grand entry, which features custom doors and a statement-making curved staircase.

A stately great room has been intentionally arranged to upgrade everyday life, with sliding glass doors providing access to the picturesque exterior space, a modern marble fireplace, and a funky bar.

The main level also includes a "chic powder room," and a private en-suite bedroom that could be well-suited to serve as a home office or a welcoming space for guests.

The remainder of the bedrooms are upstairs, including the lavish, light-flooded primary suite. The room feels like a true escape, thanks to its expansive wraparound balcony, sizable walk-in closet, and spa-inspired bathroom with an oversized shower and relaxing soaking tub.

While this property conveniently provides easy-access to everything a busy family could need, it's also the kind of place they'll want to spend as much time as possible enjoying.

The tranquil outdoor space is truly a vacation-like getaway, primed for relaxation and entertaining alike.

The lush greenery can be enjoyed from the large oversized outdoor living area. The impressive pool is certainly the trophy of the backyard, and features a spacious spa, accessible by a pair of stone steps.

A separate pool house is exceptionally versatile, with a gorgeous bathroom and space that can be utilized by guests or the residents who may want to dedicate additional room to poolside living.

There's also a four-car garage complete with custom epoxy flooring. Functional luxuries include a whole-house water filtration system, smart home technology, and solar panels that have already been fully paid-off.

#5454. Compass Sues 15 MLSs in 8 States Over Marketing Restrictions

As the next heated step in its nationwide battle against MLS incumbents, Compass filed more than a dozen federal antitrust lawsuits against 15 MLSs today, carrying out a promised threat to take a bitter, long-running dispute over restrictions on off-MLS marketing to the courtroom.

According to a release, Compass is accusing the MLSs in question of “fining and punishing agents who publicly market homes as their clients have lawfully instructed.” It also notes that said fines can reach up to $15,000.

“Only the law and the homeowner should tell agents how to market a home, and the MLS is neither the law nor the homeowner,” a Compass spokesperson stated. “Agents should be free to compete on the marketing strategies they offer.”

One of the initial complaints obtained by RISMedia targets Hive MLS in North Carolina. The 45-page lawsuit alleges two violations of federal antitrust laws, accusing the MLS of conspiracy and an illegal group boycott.

“Homeowners should be free to choose how to sell their own homes without having a competition-killing real estate industry organization tell them how to do it,” the complaint begins.

The lawsuits are against six MLSs based in California:

And six MLSs are spread throughout the country:

Several of the MLSs targeted—including Hive MLS, ARMLS, REcolorado, Canopy MLS, Doorify MLS and bridgeMLS—already sued Compass, asking a judge to preemptively declare their rules do not violate antitrust laws. They have characterized their various policies, which restrict how members can market listing off-MLS, as pro-competitive and pro-consumer, and claimed Compass is merely seeking to use its exclusive listings as a “competitive weapon.”

Compass, on the other hand, has repeatedly accused these MLSs of fighting purely to protect their own interests and claimed the MLS industry has long endured antitrust scrutiny from government regulators. It sent letters to many of these MLSs back in September, explicitly threatening to sue and force them to bear the legal costs if they continued enforcing the policies in question.

“It’s almost as if these MLSs are asking people to ignore the evidence that proves their claims aren’t true,” the Compass spokesperson said. “For years, seven of the top 25 MLSs, covering 340,000 agents across 12 states, have allowed agents to publicly market ‘office exclusives’ without fines, and none of the problems they warn about have happened. If what we are asking for is so bad, why has it worked for years in nearly 30% of the country?”

Specifically, the lawsuit targeting Hive mentions restrictions on showings for “Coming Soon” properties and focuses on governance, describing the MLS as a “contract, combination, or conspiracy of competing agents and brokers.” It also points to Hive’s alleged licensing of data to third parties, something Compass has previously criticized.

“MLSs that are comprised of or governed by brokerages and agents with traditional business models have a strong financial incentive to impair the business models of innovators and mavericks who seek to offer marketing options to homeowners that eschew immediate and automatic sharing of their listings on the MLS regardless of the circumstances or preferences of the homeowner,” the lawsuit says.

Other lawsuits viewed by RISMedia, including complaints against San Diego MLS and REcolorado, appeared to be largely similar, though they incorporated at least some unique elements (for instance, the San Diego MLS suit quotes California law as imparting a fiduciary duty of “utmost care, integrity, honesty, and loyalty” on agents, and notes that the Realtor® associations that previously owned REcolorado specifically cited worries about antitrust scrutiny when they sold the MLS to a private company back in 2024).

The lawsuits were filed right on the heels of Compass’ new Broker-to-Broker Cooperation Policy, which requires all Compass agents to cooperate with other brokers and agents unless otherwise instructed by the client in writing. Compass agents must also adhere to the policy when dealing with listings earmarked as Private Exclusives or Coming Soons.

Compass’ arguments against the 15 MLSs echo closely to the brokerage’s complaint in the ongoing lawsuit against the California Regional Multiple Listing Service (CRMLS), which it sued in mid-October.

Prior to Compass’ complaint, CRMLS took the initiative and sued the brokerage in early October. As outlined in its original complaint, CRMLS is asking a federal judge in New York to declare that the organization’s rules do not violate state and federal antitrust laws.

“The Cooperation Rules are straightforward: they require that when a broker publicly markets a property for sale—that property must also be submitted to the MLS for cooperation with other participating brokers,” CRMLS’ original complaint states. “What the rules do not permit is having it both ways—publicly marketing a property to attract buyers while simultaneously withholding that property from the MLS cooperative and the thousands of other brokers and their buyer clients.”

Compass, meanwhile, alleged that CRMLS’ rules were “illegal” and accused the organization of blocking the brokerage’s “better home marketing product to protect Compass’ competitors from having to compete,” in Compass’ original complaint against CRMLS.

“Instead of fixing its anticompetitive rules, CRMLS has escalated enforcement against Compass: by CRMLS’s own count, roughly a quarter of the CRMLS fines for public marketing in 2026 involve Compass listings,” Compass’ complaint continued.

Since then, several other MLSs have joined CRMLS in their lawsuit, or have filed their own against the mega-brokerage. OneKey MLS joined CRMLS in its legal battle late last month, while Texas-based Unlock MLS released its own letter alleging that Compass had mischaracterized its rules.

This is a developing story. Stay tuned to RISMedia for updates.

Jesse Williams contributed to this reporting.

Desirae Sin is an assistant editor for RISMedia. She graduated from the University of Connecticut in 2025 with a double major in Journalism and Political Science. Prior to joining RISMedia, Desirae wrote stories geared toward policy issues for the Connecticut Mirror. She also worked as a staff writer for The Daily Campus, UConn's student-run newspaper.

#5453. Sovereign or not? The 2026 Hyperscaler Buyer’s Guide

BREAKING ANALYSIS by David Vellante and Amit Eyal Govrin

Sovereignty is everywhere right now, and most people still can’t agree on what it means and, just as importantly, what it all means to them.

This week theCUBE Research releases its new market report, Sovereign or Not? The 2026 Hyperscaler Buyer’s Guide. In this Breaking Analysis, we’re joined by its author, Amit Eyal Govrin, lead analyst for sovereign AI at theCUBE Research and CEO of Agentcy Labs, to talk about why he wrote it, what sovereignty is and what it isn’t, and what surprised him most in the findings.

The full scores are in the report. Read the full report online: Sovereign or Not? The 2026 Hyperscaler Buyer’s Guide https://siliconangle.com/sovereign-or-not

Dave: As someone who’s been leading the thought leadership in this domain, how did you come up with the inspiration to research this topic and write the report?

Amit: To understand the how, it helps to understand the why. I’ve been thinking about this subject for a while now. It hasn’t always been called “sovereignty,” but the tenets have always been the same.

It all started around four years ago, as I’ve been a builder in this space for that long. First with Kubiya, one of the industry’s first agentic implementations, deploying agents in enterprise production environments as early as September 2023, before agents were even an industry term.

We were deploying as a software-as-a-service company, and many of those concerns were legitimate. As a software company, we got to keep our intellectual property and license it out. If we were successful, we would create dependency, which effectively meant customers lost control of their crown jewels.

When we started Agentcy Labs earlier this year, customers familiar with our work approached us, and many of these points crystallized for us. What they told us: We’re relieved you are no longer at Kubiya. It’s not that we ever doubted your technology or the value it brings. Quite the opposite. That was what they were afraid of. Kubiya creates a dependency, adoption balloons, and they lose control of their costs. Or a vendor changes the meter on them because of shareholder pressure or regulatory controls.

What clicked for us is that their resistance was never about Kubiya or our technology. It was about the loss of control of their alpha. Namely, the Agentic Operating System, the key driver of their artificial intelligence transformation, which falls under our technological pillar.

It doesn’t matter if the vendor is a startup, an AI lab or a hyperscaler. No enterprise can afford to mortgage its entire business on an external dependency on such a key issue. It’s far too strategic not to own outright.

That finding forced us to rethink the model behind software, dig deeper into sovereignty as an issue of control, and help the industry define it in a more standardized way.

Dave: So control is the heart of it. But when most people hear sovereignty, they think about where the data sits. Is that the wrong way to look at it?

Amit: Sovereignty goes well beyond territory, which is often the most misunderstood aspect. People hear sovereignty and immediately revert to the sovereign state: government initiatives, national security, on-premises air-gapped environments. That can be true in some cases. But by and large, our sovereignty discussions involve enterprises and regulated industries that have sovereignty as a core tenet of their AI initiatives.

It goes beyond buzzwords and sovereign-washing claims. Think back to the explosive Alex Karp interview on CNBC claiming enterprises are losing their alpha to frontier labs. I largely agree with that claim, by the way. Only he finished his pitch by offering customers to move it over to Palantir. In other words: Stop mortgaging your alpha to Anthropic and OpenAI, come rent it from us.

That interview was my trigger point to take up arms and educate the industry on sovereignty: what it is, what it isn’t, and most importantly, what you, as a buyer of AI, can do about it.

Dave: And you’ve been out in the field with buyers ever since. What did those conversations teach you, and how did that shape the framework?

Amit: Since then, we’ve been included in dozens of engagements with enterprises, governments and policymakers around the world, from Washington to Brussels, New Delhi, Sydney and even Riyadh. We are in the room when sovereignty discussions happen. That helped us shape our view, tease out the concerns, and focus on what really matters and why. From those discussions came the 5 Pillars of Sovereignty framework. We use it today to assess all vendor relationships, policy and regulation, and geopolitical events.

Dave: Which brings us to the report. You started with the hyperscalers. Walk us through how you approached it.

Amit: In our first edition, Sovereign or Not? The Hyperscaler Buyer’s Guide, we take the buyer’s lens and assess each hyperscaler by its sovereignty posture.

Hint: By definition, working with any hyperscaler means ceding a good portion of control over your Operational, Technological, Legal and Financial pillars. Oftentimes that’s the reality in the real world.

My view: Sovereignty is not a purity test. It’s perfectly acceptable to go with a hyperscaler, as long as it’s a known dependency you priced in as an acceptable risk. If that’s the case, let us guide you through these considerations to the best path forward for your organization.

Dave: OK, let’s get to the part everyone wants to know. Who scored what, and why?

Amit: We looked at seven hyperscalers and 40 of their offerings, from the point of view of buyers in five regions: the U.S., Europe, Asia-Pacific, Latin America and the rest, including the Middle East and Africa. Everything is scored out of 5.

The short version: The most sovereign product a hyperscaler sells is the one the hyperscaler itself can’t reach.

On these tests, sovereignty often runs inverse to how a hyperscaler is built. A shared global control plane and services the vendor runs for the customer make a cloud easy to adopt, but every layer the vendor runs is a layer the buyer does not control. Amazon Web Services and Google built their platforms around that abstraction, which becomes a hindrance once a buyer needs to run the stack without them. The grades measure how much control a buyer can take back, not the quality of the cloud.

Who came out on top, who came in last, and by how much, is in the report. And every score is backed by a source. Don’t like your grade? Publish the document and we’ll re-score it.

Fair is fair, though. Every one of the seven owns some ground:

Dave: What surprised you most when you went through the findings?

Amit: None of the hyperscalers has a practical solution for the U.S. CLOUD Act, and that alone has created a real legal clawback on non-U.S. companies.

In plain English: The U.S. government can ask an American cloud company for data it controls, no matter which country the data sits in. A sovereign cloud in Brandenburg, run by a German subsidiary, doesn’t change the answer. It’s still owned by an American company.

The vendors aren’t hiding it. AWS told us as much on the record. Microsoft’s own lawyer in France told the French Senate he couldn’t guarantee French data would never reach U.S. authorities. That’s honesty, and we don’t penalize honesty. It’s the law, and it applies to every American cloud the same way.

The fixes buyers are being sold, like keeping data local, holding your own encryption keys, or a contract promise to fight requests, don’t change who the government can go to.

Dave: So what’s a non-U.S. buyer supposed to do about that?

Amit: There’s no perfect answer today, only partial ones.

Going with a hyperscaler is fine, as long as you know the risk and priced it in. What’s not fine is believing a data center in Brandenburg, on its own merits, solved your sovereignty problem.

Dave: And this is just the first of several. Where do you go from here?

Amit: This is the first of a series: neoclouds, OEMs, telcos and specialized sovereign initiatives, wherever you happen to be, whether you’re a U.S., EU, Latin American, APAC or Middle Eastern buyer. Every edition covers the 5 Pillars, plus security, regulation and exit costs. Readers will be surprised by how deep we got, including quotes from the hyperscalers themselves and surveys of actual buyers. I truly think this will be valuable to everyone listening and reading.

Dave: That’s phenomenal, Amit. This is a cutting-edge report on a truly important and timely subject. If previously you were building on the frontier, you’re now squarely on the frontier of research. The scores, the vendor answers and the buyer data are all in the full report.

Read the full report online: Sovereign or Not? The 2026 Hyperscaler Buyer’s Guide

Amit Eyal Govrin is lead analyst for sovereign AI at theCUBE Research and CEO of Agentcy Labs, which designs and builds sovereign AI platforms for enterprises and governments. #5452. Engel & Völkers sets sights on Aruba as brokerages add agents

Engel & Völkers announced an Aruba shop, Realty of America entered San Diego, and eXp Realty added a Tampa Bay brokerage and an Ohio team.

Brokerage expansion stretched from the Caribbean to the West Coast in recent days, as firms moved into new markets and picked up agents and teams from other companies. Engel & Völkers is headed to Aruba, where it plans to open a shop in April 2027, and Realty of America reached California with Zandra Ulloa and 12 of her Team Z Realty agents in San Diego.

eXp Realty picked up a Tampa Bay brokerage and a Cincinnati-area team that spent 20 years with REMAX. Baird & Warner brought on Oak Park, Illinois, boutique Beyond Properties, and Dane Briggs teamed up with Phil Sexton at HomeSmart’s NEXT team. IRES MLS welcomed back a former staffer to run operations, and Howard Hanna Portside added an agent in Massachusetts.

Engel & Völkers expanded into Aruba with license partners Zobaida Akkari and Richard Franken, Aruba-based entrepreneurs with backgrounds in real estate, luxury sales, hospitality and tourism. The shop is projected to open in April 2027 at L.G. Smith Blvd. 330 in Palm Beach and will serve clients across the island, according to the company.

“Aruba is a compelling addition to the network’s growing presence in the Caribbean,” Stuart Siegel, president and CEO of Engel & Völkers Americas, said in a statement.

Realty of America entered California with Zandra Ulloa and 12 Team Z Realty agent partners in San Diego. Ulloa has generated more than $4.2 billion in sales volume over her 13-year career, and Team Z peaked at 72 agents and $589 million in annual volume, according to the company. Agent-owned ROA, founded in September 2024, says it has more than 3,900 agents across 26 markets.

“People around me may see what I am giving up, but I see what I am making room for,” Ulloa said in a statement.

Rene Carpena and Dana Carpena moved Florida’s 1st Choice Realty, their independent Greater Tampa Bay brokerage, to eXp Realty, where it now operates as 1st Choice Collective. The group brings more than 70 agents and support staff and recorded more than 325 transactions and $60 million in sales volume in 2025, according to the company.

Jon Bowling also brought his 17-person team in Mason, Ohio, to eXp after 20 years with RE/MAX. eXp Realty is the core subsidiary of AGNT Inc.

Baird & Warner added Beyond Properties, a boutique brokerage in Oak Park, Illinois, whose dozen agents will operate as Beyond Properties Group. Owner and designated managing broker Erica Cuneen, who founded the firm almost 20 years ago, will co-lead the group with team leader Cynthia Howe Gajewski. The group joins Baird & Warner’s Oak Park office and keeps its Marion Street location.

“This partnership will allow me to simplify the operational side of the business and spend more time doing what I love, which is focusing on our agents and clients,” Cuneen said in a statement.

Dane Briggs, an Arizona real estate veteran, partnered with Phil Sexton, founder of HomeSmart’s NEXT team, in a leadership role focused on agent workflows and AI integrations. Briggs has worked as a designated broker and title executive, founded referral brokerage Roosted and led expansion initiatives at Homie. He has also served as an Inman Ambassador.

“Before long, we weren’t just talking about what Phil was building. We were talking about what we could build together,” Briggs said in a statement.

IRES MLS, which serves Northern Colorado and parts of the Front Range, rehired Samantha Ewing as director of operations. Ewing spent 13 years at IRES as a projects manager and quality assurance tester before leaving in 2018, and she has more than 20 years of experience in MLS operations and real estate technology.

“Having Samantha return to IRES is an exciting opportunity for our team and the local industry we serve,” CEO Julie Dahl said in a statement.

Howard Hanna Portside Real Estate Group added Melissa Winter, an agent with nearly 15 years of experience who focuses on first-time homebuyers, to its Massachusetts team in Amesbury. Portside, which has more than 200 agents, entered a strategic partnership with Howard Hanna in 2026, according to the company.

“What drew me to Portside was the energy, the people, and the opportunity for growth,” Winter said in a statement.

#5451. ‘Momentum is the cure of all fear’: Mauricio and Alexia Umansky talk ‘Special Forces’

Jumping out of a helicopter into water below, rappelling down a 22-story building, enduring chemical warfare gas exposure — if you’ve never seen Special Forces: World’s Toughest Test, these are just a few of the tasks that must be completed.

It’s a reality TV show in which celebrities do physical challenges from the actual Special Forces selection process playbook. It’s like a competition show, but there are no eliminations, and no one gets voted off.

To leave, participants must voluntarily withdraw, be medically withdrawn by a DS (directing staff) due to injury or be dismissed for refusing a direct order. During the final test, the DS ejects those who fail the interrogation or selection test.

Season 5 is set in the Malaysian jungle. It features Candace Cameron Bure, Brandi Glanville, Oliver Hudson, Ruby Rose, George Santos, Bre Tiesi, Matt Barnes, and Mauricio and Alexia Umansky, among others.

At the time that this article was published, Alexia was still in the competition. Mauricio voluntarily withdrew after a rib injury sustained during a hand-to-hand fighting challenge with former NBA player Matt Barnes. Mauricio said the injury took two or three months to heal.

The following challenge involved gas, and Mauricio didn’t think his ribs could take it. He said he feared having a bad lung injury in the Malaysian jungle. Alexia agreed with the decision, saying the gas was the “most painful thing” she’d ever experienced in her life.

Inman spoke to Mauricio and Alexia midway through the season about the experience, the latest industry news and what’s next for The Agency.

What follows is the conversation, edited for length and clarity.

I think for me, 100 percent, the heat. I think I anticipated intense heat and intense humidity, but you don’t know what it’s like until you really feel it … It was so unbearably hot, and in our barracks that we slept in, there was no windows, and when you were inside, you actually couldn’t tell like what was even happening out there. But it was almost like … “Good, let me be locked in this metal box because the outside is crazy.”

Mauricio: I think for me, it was just the intensity of what a jungle really is. The first day we got there … when we were all showering and waiting to shower, there was a scorpion crawling on my leg, about to go in my boot, which I felt it and took it off just in the nick of time. Because if it went in my boot, it would have stung me, no question, right?

Alexia: It’s so hard to choose because literally every single thing was hard. Part of me wanted to say the car rides leading up to each challenge, because we didn’t know what was coming, and it was always so intense in the car. My heart would start pounding … the bottom line is the hardest part is just making sure that your mindset is correct [in] doing all these things and waking up each day and moving forward because that’s really what gets going is just moving forward and choosing to keep on going.

Mauricio: Yeah, I think Alexia nailed it. I mean, for me, it was really all about the little victories. The only way to survive is by looking at small victories, small steps … we used to say just make it to the next meal, just make it to the next day, just make it to tonight.

For me, the hardest part was leaving, was having to voluntarily withdraw. I did not want to have a medical withdrawal, so I didn’t want to go see the doctor and have them withdraw me.

Mauricio: Not one thing for me. What about you, Alexia?

Alexia: No. There’s nothing about this that’s easy.

Alexia: We loved everybody so much. I mean, we still talk all the time, and we still love each other so much. The words of affirmation we all told each other to this day are so special … But I think my first answer would have to be Candace [Cameron] Bure … she’s so strong, and we got looped together for a bunch of things because of our height similarities.

Mauricio: Well, I have to say that the person who surprised me the most was Alexia … the strength of her mind, her strength and what she did was extraordinary.

Alexia: Oh my god, yeah. Are you kidding me? All the time.

Alexia: Definitely thought it was pretty cool. It was an honor to be punched in the chest by DJ Tanner … I actually appreciated very much that she didn’t hold back because I just felt like I was treated like an equal, an individual.

Alexia: I’ve never punched anyone or anything … the second she threw the first punch, I knew she was so much stronger than me. But my goal was to just not fall down. I really didn’t want to fall down, so I was just trying to stay up the entire time. It felt like a fight went on for so long.

Alexia: I had zero plans on talking about that while we were there. Before we go into the course, they make you talk to some psychologists … they do ask you before the show, “What’s the worst thing that you’ve ever been through?”

And I remember thinking, like, “Are we gonna go there? … That would be so inappropriate. Everything’s in my power, and I’m not gonna go there” … Once I was finally in there, I understood why they asked … you’re stripped down to the very core of you, and you’re tired, and you’re pushing yourself, and you’re emotional, you’re exhausted … And Bre Tiesi, she got emotional, and [she said to me] ”I haven’t cried in years. I hate crying.”

It was really about discovering and repurposing the strength that I always felt that I had, but there was a time that I had felt that I had lost that.

And each night, as I was going to sleep, I just remember thinking to myself, “This is so rewarding, and this is so empowering, and this is so incredible for someone that has gone through what I have” … some people [feel like they] get their voice back. I always felt like I had my voice, but I feel like I got to discover a strength I always knew I had that someone had pushed me to question, and feeling that was just incredibly healing.

Alexia: No, not my parents. I had told two of my sisters before, and then, obviously, I told my dad on the course, and then, before the show aired, I ended up calling my mom and [sister] Portia to tell them because I obviously did not want that to be the first time they read it. And even though I spoke about it on the course, I’m still very, very afraid to tell them afterward, too.

Mauricio: It was extremely difficult … I was just proud of Alexia every single day, every single moment … hearing that story was just another revelation of her conquering and finally talking about something that I wish she never held back … I just wanted to reach out and just hug her. But by the same token, I also wanted to give her space and let her be her in that moment that she was sharing with everybody. So there was like a lot of stuff going through my mind.

There was anger toward this kid that did this … But [watching her let go of it] was beautiful to watch … from my perspective, it was like, “Do I reach over and become a dad and just give her a big hug, or do I let her go through this moment, psychologically speaking, of letting it all come out?”

And I was just proud of her all the way around.

In hindsight, I love that she was able to share that, get it off her chest with us, with everybody, with the world. I think it’s super powerful.

Yes, I live by a lot of different small philosophies. Certainty versus doubt. Momentum is the cure of all fears. All of these are the different things where you just have to move forward, right? In order to accomplish something, you kind of just have to move forward, right? … the moment that I went from being an agent to opening up a brokerage, you jump off the cliff; you hope the parachute catches.

To today … here we are in a really difficult real estate market. I mean, it is not fun out there right now whatsoever. Yet [The Agency is] still growing. We’re still putting money out there. We’re still doing things right. So yeah, to me that’s just a philosophy that I always live by.

Mauricio: I don’t know. We’ll just keep going. I really like that show Traitors. I would love to be on that show. That could be a fun one for me, so I’m putting that out into the universe.

Alexia: My dream would be to do a reality TV show with my family … We did Buying Beverly Hills, and we’ve done Real Housewives for like [16] years now. But we’ve never done something all of us together, just us, and I think that’ll be really cool.

Mauricio: I’m going to leave that one on the table. If anything, it’s for 2030. There’s still plenty of time to do that and make that decision. But I love LA, and I think I can help LA a lot. I think we live in an amazing city, and if the moment comes, and I’m set up in the right position in the business and I feel like I can actually win, I might do it. But I wouldn’t do it if I didn’t feel like I could actually win.

Mauricio: It’s an absolute mess, what’s going on in our in our in our industry right now, particularly with the listings. My take is, it’s quite simple. I think that there’s a lot of change that’s happening. I believe that it’s somewhere in the middle. Like I do everything.

I believe sellers should have choice, but I believe that we should be sharing those private listings amongst everybody — every agent, every brokerage firm, not just keeping it for themselves. I feel like there’s a lot happening right now in the industry where everybody’s really looking out for themselves: the MLSs, NAR, Compass.

Actually, Compass, I think, wants to collaborate, wants to share, but they’re in a big, big fight. But in the meantime, this Clear Cooperation Policy is what is allowing them to keep all the listings to themselves and not share them … The PLS is exactly what that was, and I still think that if Clear Cooperation Policy didn’t pass, it would have been an amazing business to have right now.

Mauricio: We are really positioned as the premier luxury brokerage firm outside of Compass right now. They’ve got Sotheby’s, they’ve got Christie’s, they’ve got all of those different brands, and we’re the only independent luxury brokerage firm out there right now.

So I’m excited to be in that position. Competitors make you better every single day … I’m excited in terms of where we sit, where we stand in a very difficult time; I’m not excited about the market. We really need to do some things to improve it. We’ve had three years of very, very difficult conditions, and it’s going to be very difficult for people to survive. And those that do survive will come out better.

I think we’re in a good position to survive, but we’ve got our work cut out for us over the next year, year and a half. But we’ll continue to grow. We’ll continue to expand, and I’m excited to just be a part of this industry. But man, it’s hard out there right now.

#5450. We keep coaching real estate agents to be salespeople. That was never the job

OPINION: Lance Pendleton argues that real estate agents are consultants, not salespeople. Learn what to ask before you pay for a coaching program.

I was the national head of agent development at Compass, and I’ve been in front of more than 30,000 agents since. I’ve also sold the thing I’m about to take apart, so keep that in mind while you read.

Here’s the usual scenario: You sign up for a coaching program. You’re excited, and you should be. Everybody wants to feel a little less alone in a job you mostly do by yourself, in your car.

You didn’t fail the program. The program failed you. How come?

The reason is simpler than anybody wants it to be. Nearly every coaching program in this business teaches professional sales skills to people who are not in sales. We’re consultants, advocates, advisors and educators.

Nobody has ever talked a family into a house they didn’t want to live in. What we do is help people through the largest and most emotional decision of their lives with the least amount of damage. We read a room. We tell someone the truth about their kitchen, and we hold a deal together at 9 p.m. on a Sunday when the buyer’s father has opinions.

That is not selling. We’re consultants, advocates, advisors and educators. If you can fog a mirror, you can get a license. Very few people can do those four things well, and I’ve yet to see a program that teaches them as a skill set.

This isn’t the coach’s fault. Coaches were trained the same way the rest of us were. Build the database. Reach as many people as you possibly can. Add value, and then add more of it tomorrow.

There’s a word buried in there that I think is the dumbest one in our industry, and I say that with love. Value.

We all have the same value. Every one of us can pull a comp, open a door, write an offer and get to a closing table. What almost none of us have is a point of differentiation, the thing that tells a consumer specifically what you do for them and why it ought to be you. You can follow “add value” for a decade and stay interchangeable with the other four agents the seller interviewed.

There’s a second reason the homework never gets done: Agents live in two periods of time: now and not now.

Now is the pipe that burst three hours before a closing. Now is the appraisal, the inspection, the client calling at 10:30 p.m. about something that could have been a text. Now is loud, it’s permanent, and it pays this month. Not now is quiet and pays in three years, if at all.

The trouble is that everything producing long-term income security in this business sits in the not-now column. The National Association of Realtors’ 2026 member profile puts median gross income at $88,500 for agents with 16 years or more in the industry, and $8,000 for agents with two years or less.

The veterans report a median 49 percent of their business from repeat clients and another 32 percent from referrals. For the newest agents, both of those medians are zero.

Somebody will say that’s just arithmetic, that you need a past client before you can have a repeat one. That’s the point. The whole gap is 15 years of relationships, and not one hour of that work feels urgent on a Tuesday. This is a patient business being coached like an impatient one.

We do something else I think is worse. We coach in a permanent state of enthusiasm. Everything is fabulous; every market is an opportunity; you’re crushing it; this is your year. I call that toxic positivity, and it does real damage. You sit in a hard month with two deals coming apart, you hear all of it, and you quietly conclude the problem must be you.

What would help is unglamorous. This job burns through five things: prioritization, organization, time management, impulse control and emotional regulation. By Thursday of an ordinary week, most good agents are running low on at least two.

There’s nothing wrong with any of those people. Real support builds bumpers around those five, the same reason a bowling lane for kids has them. You don’t make the gutter disappear by concentrating harder.

That work means dealing with people as they are, for who they are. Not more, more, more. Not the next great thing. One thing, chosen for that person, small enough to start on a Thursday when everything else has gone sideways.

We haven’t served this business well on that, and I include myself. I’ve sold the four-week cycle. It’s a comfortable thing to sell, because Week 1 always works.

If you’re picking a program this fall, ask what gets cut. Anybody can hand you 15 things. The one worth paying is the person who tells you which one matters and which 14 you can skip.

We’re not in sales. We never were. Until the coaching in this business is built for that job, we’ll keep running very good people through programs that leave them feeling like the problem.

You aren’t the problem. This is still the best time there’s ever been to be a great agent. We just have to stop training you for somebody else’s job.

The views and opinions expressed here are those of the contributor and separate from the Inman newsroom.

Lance Pendleton is the founder of Reframe Lab, a coaching and consulting practice for real estate agents, and the former national head of agent development at Compass in Connecticut. Get connected on Instagram.

#5449. Tech Roundup: Zillow Preview listings go live in RealScout

Can AI time savings be measured? Lofty is trying. Plus: $1.65 billion in October proptech funding, Airbnb’s AI travel agent and Zillow Preview in RealScout.

This week’s Inman Tech Roundup covers Lofty’s new monthly index, which tallies how much time its AI saves agents, a $1.65 billion October for proptech funding, Airbnb’s early-2027 launch window for its AI travel agent and Zillow Preview’s new home inside RealScout.

Lofty is launching the Lofty AI Index for Real Estate, a monthly report tracking how much time its AI tools save real estate agents. The inaugural edition found Lofty AI products, including Lofty Cowork, completed 1.13 million tasks in October, saving real estate agents 131,248 hours.

The index counts tasks Lofty’s AI completed, such as follow-ups, social media posts, homeowner check-ins and CRM updates, then estimates how long each would take an agent to do manually.

Among the findings: 387,824 leads got an AI follow-up text or email; solo agents saved 30 percent of their hours on daily planning; and agents in Michigan saved more time than any other region.

“Every AI vendor touts the time-saving nature of their AI product, but almost none of them show the data to confirm that what they say is true. We decided to cut through the smoke and mirrors around AI results and create measurable clarity with the Lofty AI Index. Each month we’ll put a number to the AI impact, show the calculations and stand behind it,” said Joe Chen, CEO of Lofty.

The time-saved figures rest on the company’s own estimates of manual task times, and the release doesn’t say how many agents are behind the totals, which makes per-agent impact hard to gauge. Since this is the first edition, there’s no prior month to compare against yet.

For real estate agents weighing AI tools, Lofty’s index is a step toward the kind of hard numbers the industry has been missing. It gives them a benchmark to press other vendors on when they make time-saving claims.

However, the most useful measure is their own: tracking whether hours freed up by AI actually turn into more conversations, listings and closings.

Note: Lofty is the official AI partner of Inman.

Proptech companies raised about $1.65 billion across 34 funding rounds in October, according to the Center for Real Estate Technology & Innovation (CRETI), which called it one of the strongest months of 2026.

The money was heavily concentrated. Construction and development took roughly $872.4 million, or 52.8 percent of the total, while residential pulled in $604.4 million, or 36.6 percent. Three deals alone accounted for nearly 75 percent of October capital: Bedrock Robotics’ $600 million Series C, Unlock’s $433.1 million debt financing and ICON’s $200 million Series D.

Debt was a big part of the story. About $588.6 million, more than a third of the month’s total, came through debt rounds. That includes Unlock’s financing for its home-equity agreement platform and CrowdProperty’s roughly $133.5 million round for residential development lending.

That means much of October’s residential funding didn’t go into software at all but into financial products tied to home equity and property lending.

CRETI noted that funding signals investor conviction, not proof of ROI, and said the bar for founders is rising to show a credible link between their technology and a material financial outcome.

The numbers suggest investors are betting less on new real estate agent-facing software and more on the expensive, physical end of housing, such as building homes faster and cheaper and financing the transactions around them.

If that capital pays off, the bigger impact on agents and brokers may come indirectly, through more housing supply and new ways for homeowners to tap equity, rather than through the tools on their desks.

Airbnb plans to roll out its AI travel agent to consumers in the first half of 2027, the company said in its third-quarter shareholder letter, firming up a timeline it had previously pegged only as sometime in the next year.

Instead of a text-heavy chatbot, the AI agent will assemble a custom interface around each guest’s request, pulling from hundreds of travel-specific components such as maps, photos, comparisons, calendars and itineraries. It will also handle post-booking tasks like reservation changes, refunds, rebooking and payment issues, which Airbnb argues outside AI agents can’t easily do.

CEO Brian Chesky told analysts that general-purpose AI agents are fine for routine tasks but not for trip planning.

“Travel is aspirational,” Chesky said. “Discovering where to go and where to stay is part of the experience.”

The announcement came alongside a strong third quarter for Airbnb. Revenue grew 19 percent year over year to $4.87 billion, beating Wall Street estimates. Airbnb raised its 2026 growth forecast to the high teens, up from the mid-teens. Chesky called it the company’s fastest revenue growth in more than three years.

Airbnb’s bet is one real estate portals and brokerages are weighing, too: that owning the search experience and the transaction behind it beats handing consumers off to general-purpose AI agents.

If a custom, visual AI agent wins over travelers, it’ll strengthen the case for real estate platforms to build their own AI home-search tools rather than relying on outside chatbots to send them buyers.

RealScout is now showing Zillow Preview listings from hundreds of participating brokerages in its collaborative home search platform, putting pre-MLS inventory in front of buyers searching with their own agents.

The integration, first announced in September, extends Zillow Preview’s reach beyond Zillow, Trulia and Realtor.com to RealScout’s network of more than 100,000 agents.

Preview listings appear in client searches and listing alerts that include Coming Soon properties. Buyers can message their agent directly about a home, and each Preview listing is replaced by its MLS listing once the home goes active. Agents and brokerages don’t need to opt in to see eligible listings.

RealScout CEO Andrew Flachner framed the move as a transparency play, with a not-so-subtle shot at private listing networks.

“Listing transparency comes down to whether a buyer can choose the agent they trust without worrying that the right home is hiding behind another brokerage’s velvet rope,” Flachner said in a statement. “With Zillow Preview listings from hundreds of brokerages now available in RealScout, agents can give their clients more of the market through the home search experience they already share.”

For agents, the integration means clients can see pre-MLS listings from participating brokerages in the search tool they already use, without signing up for Zillow or leaving the agent relationship. It also gives buyer’s agents an earlier look at upcoming inventory, which matters most in tight markets, where a few days’ head start can decide who gets a showing first.

#5448. How Daylight Saving Time Changes the Real Estate Showing Playbook

With Daylight Saving Time already ended, showings that previously took place in daylight may now happen entirely after sunset. For agents, this creates challenges, including scheduling, affecting buyer engagement and property presentation. Here are some key challenges:

Daylight Saving Time changes showing logistics for agents managing multiple buyers and listings. The clock change hurts most in the after-work window. For example, in Austin, the sun now sets around 5:30 p.m., so the 5:30 p.m. to 7:00 p.m. slot that used to cover two or three homes in daylight now covers maybe one. Agents with several active buyers have to stop routing by geography and start sorting by need. One buyer has to see a yard, a view or the street before they can decide, and another is fine walking a condo at 7 p.m. That means moving showings to weekends and lunch hours, and having that talk with buyers at the start of the week rather than in the car at 5:45 p.m.

Traditional open house strategies may or may not remain effective during shorter fall and winter days. The traditional open house was never great at selling homes. It’s great at finding buyers for the agent sitting it. Shorter days don’t change much on their own, since most open houses already run on weekend afternoons. What changes is the margin. Fewer buyers are out in November and December, so a three-hour Sunday open with no promotion behind it will be quiet. We’d rather see agents run shorter, promoted windows and invite the buyer agents who have already shown interest. The open house should be one tool in the showing plan, not the whole marketing strategy.

Agents can protect a property’s curb appeal and first impression when buyers arrive after sunset. Our honest answer is to avoid showings after dark when you can. On the buy side, we tell clients not to tour homes at night. You can’t judge the yard, the street, the drainage or the neighbors’ houses, so it’s a poor experience and usually means a second trip anyway.

On the sell side, we discourage evening showings, and that’s easier than people expect: it’s close to dinner, buyers are tired, and walking through a stranger’s house after dark just feels odd. If a buyer insists, we take the showing, because we want as many showings as we can get. When we do, every exterior light is on, including porch, landscape and garage lights, and every interior light is on too, so the house reads as warm and lived in from the curb. We also make sure the path to the lockbox is well lit, and we include daytime photos in the listing so the buyer already knows what the dark is hiding. Then we offer a daylight second look, because a buyer who liked it at night is almost always worth bringing back during the day.

Showing schedules should be designed around individual property characteristics rather than convenience alone. Scheduling for convenience treats every house the same, and they aren’t the same. A west Austin home with a Hill Country view or a big lot has to be shown in daylight, because that’s what the buyer is paying for. The rare exception is a property whose selling point is the night, like a downtown condo with a lit skyline. The listing agent should set the best showing windows at the pricing conversation and get the seller to agree to them upfront. A buyer who sees a property in the dark and walks away rarely comes back for a second look.

Brokerages can use showing data and buyer feedback to identify seasonal obstacles to buyer engagement. Most brokerages collect showing feedback and do nothing with it. Single comments don’t tell you much; the patterns do. Look at what time of day each showing happened, whether evening showings turn into second showings or offers at the same rate as daylight ones, and whether the same complaints keep coming back: couldn’t see the yard, dark street, hard to find the house.

If a listing gets plenty of evening traffic and no second looks, the problem is presentation, not price, and better lighting, better photos or a daylight window can fix it. Sellers will cut the price long before they ask why showings aren’t turning into offers, so the brokerage has to look first.

Eric Bramlett is the broker/owner of Bramlett Partners, an independent brokerage in Central Texas.

#5447. Existing-home sales sink to a 16-year low as mortgage rates bite

October was the perfect storm for existing-home sales, with a typical seasonal slowdown made worse by elevated mortgage rates, a worsening macroeconomic environment and political uncertainty.

Existing-home sales during October declined 5.5 percent month-over-month and 8.8 percent year-over-year to a seasonally adjusted rate of 3.75 million, the lowest rate since August 2010 (3.68 million). Annual sales declined in all four regions; however, the Northeast was the only region to also experience a month-over-month drop.

Despite slowing sales, unsold inventory (1.59 million units) and the median home price ($416,700) increased by 1.3 percent and 0.4 percent, respectively.

NAR Chief Economist Lawrence Yun said mortgage rates are the primary cause of current market woes.

Fixed rates experienced a rapid-fire ascent at the beginning of the fall, breaching 7 percent on Sept. 24 and then roughly a week later reaching a three-year high of 7.40 percent on Oct. 8. The catalyst had been two-fold: the Federal Reserve had hiked the federal funds rate (i.e., short-term rate) by 25 basis points during its Sept. 16 FOMC meeting and 10-year Treasury yields were rising at a historic pace.

Rates have since relaxed to the lower 7 percent range, but the short-term damage is already done.

“Homebuying is difficult when mortgage rates have climbed to their highest levels since 2000, aside from a single month in 2023,” Yun said in a written statement. “As a result, home sales fell to their lowest level since August 2010.”

Although Freddie Mac’s Primary Mortgage Market Survey saw rates drop for the fourth consecutive week to 7.11 percent, Bright MLS Chief Economist Lisa Sturtevant said she expects mortgage rates to start rising again in the coming weeks because of sticky inflation.

“There is little reason to expect rates to come down before the end of the year,” Sturtevant said in an emailed statement. “In fact, given this week’s inflation report, it is much more likely for us to see rates increase instead of decrease.”

Yun and Sturtevant said mortgage rates will continue to impact home sales — not inventory and home price growth.

“So far, we haven’t seen higher rates lead to widespread price declines. In fact, home prices are still rising in many local markets,” Sturtevant said. “Inventory is rising, but higher rates are holding back some sellers along with buyers. Because both sides of the supply-demand equation are slowing, it’s not likely for home prices to drop significantly, even if rates move higher.”

Added Yun, “It will be the highest inventory count since November 2019. We are now back to pre-COVID inventory conditions.”

Mortgage rate volatility has pushed homebuyers to slow down or pull out of the market altogether, as shown by September’s pending home sales, which declined 7.3 percent month over month and 11.3 percent year over year.

As a result, homes are sitting on the market longer, averaging 35 days. Most homesellers, Yun said, can wait for the market to turn in their favor, thanks to strong home price appreciation.

“Despite fewer transactions in October, the 88 million homeowners across the country are largely in a comfortable financial position due to sizable housing wealth accumulation,” he said. “The number of distressed property sales remains historically low at only 2 percent of all transactions.”

However, if a homeseller is in the position where they have to sell now, due to career or family changes, they’ll need to get comfortable with making a price cut.

“If the homes are not selling at the listing price, it requires a discount,” Yun said in a pre-report call Thursday morning. “The longer the days on market, the larger the discount. If the home is sitting on the market for more than 60 days, it requires a 9 percent discount … Even with this discount that is occurring, the median home price is still squeaking out a small gain.”

Yun and Realtor.com Chief Economist Danielle Hale said existing-home sales could improve in November and December — if mortgage rates continue to relax.

“Fortunately, the 10-year Treasury yield has pulled back from its early October highs, which has helped nudge mortgage rates below this recent peak,” she said. “However, several factors are likely to put a floor under how low rates can go.”

Hale said jobs and inflation trends will determine whether rates can move back toward the high sixes.

“[The] expected need for tighter monetary policy in the near term combined with sizable demand for capital from both governments and private companies, largely to finance AI-related investments [also matter],” she said. “Put simply, I expect to see more homebuyers come back into the market as we move away from recent mortgage rate highs, but the upside will be limited.”

Yun said rates below 7 percent could unleash a wave of untapped demand, allowing homebuyers to finally seize the advantage they’ve been given in terms of income growth, inventory and negotiating power.

“One wonders whether current price-declining markets will see buyers step in and stabilize the market,” he said. “We are not in a recession, and we are adding jobs. First part is prices, second is income growth. Wage growth is helping modestly on home affordability, but the big change is from mortgage rates. If mortgage rates can come down under 7 percent, we’ll see whether we see more buyer traffic.”

However, Sturtevant is less bullish on mortgage rates, noting that rate shifts don’t guarantee buyers the affordability break they seek. The Bright MLS economist pointed to the fact that home prices have continued rising in many markets, despite rates exceeding 7 percent.

“There is little reason to expect rates to come down further this year,” she said. “In fact, given this week’s inflation report, it is much more likely for us to see rates increase instead of decrease. Data on new pending contracts, showing activity and buyer traffic suggest that sales are going to continue to be anemic in the 4th quarter. It is very likely we will end 2026 with a total of fewer than 4 million existing home sales for the first time since the 1990s.”

#5445. He sold Bibles door to door. Now he runs a 35,000-home luxury exchange club in 103 countries

What do door-to-door Bible salesmen have to do with luxury real estate? For Wade Shealy, everything.

On this episode of Real Estate Insiders Unfiltered, James Dwiggins and Keith Robinson sit down with Shealy, founder and CEO of ThirdHome, the luxury home exchange club he started in 2010 with just two homes. Today it has more than 35,000 homes in over 100 countries. Shealy shares how selling Bibles and dictionaries door to door paid his way through the University of Georgia and how it led him to Hilton Head in 1984 to a career in resort real estate.

He explains why second homeowners kept coming back within five years wanting to sell and how that pattern became the idea for ThirdHome. He also walks through how he signed up his first 1,500 members and how the club’s key system works. Plus, he shares the biggest lesson he’s learned from his partner, Mrs. Fields founder Debbi Fields: Make everyone you meet feel important.

They also get into handling rejection, taking big risks and why Shealy believes very few people will buy a vacation home without a home exchange membership 10 years from now.

Shealy explains the luxury home exchange club model simply. Owners deposit unused weeks in their second home and earn credits called keys. They use those keys to book stays in other members’ homes, paying only an exchange fee of around $900 instead of thousands in rent. The club has now completed 100,000 exchanges, and Shealy says many members who would never rent out their home happily exchange it.

For agents, Shealy points to ThirdHome’s ambassador program. In Cabo San Lucas, developers began offering ThirdHome access as part of their sales pitch, and the club grew to roughly 8,000 properties there. He believes the next generation of buyers will expect mobility and experiences, not just a single vacation home.

His advice for agents: Look at what everyone else is doing, and do the opposite. Above all, keep changing, because if you’re marketing the same way you did 20 years ago, you’re already behind.
