#5408. NiCE’s next-generation Cognigy bets the hard part of AI agents is running them, not building them

GUEST COLUMN by Zeus Kerravala

The contact center has been the low-hanging fruit for the artificial intelligence industry. Ask any information technology or business leader what they want to use agentic AI for, and they will say it’s to improve the customer experience, which starts with the contact center.

However, to date, the industry has spent the past two years arguing over which AI agent is the smartest. That’s the wrong debate. Model capabilities are improving so quickly and are getting so much cheaper that raw intelligence and reasoning are becoming the least differentiated part of the stack.

The real challenge for enterprises is operating a fleet of AI agents reliably across complete customer journeys, with the visibility and control a large business requires. Without that, the human, or worse, the customer, is left connecting the dots among the outputs of the growing number of agents they are communicating with.

That’s the thesis behind the next generation of NiCE Cognigy, which NiCE Ltd. launched this week. The release includes a redesigned Agentic Experience Studio, an AI Assist companion spanning the building, testing and improvement of agents, reusable “skills” that package instructions and tools, turn-by-turn tracing and native voice-to-voice model support.

Default speech-to-text, text-to-speech and large language models are now included in the per-conversation price, with premium models from Deepgram, ElevenLabs and Anthropic available with a few clicks and billed by usage.

Ahead of the launch, I attended an analyst briefing with Nhu Ho, senior product marketing manager at NiCE Cognigy, and with Clement Boutier, director of product management, who leads the team that built the release and owns the platform roadmap.

Here are the important points from this release:

Ho opened with a chart showing how long AI can work on its own before a human has to step in. In 2020, it was seconds; in 2024, it was minutes; and this year it’s roughly 16 hours. The footnote was interesting, as it calculated that figure at a 50% success rate. “Capable and dependable do not always mean the same thing,” Ho said. “That is exactly where the platform matters.”

For CX leaders, that’s a solid benchmark to consider. A 50% success rate is a research milestone. In a contact center, it’s a churn event or a compliance violation. As models commoditize, value shifts to the system around them: testing, tracing, guardrails and deterministic fallbacks. NiCE doesn’t build frontier models, and frontier model builders don’t run contact centers. Positioning Cognigy as the layer that makes AI dependable is a smart place to plant a flag.

Cognigy earned its pre-acquisition leadership position by handling complex production deployments for large brands such as Lufthansa, Mercedes and DHL. But that flexibility and customizability added complexity. Boutier put it this way: “The large number of options when configuring an agent creates friction to get started, which slows things down.” The new studio lets a builder stand up an agent in a few clicks, with models already provisioned, while power-user tools, including full access to the agent’s system prompt, are available in advanced sections.

This is important because NiCE aims to create a “1+1=3” value proposition for its current customers. NiCE needs Cognigy to expand broadly across the CXone installed base, not just among expert teams at the largest enterprises. Boutier described three builder personas: smaller businesses building simple agents, contact center administrators and team leads, and engineers at technically sophisticated companies. AI Assist is aimed squarely at the first two.

In the demo, it built an agent, tested it, fixed the problems it found, and deployed it to WhatsApp. The flip side is that lowering the barrier means more agents built by less experienced people, which makes the governance features the real story of this release.

Despite all the agentic hype, most enterprises aren’t ready to hand over entire journeys to an autonomous agent. Boutier outlined three modes: traditional natural language understanding, hybrid and fully agentic. Hybrid “is actually where most of our customers are,” he said, while fully agentic deployments are at the “beginning of the adoption curve.” This approach lets customers ease into agentic, build confidence and move to fully autonomous at their own pace.

NiCE designed the product for that approach. An agent can serve as the orchestration layer, calling existing flows as tools. Flows can also be placed in front of agents, for example, to scrub credit card numbers or other personal data before any data reaches a model. Ho described the release as “an evolution, not a replacement,” with production deployments, application programming interfaces and integrations continuing to run unchanged.

That’s a meaningful advantage over AI-native challengers whose pitch effectively requires a rebuild. Contact centers are the fastest-moving environments, and deterministic workflows aren’t legacy baggage. They’re how a business enforces what a large language model shouldn’t be deciding.

“You can have the best builder experience, but if you don’t have any feedback loop on what you’re building, you’re never going to build a great agent,” Boutier said. The new tracing shows each turn: which skill loaded, which tool was called and with what arguments, and when the agent handed off to a flow.

The Simulator now supports multivariate testing of up to 10 variants, using an LLM-as-judge to run synthetic customers against an agent. Boutier ran the same agent on two models and found that one was faster and consumed fewer tokens. This shifts model selection from a preference to a data-backed economic decision.

Voice-to-voice support may be the first feature customers deploy. Boutier noted that buyers are open to using a speech-to-text and text-to-speech cascade, “but what they realize is that voice-to-voice models sound just better.” In the demo, the agent delegated tool calls to a separate model while continuing to talk, making the conversation sound far more natural.

Cognigy now serves as both a Model Context Protocol client and server and supports agent-to-agent connections, including one customer linking Cognigy to agents built with Microsoft’s tooling. NiCE is also co-developing the Personal Agent Protocol with Meta and Sierra, which isn’t live yet. Boutier described Cognigy as “the front door” of the contact center, where a consumer’s personal agent must authenticate before it can proceed. It’s great to see NiCE collaborating with Sierra, a direct competitor, on this, as it makes things easier for a customer.

The industry views agent identity as a shared responsibility. But as Sierra outlines, companies can also let personal agents work through their websites and APIs, so the front-door position depends on enterprises routing that traffic through Cognigy. This lets brands interact with personal agents safely.

There has been a wave of companies banning personal agents, which I think is a mistake. If something is good for a consumer, it will happen, so it’s better to be on the leading edge of enabling it rather than fighting it.

This release is less about new capabilities and more about NiCE betting on where value will accrue as AI agents mature. Intelligence is getting cheaper. Dependability, governance and the ability to blend autonomous reasoning with deterministic control are not.

NiCE is the market leader in contact center as a service, as Cognigy was in conversational AI. Now the challenge is to get an easier-to-work-with Cognigy into the hands of thousands of CXone customers without creating a sprawl of individually governed agents. This will allow NiCE to maintain its industry leadership as personal agents arrive. As it does that, the Cognigy acquisition will move from an add-on to a core component of the NiCE platform.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

#5407. Chinese Team Drops a "Game-Changer": Motphys Launches MotrixSim 1.0, Sparking Industry Buzz

BEIJING, Nov. 14, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- If the global expansion of Chinese-made robots defined the hardware boom in the first half of the embodied AI race, the second half will be won by those that can bring down the high cost of real-world trial and error and make robot training more universal and accessible. In this underlying physics engine race long dominated by Western players, a Chinese team is now bringing a potential game-changer to the field.

Recently, Chinese company Motphys was invited to attend CoRL 2026, where it showcased its fully in-house embodied intelligence simulation engineâMotrixSim 1.0. In extreme benchmark tests against leading international physics engines, MotrixSim 1.0 demonstrates extraordinary capabilities: overwhelming established open-source engines in the contact and grasping test and vastly surpassing mainstream GPU-accelerated simulation platforms in training efficiency.

In the past, simulation was primarily used for error-proof verification at the end of the design phase. But in the era of embodied AI, AI requires massive amounts of interaction experience.

"Simulation once served to validate how machines perform. Now, it is where they learn how to perform," said Zhang Heng, co-founder and CTO of Motphys. Simulation has evolved from a "post-design validation tool" into a "physical experience production system". To power this system, Motphys builds its physics engine entirely in-house, developing the core from the ground up in Rust rather than building on existing open-source engines. This equips MotrixSim 1.0 with strong memory safety and computation power, enabling it to compete with established international players at the underlying architecture level.

True technical strength is proven in extreme tests.

In a "devil-level" disturbance-rejection grasping test where a Franka arm grasps objects of different shapes, MotrixSim 1.0 is the only engine to achieve a 100% pass rate at both 2 ms and 10 ms simulation step sizes. In the microscopic critical friction point test, MotrixSim exhibits hold-and-slip behavior near the critical friction consistent with Coulomb's law, achieving 0mm slip distance.

In terms of compute and training efficiency. Through its unique pipeline supporting CPU/GPU parallel computation, MotrixSim can achieve a physics simulation throughput of millions of physics steps per second across 4,096 parallel environments. In a controlled comparison conducted on the G1 whole-body tracking task, under the same task environment configuration and the same RL algorithm, MotrixSim reaches the current tracking score in about 10.2 minutes of end-to-end time, while the Isaac Sim-based solution takes 130.8 minutesâa gap of about 12.8Ã.

Furthermore, for the Strandbeest complex closed-loop mechanism with 92 linkages, when traditional engines fail to maintain the stability of the mechanism at a large time step of 5ms, MotrixSim solves closed-loop constraints together with the multibody dynamics in generalized coordinates, so the mechanism maintains its assembly relationships during motion.

Beyond extreme physical conditions and compute, MotrixSim 1.0 has achieved breakthroughs in multimodal perception and developer experience: LiDAR simulation throughput reaches 124 million rays per second; visual synthesis maintains stable throughput even when resolution surges 16 times. In terms of developer experience and industrial deployment, MotrixSim 1.0 streamlines development with high-speed solving in a single line of code (98.42% success rate) and a "zero-conversion + AI auto-modeling" workflow. Forge is also launched as the industry's first Blender-based extension tool, enabling AI Agents to automatically generate physics scenes.

Zhang Heng emphasized that the core proposition of Physical AI is to transform expensive and slow "real-world physical experience" into digital learning resources that can be generated at scale.

Motphys's relevant research has been accepted to top international conferences such as RSS and CoRL, and the company has built a simulation and real-robot training center for embodied AI in China. Currently, the world's leading physics engines primarily include Google's MuJoCo and NVIDIA's Isaac Sim.

#5405. SmallRig Joins Art World Figures to Discuss Creativity and Authenticity in the AI Era--and How Art and Technology Can Drive Innovation

SHENZHEN, China, Nov. 14, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- As generative AI changes how images are made, one question grows more urgent: what still belongs to the human behind the lens? On November 11, Shenzhen International Art Museum and SmallRig, the imaging-gear brand built for creators, took up that question together by hosting an international exchange on how art and technology ecosystems are being reshaped in the AI era.

The conversation brought together leaders of Chinese art museums, Anett Holzheid, senior curator at Germany's ZKM Center for Art and Media Karlsruhe, artists and SmallRig co-founder Gao Haiyan.

Zhang Zikang, director of Shenzhen International Art Museum and professor at the Central Academy of Fine Arts, said art and technology are a key direction for the museum, rooted in Shenzhen's tech environment. Wang Shaoqiang, director of the Guangdong Museum of Art, described using AI to produce short films about classic works, which cut cost and production time, yet stressed that art must return to personal growth, understanding of the world and the expression of Eastern aesthetics. Holzheid views exhibitions as shared ground for artists, audiences and curators, and sees AI widening perception and enabling collaboration across disciplines.

Zadok Ben-David used AI to explore bird forms for an installation, repeatedly refined the images and selected some for the work, determined that it retain an artist's character, emotion and humanity. A photographer set an AI-generated lightning strike against a desert he had photographed himself, gaining new ideas but noting that generated imagery tends toward sameness, while real presence at a scene cannot be substituted. Spatial artist Feng Yu championed honesty of material, where imperfection and unplanned outcomes can carry sincerity.

Speaking for SmallRig, Gao noted that technology has opened imaging to everyone, but "AI cannot replace real-life experiences or the act of capturing them." AI can be an efficient, enabling creative tool, he said, but it cannot meet the human need for real images.

In SmallRig's view, technology helps more people express what is real, while art and creator's real needs give innovation its direction. The company will therefore move closer to creative scenes and the creators themselves, developing solutions faster for people who make real images.

After the forum, guests visited SmallRig's headquarters to unveil Ode to the Orchid, an installation co-created with Feng Yu and the first of his works placed in a corporate workplace. Instead of sponsoring an exhibition or releasing a co-branded product, SmallRig placed art in everyday spaces, so people meet it in passing rather than behind museum walls.

Gao said companies often move from manufacturing to technology, while SmallRig also wants to merge with art and creativity. The space is only the surface. The real aim is an open, diverse, inclusive and creative culture, and a lasting bond with creators built on shared taste. SmallRig will keep working with artists, exploring art IP and cultural products, and linking products, content and services into one ecosystem. More activities to support creators are also on the way, bringing the meeting of technology and art into everyday creative practice. Real images remain where SmallRig starts, and where it hopes to innovate alongside creators.

#5403. Nearly Half of the Stolen Binance Basket Had a Freeze Button

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Tether, Circle and Ripple could freeze their tokens within hours of the Binance theft, and they did.

There is no one to call for the stolen bitcoin, ether and TRX, which makes up most of the money Binance is unlikely to get back.

In most hacks, the stolen total is the headline. In the Binance breach, the more useful number is how much of the stolen money could be stopped.

On-chain trackers estimate the stolen basket at more than $5.6 billion. Binance itself has put the estimated impact at $6.3 billion and says nearly $3 billion is frozen. That freeze was possible only because of how the stolen money was made up.

Almost half of it was in tokens whose issuers can freeze them. The rest was in assets that no company, foundation or council can stop on their main blockchains.

That second half explains why recovery stalled at about $3 billion despite a fast industry response. It is also the part Binance will most likely have to pay for itself.

The per-asset breakdown from on-chain trackers is:

Sorting by whether the issuer can freeze the token gives a near-even split:

That one division shaped everything that happened after the theft.

The response on the freezable side was unusually fast:

The pattern is the same in every case. A company that issues a token on a public blockchain usually keeps a way to block specific addresses from moving it. Critics see that power as a central point of control, but in this theft it worked. Within hours, the largest dollar-value block of the stolen money could not be moved.

There was one notable intervention outside the token issuers. On Arbitrum, the Arbitrum Security Council took emergency action and moved 74,559,805 ARB and 8,425 ETH, about $30.5 million, out of an address connected to the exploit.

It shows that some layer-2 networks keep emergency powers their base layers lack. The amount was small next to the size of the theft.

The other half is a different story. Bitcoin has no issuer. Ether on Ethereum's main network has no admin key. TRX is Tron's native coin, and no token issuer sits between the holder and the blockchain. Once these assets reached the attacker's wallets, stopping them depended on exchanges refusing deposits and investigators tracking the funds, not on any freeze function.

Together, the $1.45 billion in BTC, $875 million in ETH and $234 million in TRX make about $2.56 billion. That is close to Binance's own numbers: about $3 billion frozen out of a $6.3 billion estimated impact leaves roughly $3.3 billion still in play, and most of it is in assets nobody can freeze.

The bitcoin figure is the most contested part of the basket. Some BTC moving out of Binance-linked wallets during the incident may have been Binance moving its own reserves to safety rather than attacker withdrawals. So the true unfreezable total could be lower than $2.56 billion, but the split between the two groups is unlikely to change much.

The attacker appeared to understand this difference and acted on it right away.

On-chain records show the main sweep on Ethereum used an EIP-7702 delegation. This feature lets a regular wallet hand control to a smart contract. Within minutes, the drained hot wallet's contents, including more than 1.6 billion USDT, had moved to attacker-controlled addresses.

The clearest example of the next step is on Aave. According to Aave's governance forum update from risk manager LlamaRisk, one wallet in the exploiter's cluster acted between 20:58 and 21:01 UTC:

That trade left freezable USDT locked inside Aave as collateral and gave the attacker wrapped ether, which no issuer can freeze. The position stays over-collateralized, and LlamaRisk said it "does not put Aave suppliers at risk." The ETH, however, was already gone.

Aave responded on a large scale. Between 21:42 and 23:04 UTC, its guardian multisigs froze:

The freezes blocked new deposits and borrowing. Reports also describe stablecoins being swapped for ETH on Uniswap.

The race was easy to see in the timeline. Each hour before an issuer froze its token was another hour to swap that token for ether. Tether and Circle reacted within the first hour, so most of the stablecoin stash was frozen before it could be converted.

A freeze stops the attacker, but it does not put money back in Binance's accounts. Frozen tokens stay locked at the attacker's addresses until the issuer decides what to do with them. In past cases, issuers have destroyed frozen tokens and reissued the same amount to the rightful owner, usually after legal or law-enforcement checks. That process takes time, and each issuer has its own procedure.

Binance has said that its initial investigation points to a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop. According to the company, that laptop let the attacker reach a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions. Binance said it found no evidence that wallet private keys were leaked, and that it has revoked the affected address authorization and is working with law enforcement and blockchain intelligence firms.

Deposits and withdrawals were suspended while security checks continue. Binance has not yet given a date for reopening them.

Binance has said it will cover all losses using its SAFU fund and its own money. Grouping the stolen basket by freezability gives a rough picture of what that bill could be.

The roughly $3 billion that is frozen should eventually be recovered, depending on how and when each issuer releases or reissues the tokens. The bitcoin, ether and TRX are another matter. Unless exchanges block deposits and investigators recover funds as they are laundered, that part is effectively gone. It accounts for most of the money Binance will have to cover from its own reserves.

The theft also raises a question for the whole industry. The assets that limited the damage were the issuer-controlled tokens that crypto purists often criticize. The assets that caused the real loss were the ones built so that no one can stop them. Exchanges have long decided hot-wallet sizes by liquidity needs. After this theft, they may also consider which assets in those wallets can still be stopped once they leave.

On the other hand, traders are increasingly looking toward $2,200 as the threshold for a meaningful recovery. Until ETH reclaims that level, any bounce risks becoming another temporary relief rally.So, buy, hold, or time to sell?

Ethereum’s latest decline has erased much of the optimism surrounding its August recovery. The second-largest crypto has slipped back toward the price region that previously supported its breakout.

That makes the current setup particularly important. The $1,900–$2,050 range previously acted as resistance before buyers pushed ETH higher. But can this resistance become support?

The technical picture remains uncomfortable for bulls. Ethereum has continued forming lower highs, and it can be interpreted that sellers are still controlling the short-term trend. A move below $2,000 would put the lower end of the previous breakout base under pressure. The $1,900 area would then become an important downside level to watch.

Ethereum investors now face three competing strategies as ETH revisits a previous breakout area. ETH is not trading at an unfamiliar support level. If buyers defend $2,000, bargain hunters could view the correction as an opportunity to accumulate.

Long-term holders may prefer to wait. Ethereum’s underlying ecosystem continues developing, with experiments involving zETH and Activity Markets bringing fresh attention to on-chain participation.

These projects explore ways to measure and reward Ethereum activity, including trading, lending, borrowing, staking, and restaking. Reclaiming $2,200 would provide stronger evidence that buyers are regaining control. It would also help invalidate the immediate bearish structure created by successive lower highs. Until this happens, aggressive dip-buying carries the risk of catching a falling market.

The bearish scenario becomes more convincing if Ethereum loses the $2,000 price level decisively. A breakdown could expose $1,950 before bringing the $1,850 support in view.

Ethereum has two important levels to watch. $2,000 could determine whether buyers can prevent another breakdown, while $2,200 could confirm whether the recovery has enough strength to continue.

Ethereum isn’t the only crypto opportunity attracting investors. Bitcoin Hyper ($HYPER) is counting down to its November 26 token launch, with just 14 days remaining for early participants to secure tokens through its presale.

The project has raised more than $33.2 million, with its presale price listed at just $0.0136. Its staking program also offers rewards of up to 35% APY, giving early buyers another incentive to accumulate before launch.

Bitcoin Hyper aims to bring faster transactions and smart contract functionality to Bitcoin using the Solana Virtual Machine (SVM). Its architecture combines a Bitcoin bridge, Layer 2 execution, and zero-knowledge proofs to support decentralized applications.

Developers are already working on the project’s public testnet infrastructure, including an RPC endpoint, block explorer, wallet functionality, and bridge components. The goal is to create an ecosystem where developers can build applications while leveraging Bitcoin’s underlying network.

There is a parallel with Ethereum’s early days. ETH eventually grew beyond its original payment-token narrative by attracting developers, applications, and liquidity. Bitcoin Hyper is pursuing a similar ecosystem-building strategy around Bitcoin.

HYPER isn’t competing with Ethereum’s market size today. That’s precisely where its speculative appeal lies. A smaller starting valuation could offer greater percentage-return potential if adoption accelerates, while staking rewards provide an additional attraction for early participants.

#5400. FAA grounds all domestic flights after reported network outage

The Federal Aviation Administration today grounded all domestic flights in the U.S.

The rare order was issued by the Air Traffic Control System Command Center, or ATCSCC. It’s an FAA facility in Northern Virginia that is responsible for monitoring air traffic and mitigating potential risks. When ATCSCC identifies issues such as airport congestion, it provides local officials with guidance on how to address them.

The ATCSCC sent today’s ground stop order to all 22 regional air traffic control centers in the U.S. The memo explained that the move was “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.”

U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy elaborated in a post on X that the FAA “issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers. FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide immediate updates as we have them.”

The post didn’t provide any details about the communication issue. According to CBS News, the problem affects a “private communications network” that connects components of the U.S. air traffic control system. The outlet cited sources as saying that an update caused the network to reboot, which in turn led it to crash.

On Tuesday, the FAA announced that it was expanding its use of an artificial intelligence system called SMART. The software analyzes weather patterns, flight paths and related data points to generate air traffic scheduling recommendations. The FAA says that the software is designed to reduce delays and fuel consumption.

The agency last issued a national ground stop in January 2023. It was a response to an issue in the FAA’s NOTAM system, which it uses to notify pilots about hazards such as closed runways. The shutdown lasted about two hours and grounded 9,500 flights.

The current shutdown is already much longer, having started at 3:54 p.m. EST. More than 13,000 flights have reportedly been delayed or canceled. Eurocontrol, an organization that helps European Union member states coordinate air traffic, suspended flights to the U.S. at the request of the FAA.

FAA officials said that inbound international flights will be “handled on a case by case basis.” American Airlines, meanwhile, stated that flights already airborne will proceed to their destinations. The airline reportedly expects the disruption to last all day.

The breakdown puts a major psychological level in view, with traders watching if bulls can reclaim $1,000 before another wave of selling hits. Zcash is also approaching its 0.5 Fibonacci retracement level, an area that could attract buyers looking for a potential relief rally.

Strangely enough, the decline comes despite Grayscale committing $1 million to support the Zcash ecosystem. Its investment campaign and development funding have failed to reverse the selling pressure. A technical bounce will depend heavily on Bitcoin stabilizing after its own recent weakness. If BTC continues falling, ZEC could struggle to find enough demand to establish a lasting bottom.

Zcash price latest decline has erased much of its September rally, when ZEC climbed toward $1,700 before momentum started fading. A sustained move above $1,000 could open the way toward $1,100, followed by the $1,200 region. The latter also aligns with an important technical recovery area after the recent breakdown.

But the bearish scenario remains firmly on the table. If ZEC loses its 0.5 Fibonacci support, traders could start looking toward $900 and potentially the $800 region. That would extend the correction and give September’s rally further room to unwind.

The Relative Strength Index is also approaching oversold territory, with recent readings near 34. This shows that selling momentum has become stretched, although it does not guarantee an immediate reversal.

$1,000 remains the level bulls need to reclaim, while the 0.5 Fibonacci retracement could determine whether the latest correction is nearing exhaustion or has another painful chapter ahead.

#5393. AT&T uses agentic AI to reinvent business processes from the ground up

CASE STUDY by Paul Gillin

AT&T Corp. is moving beyond using artificial intelligence to improve employee productivity, increasingly applying autonomous agents to redesign how its business operates. Nearly 500 agentic workflows are already in production, and the telecom giant plans to triple that number next year.

AT&T now processes about 45 billion AI tokens daily across the company, according to Luke Corbin (pictured, below), assistant vice president of digital transformation and AI at AT&T Business. Its agentic AI platform handles more than 1 million transactions monthly. Many of those workflows now operate autonomously, handling tasks ranging from customer provisioning to sales prospecting.

Speaking at an Amazon Web Services Inc. event in Boston earlier this month, Corbin said the company’s approach emphasizes rethinking entire processes rather than simply automating individual tasks. AT&T has moved quickly from experimenting with generative AI to systematically identifying business processes that can be redesigned around agentic capabilities.

At the heart of the transformation is Business Agent Foundry, a group established in early 2025 to work with individual business units. Rather than soliciting isolated automation ideas from employees, the foundry maps business processes using industry frameworks and identifies opportunities to eliminate unnecessary steps, organizational handoffs and legacy application dependencies, Corbin said.

One early initiative involved automating interactions with AT&T’s mainframe computers. Changes to customer fiber installation orders previously required employees to retrieve tickets from queues, manually update records and return them to the workflow.

Agentic automation eliminated portions of that manual process, reducing delays and accelerating service delivery.

“It was kind of cool having some of the most advanced technology talking to some of the oldest that we have,” Corbin said.

In another example, AT&T halved the time required to provision dedicated internet connections in buildings where fiber infrastructure was already installed.

AT&T’s architecture breaks from conventional approaches that build large numbers of independent, specialized agents. Instead, the company maintains a relatively small set of agents that execute business workflows using centrally managed business logic.

“We store the business logic in context or in memory,” Corbin said.

Retrieval agents identify applicable knowledge, while planning agents determine the actions, tools and data needed to complete a task.

“We’ve democratized agents to the point where people can use them for personal productivity, but not to where you would drive business workflows that could touch your customers or materially have an impact on your business,” Corbin said.

Every production workflow initially includes human oversight. Only after accuracy reaches the mid- to high 90% range within a permissible risk profile can agents operate autonomously. Continuous monitoring evaluates performance and detects drift.

Success metrics include labor savings, revenue generation, operating costs and customer satisfaction. Corbin said production AI investments are achieving fivefold returns within a year.

A 151-year-old company that has been using computers since they were invented “is built on a lot of legacy processes and applications,” Corbin said. “The cost of maintaining those applications, training employees to use them and ongoing maintenance is very high. When you can offset some of that with simpler generative workflows, you’ve got a business case that’s built for itself.”

Sales prospecting is one beneficiary. Agents identify promising customers by validating their locations and checking fiber availability before representatives invest time pursuing sales opportunities.

Scaling up those capabilities requires more than AI models. AT&T has had to consolidate fragmented data and provide reliable connectivity across data centers, cloud infrastructure and mobile workers.

“We’ve been through a lot of mergers and acquisitions,” Corbin said. “You can imagine what our data infrastructure looks like.”

Encouraging employees to come forward with ideas for using agents has helped limit resistance from those who worry AI could replace them. So has the opportunity to replace inefficient processes.

“There are a tremendous number of people in the organization who have knowledge and passion about the business process that they used to use but that they didn’t like,” he said.

Corbin said AT&T is now shifting its focus from improving existing processes toward using agents to launch services, enter markets and support new sales channels.

Ultimately, Corbin said responsibility for AI-driven business transformation should be distributed throughout the organization, rather than concentrated in a specialized team like Business Agent Foundry.

“I feel privileged to have the team that I do, but in the long run, my team shouldn’t exist,” he said. “What we do should be completely distributed.”

#5389. Reconciling the OCC’s Final Stablecoin Reserve Floors Against the Fed’s Proposal

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The OCC's final GENIUS Act rule sets a 5% cash floor and a 40% cap on any one counterparty. The Fed's open proposal uses neither figure, and its comment window runs until November 30.

Issuers now face two sets of reserve rules that share a redemption deadline and differ on almost everything else.

Ask a stablecoin issuer what its reserves must look like in 2027, and the honest answer is now: it depends which regulator you ask.

The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) gave its answer on October 21, the final rule implementing the GENIUS Act. Our October 19 piece on staggered agency filings expected that rule "before the end of October," and it came two days later. The rule sets specific numbers: at least 5% of reserves in demand deposits or similar instant-access funds, and no more than 40% of reserves with a single counterparty.

The Federal Reserve's answer is still a proposal. Its GENIUS Act rulemaking remains open for comment until November 30, and it contains neither of those numbers. Until the Fed finalizes its rule, any company planning to issue under both agencies' rules, or deciding which one to apply to, is working with one fixed set of numbers and one open-ended set of principles.

The OCC's final rule was published in the Federal Register on October 23 and takes effect on January 18, 2027, the same day as the GENIUS Act itself. Comptroller Jonathan V. Gould called it "a clear, practical framework for payment stablecoin innovation, with strong standards for reserve backing, redemption, and risk management."

The reserve rules are looser than the March proposal in several places:

The OCC also removed the rebuttable presumption that some affiliate yield arrangements break the GENIUS Act's ban on paying interest, though it kept its broader anti-evasion powers. The agency received about 328 comments.

For existing issuers, the timeline is short. Under OCC Bulletin 2026-51, firms already operating in the United States that file a "substantially complete" application by January 18 can generally expect a waiver of the prior-approval requirement.

The Fed released its two proposals on September 24. They were published in the Federal Register on September 29 under Docket No. R-1899, and comments are due November 30.

The main requirements proposal would require Board-supervised issuers to "fully back their stablecoins with certain permissible reserve assets". The reserves' fair value would have to equal or exceed the stablecoins' outstanding value at all times. Permissible assets include:

On diversification, however, the Fed sets no numbers. Reserves must be "sufficiently diverse" to keep one-to-one backing at all times, and issuers must manage concentration in uninsured deposits and repo counterparties. The Board says it generally expects reserves to be mostly Treasuries, but it sets no cash floor and no counterparty percentage.

Redemption is where the two agencies agree most closely. Both define timely redemption as no later than two business days after a request. The difference lies in what happens under stress.

The FDIC, in its own proposal, uses a third approach: issuers would report on their own when redemption requests exceed 10% of issuance within 24 hours.

The clearest conflict is not about how much cash an issuer must hold, but how each agency treats bank deposits.

Under the OCC rule, at least 5% of reserves must be held in demand deposits or similar balances. That is a direct requirement to hold bank money.

The Fed proposal has no deposit floor. Instead, it would charge 2% capital against reserves held as uninsured deposits at an insured bank, and the same charge applies to undercollateralized reverse repo. One agency requires a minimum amount in deposits, and the other makes issuers hold extra capital against the deposits they choose to keep.

Concentration works the same way. An issuer with 60% of its deposit reserves at one bank would breach the OCC's 40% cap, unless one of the custodian or government exemptions applies. Under the Fed's current text, that issuer would face only a judgment by its supervisor about whether it has managed concentration risk properly.

The rules for a reserve shortfall also differ:

The difference is largest on capital. The OCC sets an individualized capital requirement measured in GAAP tangible equity. It has a $5 million floor that now lasts for the issuer's whole life, plus an operational backstop equal to 12 months of total expenses, up to half of which can be funded with qualifying subordinated debt.

The Fed proposes a fixed formula. On top of the 2% charges on deposits and repo, it adds an operational-risk charge on outstanding issuance:

It also adds 25% of three-year average revenue from sources other than reserves, adjusted by a loss scalar.

For an issuer with $50 billion in circulation, the issuance charge alone works out to $850 million under the Fed's proposal, before the revenue add-on. The OCC rule has no comparable fixed figure. Its capital depends on the issuer's own risk profile, with the $5 million floor as the only set minimum.

For now, the OCC's figures are final and the Fed's are not. Issuers and banks that hold reserves can still argue for changes until the Fed's comment period closes on November 30, and the Fed has asked 277 questions.

The decisions that matter most are clear from the comparison above:

Both sets of rules apply from the same date, January 18, 2027. If the Fed's final rule keeps its current approach, the United States will begin regulating stablecoins with a common redemption deadline and two different reserve rulebooks, decided by which agency charters the issuer.

#5388. La Dahua Pro Challenge 2026 celebra l'esperienza globale degli installatori e la collaborazione a lungo termine

HANGZHOU, Cina, 15 novembre 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Dahua Technology, fornitore leader mondiale di soluzioni e servizi AIoT incentrati sui video, ha riunito i partner installatori di tutto il mondo per Pro Challenge 2026: un'occasione di riconoscimento per la loro competenza professionale e di rafforzamento della cooperazione all'interno della rete globale di partner. L'evento ha incluso dimostrazioni tecnologiche, esperienze pratiche e scambi, esaltando i partner che integrano le tecnologie di Dahua in applicazioni concrete e forniscono assistenza clienti nei mercati locali.

Coinvolgere la comunitÃ  globale degli installatori

All'insegna del motto "Build It. Show It. Win It.", Pro Challenge 2026 ha presentato la Social Media Video Challenge e la nuova Partner App Scan Challenge. I due percorsi hanno offerto ai partner diverse modalitÃ  di partecipazione, in modo da condividere la propria esperienza con i prodotti e le soluzioni Dahua e ed entrare in contatto con la comunitÃ  allargata di installatori.

Durante la cerimonia di apertura, Fu Liquan, Amministratore delegato di Dahua Technology, ha salutato i partner e li ha ringraziati per la fiducia e il supporto continuati. Ha sottolineato il ruolo degli installatori nel tradurre le tecnologie AIoT in applicazioni pratiche che soddisfino le esigenze dei clienti e creino valore. "Solo attraverso una cooperazione aperta e la complementarietÃ  dei punti di forza possiamo cogliere al meglio le opportunitÃ  offerte dal cambiamento tecnologico", ha dichiarato.

Jason Zhao, Presidente di Dahua Technology, ha delineato tre prioritÃ  per la cooperazione: una maggiore conoscenza dei clienti, un supporto piÃ¹ solido per la crescita dei partner e collaborazioni piÃ¹ durature. Ha sottolineato l'importanza di ascoltare l'esperienza diretta degli installatori e di combinare le tecnologie e le risorse di Dahua con la loro conoscenza del territorio e le loro capacitÃ  di assistenza professionale.

Far dialogare tecnologia e competenze locali

Presso la sede centrale e lo showroom globali di Dahua, i partner hanno potuto esplorare prodotti e dimostrazioni tecnologiche relative alla percezione video e alle applicazioni AIoT. Sessioni pratiche e discussioni con esperti Dahua incentrate sulle funzionalitÃ  del prodotto e sul loro utilizzo nei progetti dei clienti. Una visita al parco industriale AIoT di Dahua ha permesso di osservare da vicino le attivitÃ  produttive e le capacitÃ  di produzione dell'azienda.

Queste attivitÃ  hanno offerto ai partner installatori l'opportunitÃ  di discutere con i team di Dahua di esigenze del mercato, sfide di implementazione e aspettative dei clienti. Sfruttando la loro esperienza diretta nella selezione dei prodotti, nell'integrazione dei sistemi e nell'assistenza post-vendita, gli installatori hanno condiviso spunti pratici su come i prodotti, le soluzioni e il supporto di Dahua possano rispondere al meglio alle esigenze locali. Questi scambi hanno inoltre permesso ai partner di acquisire conoscenze tecniche e di imparare dai colleghi di diversi mercati.

La cerimonia di premiazione e il gala Golden Pro Award 2026, tenutisi il 12 novembre, hanno premiato i risultati e i contributi dei partner alla comunitÃ  globale di installatori di Dahua. Anche i rappresentanti degli installatori hanno condiviso le loro esperienze, mettendo in evidenza le competenze professionali e le conoscenze pratiche alla base del loro lavoro.

Questo riconoscimento riflette il costante impegno di Dahua nello sviluppo di partnership a lungo termine. Grazie a formazione e certificazione professionale, strumenti digitali, risorse di marketing localizzate e assistenza post-vendita globale, Dahua offre ai suoi partner un supporto continuo per rafforzare le loro competenze e rispondere al meglio alle esigenze in continua evoluzione dei clienti.

Unendo le competenze tecniche e le risorse di Dahua e la conoscenza dei mercati locali da parte dei partner, l'azienda mira a rafforzare la cooperazione a lungo termine e a supportare un'efficace realizzazione dei progetti e un servizio clienti di qualitÃ  in tutti i mercati.

#5386. Jensen Huang Resigns: NVDA Crashes, Sending Shockwaves to The Crypto Market

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Nvidia (NVDA) shares plunged nearly 10% as CEO Jensen Huang resigns, triggering a wave of selling across technology and crypto markets. Bitcoin also tumbled below $72,000 as investors pulled back from risk assets.

Huang’s departure ends a 33-year leadership run at the company he co-founded in 1993. Nvidia’s board confirmed his immediate resignation as president, CEO, and board director minutes ago.

BREAKING: Nvidia, $NVDA, CEO Jensen Huang has resigned as CEO, President, and member of the Board of Directors, effective immediately. pic.twitter.com/IJE8wWvcrR

The company appointed Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim CEO while beginning its search for a permanent replacement. Harvey C. Jones, former Synopsys CEO, will become Nvidia’s first-ever board chairman.

The leadership shake-up has rattled investors across multiple markets. Nvidia sits at the center of the artificial intelligence boom, making its sudden leadership change a major shock for technology stocks and crypto traders.

Just minutes after Jensen Huang resigns, Nvidia’s sell-off quickly spread into crypto derivatives markets, where traders can access tokenized exposure to traditional stocks around the clock. NVDA perpetual futures on Hyperliquid plunged nearly 12% to $160.99 as news of Huang’s departure spread.

Similar losses appeared across centralized exchanges, including Binance, OKX, and Bybit. Cumulative trading volume across Nvidia perpetual futures markets has surpassed $7.8 billion, according to CoinGlass. Binance accounted for approximately 44% of that activity.

Nvidia-linked contracts have also become a significant market on Hyperliquid. They ranked fourth in open interest, behind Bitcoin, Ethereum, and HYPE futures. This growing exposure puts decentralized derivatives traders directly in the path of major developments involving Wall Street’s biggest companies.

Uncertainty grows around Nvidia’s AI ambitions. The company supplies critical computing hardware for major technology firms, cloud providers, and artificial intelligence developers. The disruption has, as expected, influenced sentiment across the entire AI investment trade.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

Bitcoin extended its decline on Thursday, dropping below $72,000 as selling pressure spread across cryptocurrency markets. Ethereum also weakened, trading under $1,900 as investors reduced exposure to riskier assets. https://cryptonews.com/news/ethereum-price-2000-scoop-hold-dump/

Bitcoin’s decline also comes as Nvidia-linked derivatives expose crypto traders to volatility originating outside traditional digital assets. The relationship between AI stocks and crypto markets has become increasingly important as institutional investors move between technology equities and digital assets.

With Bitcoin now below $72,000 and NVDA facing a major leadership transition, both markets are entering a critical trading period.

#5383. Nvidia had no succession plan when Jensen Huang quit. Former Fortune 500 CEOs call it ‘preposterous’

Nvidia’s total lack of the settled succession plan that’s a cornerstone of all well-run companies exposed a shocking weakness in its corporate governance. That’s the view of three former Fortune 500 CEOs, and a leading consultant, whom Fortune interviewed on arguably the most consequential leadership earthquake ever to rock the business world. Each of the former CEOs serves on prominent corporate boards.

On November 12, the Nvidia board issued a press release announcing Jensen Huang’s resignation shortly after reports of the CEO’s second affair emerged. Nvidia stated that longtime CFO Colette Kress will immediately start serving as “interim CEO” while the directors conduct a “search for a permanent Chief Executive Officer and will consider internal and external candidates.”

Kress has spent a quarter century in Big Tech financial roles, including thirteen years at Microsoft, before joining Nvidia in 2013. According to her resume posted on the Nvidia website, Kress’s past jobs don’t include any positions where she’s run a business or been responsible for a P&L. Hence, it’s highly probable that she’s a temporary pick, not a candidate to replace Huang.

It’s not clear if Nvidia had an emergency succession plan in place where Kress would temporarily take the top job in a crisis, or whether it had no plan at all and just improvised. In the opinion of one of the retired CEOs Fortune interviewed, it’s the latter. (They’re identified here as ex-CEOs 1, 2, and 3.) “It seems like a knee-jerk, panic reaction where the board’s saying, ‘We’ve got to name someone!'” says ex-CEO 3. “You’ve got to ask why a tech company would go with a financial person.”

It astounds these sources that the world’s second-most-valuable company, in business 33 years and public for 27, didn’t have a seasoned leader long groomed for the role ready to step in—especially given that Huang will turn 64 in February, and is already the oldest CEO by far in the Mag Seven. For these observers, that failure is the ultimate sign of poor corporate governance, and a shocking disappointment for an enterprise that until now, seemed to be doing just about everything right.

The sources identified four red flags warning that if its co-founder and America’s most celebrated tech CEO suddenly exited, Nvidia would face a stunning vacuum of leadership.

Huang’s feat of hiking Nvidia’s valuation by well over $5 trillion in just four years to a peak of $5.8 trillion in early October—the highest summit ever reached—has never been equaled. But that record so intoxicated investors that they didn’t install the safeguards that should have protected Nvidia should this ultimate “key man” depart in a crisis.

“No one peeled back the layers on how Nvidia was run because they were so successful,” says ex-CEO 1. “No one looked behind the curtain. Their success lulled people into a false sense of security.” This person notes that Huang’s obsession with occupying center stage, with casting himself as the leather-jacketed face of AI, and his otherwise slick salesmanship should have stirred doubts. “This is preposterous,” says this interviewee. “When you have a celebrity CEO, that person merits a closer look, especially when you have a leader who’s always putting on a show.”

Unlike Elon Musk at SpaceX, Sergey Brin and Larry Page at Alphabet, and Mark Zuckerberg at Meta Platforms, Huang does not own a special class of supermajority stock that gives him control over the board. On the contrary, Nvidia has a single category of Class A shares that each carry one vote. In terms of percentages, its ownership resembles the profile at many Fortune 500 members: Nvidia’s largest shareholders are the big institutions; Blackstone leads at 8.1%, followed by Vanguard (6.5%), State Street (4.2%), Fidelity (3.9%), and a combination of Morgan Stanley, T. Rowe Price and J.P. Morgan at around 5%. Huang holds “just” 3.5%.

Despite this highly diverse, non-concentrated ownership, it appears that Huang totally controlled the board. “In any company that runs well over time,” says ex-CEO 2, “you’ll find the board has lots of current or retired CEOs, and credible outside senior executives. When you see a board that looks like a lot of old friends and people who’ve been there for decades, it flashes danger.”

Of the seven directors excluding Huang, none has served as CEO of a Fortune 500 company, and four are mainstays of between 13 and 29 years. “The board wasn’t paying attention to how the company was run,” says ex-CEO 2. “When you have a CEO leave and everybody is asking what is the succession plan, the directors aren’t doing their job.” Ex-CEO 2 avows that indeed, the board’s first responsibility is preparing a successor: “It’s the most important thing the board does by a mile. The ground has to be plowed for succession. The board likes to talk about M&A and all these exotic things but they pale beside succession. The directors should be meeting regularly on the succession subject and talking about the best prospects at the next level, and level below that. They should be making sure those candidates get the best roles to prepare them.”

Ex-CEO 1 states that in the first year or two of a relatively young CEO’s reign, the board may not yet have anointed their permanent replacement. But, the ex-CEO adds, “you’re moving people through different settings to see if they can grow, moving towards choosing the heir.” Hence, after a short interim period, a highly qualified candidate will ascend from a super-strong bench. Far more often, a permanent replacement stands in the wings, ready to take charge in the event the current CEO suddenly departs.

Echoing ex-CEO 1, ex-CEO 3 intones that “Boards have all kinds of governance rules but just two major responsibilities. First, don’t do a deal that kills you, and second, have the right person running the place and a backup plan to replace them. Nvidia’s board failed on one of the two big items.”

The leading consultant highlights the dangers of the Nvidia predicament. “The lesson from Nvidia is that emergencies happen more often than you think and it’s a big mistake to have a structure and mindset that assumes they won’t happen to you,” notes this person. “That Nvidia has no obvious successor imposes a real cost.”

Huang talked proudly about overseeing around 60 “direct reports,” extolling the supposed virtues of a “flat” organization. What appears to be an extreme division of responsibility may account for the lack of a leader ready to lift the mantle from the legend. “It’s highly possible that none of those lieutenants had enough responsibility to have actually been tested,” notes ex-CEO 3. Adds ex-CEO 1, “In big companies, the optimal number of direct reports is 8 to 12. The presence of 60 direct reports that Huang was making a big deal about tells you the board wasn’t doing its job.”

The issue also struck the consultant as a major negative. “The downside of having a very high number of direct reports is that none have been exposed to top roles in a deep and meaningful way. So it’s hard to imagine anyone internally who is ready to take over.”

The consultant reckons that training an insider would prove a big challenge. “They’d have to telescope the training to get the candidates up to speed in a hurry since it appears they haven’t been doing that and need to catch up,” says this person. Or, Nvidia could look outside. Ex-CEO 3 believes they’d go not for a veteran in, say, their early 60s, but a young tiger in their 40s or early 50s. “They’d want someone who is, say, 50 and wants to show the world something,” says this observer.

Ex-CEO 2 concludes that the board was so excessively lax that, “If Nvidia hadn’t been performing well, it would have been exhibit A for an activist attack.” The fall of Jensen Huang unleashed another kind of broadside that exposed a big need for reform, and hopefully, it will have the same legacy as a raid from outsiders: A new era where this exceptional performer masters what it’s sorely lacking, and what most of the Fortune 500 already does far better: strong corporate governance.

Shawn Tully is a senior editor-at-large at Fortune, covering the biggest trends in business, aviation, politics, and leadership.

#5382. Trevor Noah on AI

by Oren Etzioni on Nov 8, 2026 at 9:52 amNovember 8, 2026 at 9:52 am

On Oct. 19, Trevor Noah launched Luminaries, a science conversation series at Boston’s Museum of Science. I joined him onstage, and Rana el Kaliouby moderated. Rana is a pioneer of emotion AI, software that reads human emotion, and the host of the Pioneers of AI podcast. She wrote afterward that she expected Trevor to be witty and funny, but “didn’t expect to be so blown away by his humanity and depth of ideas.”

Here are a few of his insights with his own words highlighted.

When an AI matchmaker Rana built in ChatGPT picked Trevor as her match, he pointed out that it knew very little about either of them. It assembled a plausible answer from what’s on the internet.

Trevor added that when you tell AI it made a mistake, it thanks you but often fails to correct the error: “It’s like a friend who’s been to a lot of therapy but doesn’t actually change.”

When asked how we protect ourselves from AI’s downsides, Trevor said the answer “goes back to something that is very un-technological and very un-AI.” He cited Robert Putnam’s book Bowling Alone, noting that places where communities form accrue many surprising benefits including more accountable governments.

I pushed back that communitarianism, the 1990s movement my father helped found to foster communities, had failed. Trevor responded that we hand too many ideas to intellectuals, who then “apply too much academia” to them. Communitarianism failed, he deadpanned, “because it’s called communitarianism.” An overly academic name.

He noted that nobody calls a phone a failure when the first version doesn’t sell; companies keep re-releasing it. He vowed never to stop investing in community.

Despite his concerns, Trevor has “yet to see a technology that blew up and then left everyone behind.” Cars, computers and the internet all spread to ordinary people.

AI has reached what he calls “work intelligence”: it can do the jobs we invented, but we keep inventing new ones. Salt and ice used to be precious. Now restaurants hand them out for free. What we value changes, and in Trevor’s view, we’re expendable only if we define being human by the tasks we value today.

Our conversation turned to AI’s impact on jobs.

Touring as a comic, Trevor saw towns hollowed out after Kodak and the automaker Studebaker left. Factory workers were told automation was progress. “White-collar workers are now experiencing what many blue-collar workers experienced for decades,” he said. The difference, he argued, is that white-collar workers are closer to power, so newspapers are covering it.

Trevor is confident new jobs will come, as they did after telephone exchange operators disappeared. What worries him is the gap. His analogy is the highway, where the following distance is the space that lets you stop before you hit the car ahead:

Trevor tells tech leaders that “it’s easier to be patient when you are in a position of privilege,” and added, “But ironically, they don’t have patience when it comes to quarterly earnings.”

After ChatGPT took off, show hosts kept telling him weak jokes that ChatGPT had written in a pale imitation of Trevor’s style. He rattled off four reasons AI struggles with humor: there isn’t enough comedy data, the model is a frozen snapshot while what society finds acceptable keeps shifting, comedy depends on knowing your audience (there are jokes you know are funny but you wouldn’t tell your mom), and companies have made models risk averse.

In addition to being the former host of The Daily Show, an award-winning author and a sought-after comedian, Trevor Noah is Microsoft’s Chief Questions Officer.

I reminded him of Picasso’s famous verdict on computers, “They are useless. They can only give you answers,” and joked that as Chief Questions Officer he has something rare these days: job security. He chuckled. Of course, his real job security comes from his depth and humanity, which feed his exceptional humor and wit.

Rana noted that everybody’s getting replaced by AI, but Trevor had played an AI, voicing Griot in Black Panther: Wakanda Forever.

He quipped: “Yeah, I’m coming for AI’s job.”

In just a few weeks, AWS re:Invent brings advanced and expert-level sessions on the services you build on every day, from serverless and containers to databases and developer tools. Go hands-on with new launches the same week they’re announced, and hear directly from the engineers who built them. Experience the depth you won’t find anywhere else.

#5381. $970 million Pacsun CEO says Gen Alpha and Gen Z are ‘greatly misunderstood’—so she made a board of 13- to 22-year-olds to give her advice

Bosses and senior staffers often moan about how young professionals are disengaged and lack initiative. But Brieane Olson, the CEO of Pacsun, warns against overlooking Gen Z and Gen Alpha—and she’s even ensuring they get a seat at the table of the fashion giant that hit $970 million in sales last year.

“I definitely felt, having spent so much time on the front-line with young consumers, that Gen Z and Gen Alpha were greatly misunderstood,” Olson tells Fortune. “And so, what could we do as a brand that caters to young people to really give them a seat at the table and to build something meaningful and really put community first?”

Once every year, Pacsun’s Youth Advisory Council gathers with company executives to discuss big business concerns.

The mini board of directors—comprised of 15 Gen Alpha and Gen Zers aged 13 to 22 who are rotated in each year—weigh in on pressing industry needs, what Pacsun should do differently, and the best paths moving forward.

The country’s youngest minds bring critical feedback directly to Olson and other company executives, touching upon everything from the customer experience to the way stores operate.

“I think one of the things that has taught me personally about working with this council over the last two years, is really that working with these younger generations requires sometimes giving additional context. And so it’s really important to bring them along for the journey and to answer the whys before they become a why,” the CEO says. “The most important thing is to truly listen—allow to have a dialogue, be a part of the reasoning, the why, the discussions—and you get a much better return.”

Pacsun’s youth council quickly gained popularity among young generations wanting their voices to be heard.

The company hand-selected participants in its first year spanning between 2024 and 2025, but when it opened the floodgates to young people across the country, almost 1,000 people applied to the 2026 to 2027 cohort. The surge of interest ended up fueling an entirely new ambassador program, giving even more young people an opportunity to influence the brand.

The company now works with about 300 13- to 22-year-olds who weigh in on business areas they’re most passionate about—including design, styling, visual arts, and emerging trends. Olson says Pacsun’s young advisors have helped with everything from redesigning how store flows should work, to analyzing and contrasting what retail competitors are up to. While some employers scrutinize young generations for being disengaged or unwilling to contribute, Pacsun’s CEO recognizes how motivated they are to have an impact, and is giving them the floor.

“They really do have a true seat at the table,” Olson says. “They have a direct line of communication with myself and all of the other leaders…”

“In return, they’re also getting great mentorship, and they’re getting opportunity and access and the ability to help co-create the future of the brand. And I think there’s a lot of shared benefit to bringing young people in, and helping also to fight the stereotypes that these younger generations are facing.”

Pacsun has also been hosting a Purpose Summit for the past two years, bringing brand partners together with the company’s youth council.

Olson says tech partners from Snapchat, Pinterest, and TikTok have all attended, as well as philanthropic collaborators like Selena Gomez’s Rare Impact Fund. Executives, creators, cultural leaders, brand partners, and young voices exchange ideas, discuss industry hurdles, and strategize how to lead a business with purpose at the day-long event.

Additionally, Pacsun releases a youth report every year that captures a snapshot of the attitudes, behaviors, spending habits, and cultural interests of thousands of Gen Z and Gen Alpha survey participants.

“Creating moments and opportunities for us to pause and really think about how we’re leading and what we need to do differently is important,” Olson says, adding that Pacsun’s youth research helps the company do a “better job to collectively create a future that is a better place for the youth.”

Emma Burleigh is a reporter at Fortune, covering success, careers, entrepreneurship, and personal finance. Before joining the Success desk, she co-authored Fortune’s CHRO Daily newsletter, extensively covering the workplace and the future of jobs. Emma has also written for publications including the Observer and The China Project, publishing long-form stories on culture, entertainment, and geopolitics. She has a joint-master’s degree from New York University in Global Journalism and East Asian Studies.

#5380. From paper routes to fighter jets: Shield AI’s bet on Seattle is a homecoming for its co-founders

by Todd Bishop & John Cook on Nov 9, 2026 at 6:36 amNovember 9, 2026 at 6:36 am

As a kid on Mercer Island, Brandon Tseng delivered The Seattle Times and the Mercer Island Reporter for extra cash. Now he and his older brother, Ryan Tseng, are making news of their own in the Seattle region.

Shield AI, the San Diego defense tech company the brothers co-founded in 2015, announced a deal last week to buy Kirkland, Wash.-based radar maker Echodyne for up to $5.3 billion. Shield, now valued at $28.8 billion, had already unveiled plans in September to build its AI-piloted X-BAT fighter jet at a factory south of Seattle.

“I believe we will become one of the largest, or at least the fastest-growing employer in this region over the next several years,” Brandon Tseng said in an interview with GeekWire in the hours after the Echodyne acquisition was announced.

The company projects that it will employ about 4,000 people in the Seattle area by the early 2030s. It estimates the X-BAT could support about 8,000 jobs across the region in all, including jobs at Shield and its suppliers, according to an economic analysis drawing on company figures.

Tseng said Shield expects to have “well north of a million square feet” in the area before long, up from its initial 420,000-square-foot facility in Des Moines, Wash.

“That will really just be the beginning,” he said.

Brandon Tseng said the biggest reason Shield chose the Pacific Northwest for X-BAT production was the region’s “density of engineering and manufacturing talent,” pointing to Boeing, Microsoft and Amazon.

Inside the Echodyne deal: Shield believes the defense tech companies that succeed will need products that “sense, think, and act,” Tseng said. Its Hivemind autonomy software handles the thinking, and its V-BAT drone and X-BAT jet will handle the acting.

Echodyne becomes “the cornerstone of the sensing piece,” he said.

Tseng said Shield got a closer look at the market for sensors when it bought Australian optics company Sentient Vision Systems in 2024. That led the company to start looking seriously at other sensor makers, and eventually to Echodyne.

Shield and Echodyne had first crossed paths in 2016, when both were fledgling companies in the Department of Homeland Security’s Silicon Valley Innovation Program.

Nearly a decade later, the two companies’ teams were talking about working together when Echodyne began exploring a sale, Tseng said. The deal came together over several months. Tseng was at Echodyne the day it was announced last week, as the companies held all-hands meetings with their teams.

It’s an unusual deal: one venture-backed startup buying another, funded in part by a new venture round. Shield is raising $2.5 billion to help pay for the deal, including $1 billion in new funding at the $28.8 billion valuation — more than double what it was worth in March.

Echodyne has about 400 employees, after opening a $40 million radar factory in Woodinville in July. No layoffs are planned, the companies said. Eben Frankenberg, Echodyne’s co-founder and CEO, will stay in that role, reporting to Shield CEO Gary Steele. The combined company will have about 2,700 employees.

The deal is expected to close in early 2027, pending regulatory approval. Tseng said Shield plans a light touch for roughly the first year after that. Echodyne will keep selling radar to other manufacturers, many of them in counter-drone systems, while pursuing performance targets that could add $500 million to the price.

Deeper product integrations will be announced later, he said.

“They’ve been on a tear growth-wise, and we don’t want to get in their way,” Tseng said. “We don’t want to slow them down. We just want to supercharge them.”

He called the two companies’ cultures a strong match, describing both as mission-oriented and engineering-first. Echodyne’s best-selling radar, EchoShield, is designed to protect U.S. and allied service members from incoming drones.

Echodyne spun out of Intellectual Ventures, the Bellevue invention lab, in 2014 with a $15 million round led by Bill Gates and Madrona. Madrona and other Echodyne investors will become significant Shield shareholders.

Tim Porter, the Madrona Venture Group managing director who has served on Echodyne’s board since 2014, called the deal another sign of the defense tech industry’s rapid growth in the Pacific Northwest.

Echodyne “rarely, if ever, showed up on lists of the hottest defense tech companies,” he wrote. Now it’s “under the radar no longer.”

X-BAT bet: Much of Shield’s growth in the region depends on an aircraft that hasn’t flown yet. Shield unveiled its first full-scale X-BAT prototype this month and shipped it to Kansas for flight testing, with first flight targeted by the end of the year. Shield has said low-rate production will start in Des Moines in mid-2027, with the first locally built jet due in early 2028.

The Pentagon and Shield have committed a combined $400 million to X-BAT’s development, but Shield hasn’t announced any production orders.

Ryan Tseng, speaking to Breaking Defense on the sidelines of the International Fighter Conference in Munich last week, said Shield expects to announce European X-BAT orders and partnerships but declined to discuss quantities, saying only, “Watch this space.” Andrew Hawkes, Shield’s X-BAT director for Europe, told Breaking Defense the company has “several active” sales campaigns there but declined to name customers.

Asked about the X-BAT schedule in the interview last week, Brandon Tseng acknowledged the challenge but pointed to the engineering and manufacturing teams that brought the prototype together in about a year. “There was no quit in them,” he said.

“It’s hard as hell, right? Just to move out on production that fast, but you have to be confident,” he said. “I’m confident.”

Tseng, a Naval Academy graduate who deployed twice to Afghanistan as a Navy SEAL, compared Shield’s pace to that experience, when small, mission-driven groups with the right tools and resources would “do things that people didn’t think were possible.”

Ryan Tseng, an electrical engineer, previously founded wireless charging company WiPower, which was acquired by Qualcomm. The brothers started Shield with Andrew Reiter, Shield’s first CTO, who returned to the company this year.

Seattle roots: The Tseng brothers and their sister grew up on Mercer Island. Brandon Tseng spent summers swimming in Lake Washington and played water polo for Mercer Island. Ryan Tseng, who was Shield’s CEO for about a decade, graduated from Mercer Island High School, and their sister graduated from the University of Washington.

Their father, Carlos Tseng, was CEO of Seattle-based Foss Maritime from 1996 to 2001, according to Tseng and Shield. He would stop at Pike Place Market on the way home from work, and the family “probably ate salmon every other day,” Brandon Tseng said.

The family moved to Florida in 2001. None of the Tsengs live in the area anymore, but Brandon Tseng still has friends here from middle school and high school and stops by Mercer Island when he has time on his visits to the region.

Shield’s Washington state connections go further. Steele, the company’s CEO since May 2025, grew up in Yakima and graduated from Washington State University.

Brandon Tseng called Shield’s expansion in the region “a fun homecoming” for him, his brother and Steele. He is based in Washington, D.C., but expects to spend more and more time in the Seattle area.

Tseng delivered the Times, then the afternoon paper, seven days a week from age 10 to 14, making his rounds every day after school and on weekends. He credits those routes with teaching him about hard work.

“It’s always felt like home,” he said. “It’s great to be back here.”

Go hands-on with new launches the same week they’re announced, and hear directly from the engineers who built them. Experience the depth you won’t find anywhere else.
