#5379. Exchange Ledgers in the Middle as CFTC and SEC Diverge on What “Delivery” Means

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

A customer buys a token on a U.S. exchange and the app shows the balance. Under the CFTC's December 14 framework, nothing has been delivered yet.

Under the SEC's crypto proposal, delivery doesn't decide the question at all. An October 27 comment letter asks the two agencies to settle on one answer.

Open almost any crypto exchange app after a purchase and you'll see a clean number: 1.0000 ETH, available. To the customer, the asset is theirs. To the exchange's database, it's a row in an internal ledger. To federal regulators, that row is now being judged by two different tests that don't agree on what it means.

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has opened an advance notice of proposed rulemaking on what it calls Regulation Crypto Asset Transactions (CTX) and Regulation Crypto Asset Markets (CAM). It sets out the agency's first formal view of "actual delivery" for crypto since it withdrew its 2020 guidance last December. Comments close on December 14.

The Securities and Exchange Commission's Regulation Crypto Assets proposal takes a different view of the same moment. Then, on October 27, a comment letter on the SEC's file raised the gap directly. It described the situation as "two conflicting definitions of the same physical facts" and asked the agencies to "please coordinate the definitions."

Delivery matters because it decides which rulebook applies.

For the CFTC, the answer comes from Section 2(c)(2)(D) of the Commodity Exchange Act. A leveraged, margined or financed retail commodity trade is treated like a futures contract unless "actual delivery" happens within 28 days. If delivery happens in time, the trade falls outside futures rules. If it doesn't, the exchange is effectively running a futures venue.

For the SEC, the question is whether a token is still part of an investment contract. Under the August proposal, a covered investment contract ends when the issuer has finished or permanently stopped its essential managerial efforts and files a Form TR transition report. Whether the buyer has received the token is not part of that test.

So one agency treats delivery as the deciding question, and the other barely considers it.

The CFTC's position is still preliminary, but it is detailed. Published in the Federal Register on October 13, the notice relies on the Monex case standard: actual delivery requires "the transfer of some meaningful degree of possession or control."

For crypto, the agency suggests that possession and control "may require possession of the credentials (e.g., private key(s))." It takes three positions that matter most to exchanges:

The agency is also asking whether control has to be exclusive, whether delivery can happen while a lien or security interest is outstanding, and how financing offered in an exchange's standard account documents affects whether a trade is covered at all.

The SEC's proposal, released on August 18, deals with a different question. It creates offering exemptions, including a $5 million startup exemption over four years, and a safe harbor for when a crypto asset's investment contract ends. Neither depends on where the token sits.

Under the proposal, a token held in a customer's self-custody wallet and a token recorded on an exchange's books are treated the same way. In both cases, the investment contract question depends on the issuer's managerial efforts and its filings.

That is the gap the October 27 letter tries to close. Its author, who describes themselves as a fintech founder designing a consumer platform, argues that "where the customer holds the private keys or execution is on-chain, with custody evidence, the asset should be treated as delivered and the covered-investment-contract analysis should end there."

Running four common exchange transactions through both frameworks shows where the tests split.

Trade one: a fully paid purchase left on the exchange.

Trade two: the same purchase withdrawn to a self-custody wallet on day three.

Trade three: a margined purchase kept on the exchange's ledger for 30 days.

Trade four: an on-chain swap that settles directly into the user's wallet.

The pattern is consistent. Self-custody is the only position that clearly counts as delivery under the CFTC's view and also ends the analysis under the letter's proposed SEC fix. Everything left on an exchange's internal ledger stays in an unclear position. The CFTC treats it as undelivered and the SEC's text doesn't address it.

The letter was filed on October 27, a week after the SEC's October 20 comment deadline. It is anonymous and brief, but its main concern is practical. If the definitions stay separate, it warns, founders will have to design products around whichever rule is stricter.

It is the only filing on either docket so far that sets the two definitions side by side.

The CFTC process is still at the advance-notice stage, so a formal proposal will follow. For U.S. platforms, though, the direction is clear. Under the CFTC's preliminary reading, an exchange that keeps customer assets in internal ledger accounts has not delivered them. If that exchange also offers margin or financing, it is on track to be treated as a futures venue.

The SEC's final rule could adopt the letter's custody-based approach or keep delivery out of its analysis entirely. Until one of those happens, the same ledger entry can be undelivered for one regulator and irrelevant for the other.

Exchanges and their customers have until December 14 to say which definition should prevail. The real decision is whether "delivered" ends up meaning the same thing at both agencies.

#5377. Nebraska rushed Medicaid work rules. Then a cancer patient was told he’d lost coverage

Eli McCreary of Omaha, Nebraska, said he had recently been diagnosed with kidney cancer when he got a call from a local hospital run by CHI Health. He said he was informed that he wasn’t insured anymore under Medicaid — and that the hospital would cancel his appointments unless he paid out-of-pocket.

McCreary, who was 64 at the time, said he phoned a call center for help. He said he was told his benefits under Medicaid, the government health program for people with low incomes or disabilities, now required that he have a job.

“You’re required to do work to stay on,” McCreary said a representative told him. “And you haven’t fulfilled your work requirement.”

For decades, McCreary said, he has battled drug addiction. A substance use treatment program discharged him in March, and in June he was diagnosed with cancer in his right kidney, according to documents reviewed by KFF Health News. He also has diabetes and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.

“I don’t understand what job I can get,” McCreary said. “I can’t walk. I can hardly breathe. I can’t move around. What job am I going to get?”

McCreary said he canceled a CT scan and other tests at the hospital, which is part of CommonSpirit Health, the nation’s largest Catholic health system. He also delayed a cancer-related appointment with a physician who travels back and forth to Omaha. “I missed my window of opportunity with him for another month,” he said.

Taylor Miller, a spokesperson for CHI Health, declined to answer questions about McCreary’s experience. In an emailed statement she said that “CHI Health is committed to helping patients understand their health care coverage and access to care, including available financial assistance resources.”

Determined to be the first state to enforce Medicaid work requirements under President Donald Trump’s signature One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Nebraska launched the new rules May 1 — eight months before most states will do the same. With their newly elected majorities in Congress, Democrats have said they plan to repeal the changes to Medicaid in their first 100 hours in office in January. But it is unclear whether they will be successful, because Trump could veto the measure.

Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen said in December that state officials “certainly appreciate President Trump and his whole administration for delivering this key reform.” Pillen spoke alongside a videoed-in Mehmet Oz, the Trump administration official overseeing Medicare and Medicaid.

“We’re excited to be able to be the first to make it happen,” the Republican governor said.

Laura Strimple, a spokesperson for the governor, didn’t respond to requests for comment. Jeff Powell, a spokesperson for Nebraska’s Department of Health and Human Services, said its rollout “has been very successful.” He pointed to state data showing 86% of affected applicants met the requirement or qualified for an exclusion and 93% of existing enrollees kept their coverage.

Health clinics and organizations advocating for poor and working-class Nebraskans say the rollout has been rife with problems — many due to poor training and inadequate staffing.

About 70,000 adult Medicaid recipients in Nebraska are subject to the work requirements. They must prove they’re working or participating in a similar activity for 80 hours a month, unless they qualify for an exemption. State officials and consultants advising them have said the May 1 date was challenging to meet.

To deploy the law’s Medicaid coverage restrictions, Nebraska budgeted millions of dollars for government contractors, according to state documents KFF Health News obtained via a public records request. Documents from Nebraska’s health department outline $8.2 million in contractor costs to enact Medicaid changes, including work requirements and more frequent checks for whether people still qualify.

Nebraska operates the information technology system that determines who in the state qualifies for Medicaid, unlike most states, which outsource the work to companies under contracts often worth hundreds of millions of dollars. But Nebraska’s health department nonetheless relies on the private sector to help administer its Medicaid program.

The $8.2 million in costs span two years. They stem from two companies that Nebraska uses to increase agency staffing: Public Consulting Group, based in Boston, and Atlanta-based Covendis, which supplies information technology staffers.

One of the companies has praised Nebraska’s implementation of work requirements. A post on Public Consulting Group’s website quotes senior consultant Latanya Michaux. “I really cannot brag enough about how well Nebraska handled this requirement,” Michaux said, crediting the firm’s “incredible relationship” with the state.

Covendis executives did not respond to requests for comment. Powell said the health department “uses contracted staff when hiring a state employee is either uneconomical or impractical because of time constraints, or when the role requires highly specialized skill sets.”

Advocates who work with Medicaid enrollees in Nebraska say that participants are confused and don’t know whether the rules apply to them. These advocates say enrollees also have received inaccurate information. In December, Pillen said the state “won’t be adding workforce” to implement the work requirements, a decision those advocates have criticized. Pillen in July also instituted a government-wide hiring freeze.

Nebraska listed at least half a dozen contractors costing more than $250,000 each, including one person whose compensation exceeds $1.8 million, the documents show. Nebraska submitted the records to federal Medicaid regulators as part of a routine process to secure federal money. Powell said the funding requests “may not reflect actual expenditures.”

Sarah Maresh, a program director with the social justice advocacy nonprofit Nebraska Appleseed, said the amounts were “shocking.”

“When you put in complicated policies like this, there are large corporations making money behind the scenes,” Maresh said. “This just further confirms that it’s happening in Nebraska quietly.”

The Medicaid work requirements in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and other changes shepherded by Republicans will curtail insurance gains that came from the Affordable Care Act, also known as Obamacare. The GOP tax and spending law, which the Congressional Budget Office estimated would reduce federal Medicaid spending by more than $900 billion over a decade, adds reporting requirements and restrictions making it harder for people to stay enrolled.

As of early July,  most denials related to the work requirements among Nebraska adults applying for Medicaid were due to unsubmitted paperwork, according to internal documents from Nebraska’s health department that KFF Health News obtained through a public records request. The state wrote this was “expected.”

State data shows that average wait times at a Nebraska health department call center nearly doubled between May and July, going from about 13 minutes to 26 minutes, before declining in August. In interviews, advocates for Medicaid enrollees said they’ve encountered people who have waited on the phone for hours.

Nebraska received more than 101,000 calls in August, a 66% jump from May.

“If people are working, they just don’t have time to be sitting on the phone to go through all of this stuff,” said Kenny McMorris, CEO of the Charles Drew Health Center, a federally qualified health center in North Omaha. He said roughly half of Charles Drew’s 13,385 patients are on Medicaid, and of those, 42% are in the population subject to the work requirements.

“You can leverage the technology, but you still got to have people there to help,” McMorris said.

Then there are experiences the official data may not catch, like what happened to McCreary — saddled with figuring out what happened with his Medicaid benefits amid a health crisis, and whether it was even true that he had to work to keep them.

McCreary had heard about the Medicaid work requirements but didn’t know they might apply to him. Powell confirmed McCreary was eligible for Medicaid because of the ACA — putting him in the population subject to work requirements.

His ordeal underscores the fallout from being caught in confusing government systems and silos that aren’t obvious to the public.

“This cancer ain’t going to stop just because I ain’t got insurance,” he said. “It’s going to keep working on me.”

When he received the call from the hospital about his coverage, “I was really in despair,” McCreary said. Eventually, he said, he called for help.

Nebraska’s health department runs AccessNebraska, a call center for help with safety net benefits such as Medicaid and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, commonly known as food stamps. But the number McCreary recalls dialing ended up not being AccessNebraska — it was for a different call center, one for SNAP accounts that Nebraska outsources to a private company. Powell said the state has no record of McCreary calling the health department.

McCreary said the worker didn’t have a good explanation for why the Medicaid work requirements would apply to him. Before his health deteriorated, McCreary worked as a driver for an asphalt services company. He said he worked “until I couldn’t do the job anymore.”

“I really had hoped to work longer,” he said. “I kind of enjoyed that job.”

Attorneys and policy professionals who work with people on Medicaid and other public benefit programs said that McCreary’s substance use treatment, lasting four months starting in November 2025, and other health conditions should have exempted him.

The federal law outlines categories of exemptions, such as being too sick to work. People who are considered too ill include those who have a serious medical condition or a substance use disorder.

Nebraska’s health department said it sent tens of thousands of letters, text messages, and emails to inform enrollees about the new requirements. According to state documents, Nebraska said it would “implement enhancements” to its computer system and online portal, including allowing people to submit documents online and having “clear, plain-language” enrollee notices. McCreary, however, doesn’t have an account on Nebraska Medicaid’s online portal, preferring to handle things over the phone or in person.

He also said it’s possible he missed letters from Nebraska Medicaid about his coverage.

“I don’t know if it’s my fault or not,” McCreary said.

The Cornhusker State’s experience could be a harbinger of things to come. Next year, work requirements will apply to millions of adult Medicaid enrollees in more than 40 states.

The nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office has estimated the policy will lead to 5.3 million more people being uninsured in the U.S. by 2034.

The One Big Beautiful Bill Act’s Medicaid changes are the most complicated in years — changes that government benefit experts say will strain and exacerbate long-standing problems with state technology systems for health benefits.

“It’s already a shaky system, and now you’ve added more burdens on top of that,” said Gelila Selassie, director of health advocacy for the nonprofit Justice in Aging.

Nebraska and federal officials, as well as consultants advising the state, detailed the difficulties and successes with the state’s May 1 launch during an August panel discussion at a national conference in Oregon.

“They said, ‘We’re going to go live May 1.’ To which CMS said, ‘Oh, my God!’” Brent Weaver, an official who specializes in Medicaid IT at the U.S. Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, said about Nebraska.

Nebraska officials knew “they weren’t as agile as they probably would have liked to have been,” Weaver said, “but they didn’t let that stop them.”

“If they fail, we looked at it as a failure,” he added in comments that broadly praised the state’s approach.

CMS did not answer questions from KFF Health News about Nebraska’s rollout and Weaver’s remarks.

In Nebraska, a group of 60 people held hours-long meetings three days a week that were “very exhausting,” Michaux, of Public Consulting Group, said during a different session at the conference.

“Our calendars were cleared, and that was the focus,” Michaux said.

Because CMS had not yet issued regulations outlining key details such as how people could get exemptions — it would do so June 1 — Nebraska officials said they had to rely on the law’s broad language to make initial decisions.

“We had to get comfortable being uncomfortable,” Jacob Kawamoto, a deputy director at Nebraska’s Medicaid division, said at the conference.

Public Consulting Group said it worked with the state to develop new guidance and “process guides” — materials for Nebraska eligibility workers with instructions on how to process Medicaid applications or renewals. Training materials for Nebraska caseworkers reviewed by KFF Health News refer to those guides.

“The training was very robust, and the process guides were very robust,” Michaux said.

Maresh disagreed with that characterization. “There are gaps” in the state’s training materials, she said, and caseworkers “are confused” about work requirements.

Public Consulting Group also helped the state institute changes to Nebraska’s Medicaid IT system, according to the company. “We are preparing for future updates and enhancements,” Michaux said.

In response to questions, Public Consulting Group spokesperson Alyssa Brown said the company “has supported Nebraska Medicaid via a broad range of consulting services since 2019, including work on federal and state compliance initiatives.” She said Michaux “discussed” the process guides at the conference but Nebraska developed them. Similarly, Brown said the company did not develop training.

Federal taxpayers will largely bear the costs of implementing the One Big Beautiful Bill Act’s Medicaid policies in Nebraska and elsewhere. Congress allocated $200 million in one-time funding to states. Under federal regulations, the U.S. government picks up most of the tab for state IT system changes, paying as much as 90% of the cost.

“Even though it was not so easy,” Michaux said at the conference, “we definitely had fun standing up the Medicaid work requirement program.”

Public Consulting Group’s employees, Brown told KFF Health News, are “passionate about public service and helping our clients improve the lives of the people they serve.”

As of August, roughly 1,100 Nebraskans had been denied benefits because of Medicaid work requirements. Most denials were because people did not respond to requests for information.

Nebraska’s total Medicaid enrollment has declined by roughly 4,600 people since May, a drop of 1.4%, according to an August report.

As for McCreary, the Nebraska health department’s Powell maintained he experienced “no lapses in coverage” and said he was disenrolled from Medicaid after turning 65. Despite what McCreary said he was told, Powell said, Medicaid work requirements weren’t the reason: He aged out of Medicaid and into Medicare before they could be applied to him.

Selassie, of Justice in Aging, said McCreary’s care shouldn’t have been disrupted.

McCreary is now enrolled in Medicare, and Medicaid covers some of his health costs. He was able to reschedule his canceled appointments.

He had surgery in early November to remove his right kidney.

KFF Health News correspondent Samantha Liss contributed to this report.

#5376. New tax incentives give Washington’s sustainable aviation fuel industry a boost

Challenges, breakthroughs and big ideas in the race to protect our planet. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 9, 2026 at 9:38 amNovember 11, 2026 at 7:41 am

Washington has cleared a milestone in its effort to become a hub for lower-carbon jet fuel, unlocking tax incentives aimed at attracting production to the state.

Gov. Bob Ferguson announced Friday that Washington has reached the capacity to produce at least 20 million gallons of sustainable aviation fuel annually. That triggers incentives taking effect Jan. 1, including a tax credit starting at $1 per gallon for qualifying fuel. The credit rises to as much as $2 for fuels with greater emissions reductions.

The Department of Ecology recently surveyed potential producers and confirmed that Phillips 66’s Ferndale refinery alone has enough capacity to meet the threshold. The benchmark measures production capacity, not actual output.

Sustainable aviation fuel, or SAF, is widely seen as one of the most promising near-term options for cutting aviation’s carbon emissions because it can be blended with conventional jet fuel and used in existing aircraft. But it remains more expensive than petroleum-based fuel, and production is orders of magnitude below the industry’s needs.

“We have so many unique assets in Washington that position us to be global leaders in the SAF transition, and this tax incentive is the final element needed to really unleash the tidal wave of opportunity,” said Jake Gentry, executive director of the Cascadia Sustainable Aviation Accelerator, in a GeekWire interview.

The accelerator launched in January, bringing together airlines, SAF producers, public officials, researchers and others to promote the industry in the Pacific Northwest. Its work includes helping producers secure financing, develop feedstock supplies and connect with customers.

SAF can be produced from used cooking oil, grease and fats, plants and agricultural waste, and captured carbon. Its climate benefits depend on the raw materials and energy used to make it.

The fuel still produces carbon dioxide when burned. But unlike petroleum-based jet fuel, which releases carbon that would otherwise stay trapped underground, SAF recycles carbon already in circulation in plants, animals and the atmosphere. Washington’s per-gallon tax credit requires emissions at least 50% below those of conventional jet fuel.

Washington’s production capacity is below that of some larger facilities elsewhere. A Diamond Green Diesel plant in Texas can produce up to 235 million gallons of SAF annually, according to its partner Valero. That figure also represents capacity, not actual production.

With the minimum threshold being met, all Washington SAF producers will be eligible for the tax credit regardless of their volumes.

A startup called Twelve is already making the fuel in the central Washington city of Moses Lake. The company opened its AirPlant One facility last year and began commercially producing SAF this summer from captured carbon dioxide and water. The technology has the potential to create the most climate-friendly SAF available, potentially unlocking the largest state tax credits.

Nicholas Flanders, Twelve’s CEO and co-founder, welcomed the announcement.

“This is an extraordinary signal of support for our industry,” Flanders said via email. “Washington is building the leading foundation in the country for next-generation domestic fuel production, and Twelve is ready to build upon it.”

Twelve’s first-of-its-kind facility is designed to make up to 50,000 gallons of SAF per year. AirPlant Two, a much bigger plant that would make tens of millions of gallons a year, is in development. The company hasn’t said where it will be located.

Dutch-owned SkyNRG is building a SAF facility in Walla Walla, Wash., and plans to use renewable natural gas that’s captured at landfills and from dairy waste as a feedstock. Earlier this year, leaders said the company had secured key environmental approvals and plans to start commercial operations in 2030.

Washington’s relatively affordable hydroelectric power has historically helped attract climate tech companies. But growing electricity demand, including from data centers, is putting pressure on the region’s power supply.

Washington also faces competition from other states offering SAF tax incentives. Illinois and Minnesota already offer credits, and Nebraska’s program starts next year. Meanwhile, a federal credit was reduced from $1.75 per gallon to $1 after President Donald Trump returned to office.

Washington leaders tout other perks that could attract SAF production. It’s the only state that offers both a SAF tax credit and a clean fuel standard. Together, the policies help make cleaner jet fuel more cost-competitive by providing tax benefits and allowing SAF producers to earn credits they can sell to other fuel suppliers that need to meet the state’s emissions requirements.

The accelerator also supports efforts with Washington State University to develop regional feedstock supplies, including waste from logging and agriculture.

“Between our long history of aviation innovation, our intentional investments into the sector and our climate-forward policies, we’re making sure Washington is the best state in the country to produce sustainable aviation fuels,” Ferguson said in a statement.

The Climate Pledge is a commitment to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2040, co-founded by Amazon and Global Optimism in 2019.

Seven years later, the community has grown to over 700 signatories across 62 industries and 49 countries and territories, reducing emissions, scaling emerging climate solutions, and addressing challenges across operations and value chains.

#5375. Meet the short seller that flagged Nvidia’s ‘significant China problem’ six months ago—including ‘uncomfortably close’ ties with Alice Huang

Six months ago, Nvidia stock peaked at $235.74 a share. But while others were focused on the AI boom and Nvidia’s growing market cap, one research firm saw a China-sized crack in the foundation.

Now, Nvidia is down 27.9% since then, and Jensen Huang has been ousted as CEO following his romantic affair with a suspected Chinese spy.

In a report in May, short seller Culper Research raised concerns about Nvidia’s exposure to China—including Huang’s relationship with the suspected spy, Alice Huang.

“This is not a bet against AI. We are short Nvidia for one reason: the Company has a significant China problem,” the report read.

Culper Research did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Fortune regarding the return on its short bet.

The central allegation in Culper’s report was that more than 20% of Nvidia’s fiscal 2026 compute revenue was driven by Chinese demand, despite assertions from the company that its China business had fallen to zero following U.S. export restrictions in April 2025.

Culper alleged the revenue came through the smuggling of restricted GPUs to Chinese customers and via Southeast Asian intermediaries that purchased Nvidia hardware and provided computing capacity to Chinese companies.

The research’s allegations focused on Singapore-based Megaspeed International, which it says was secretly financed by China’s Alibaba through a network of shell companies—potentially allowing Chinese companies to access Nvidia’s advanced AI chips.

The problem in relying on this undisclosed China-based revenue was that Beijing has since blocked Nvidia imports in favor of its own domestic chipmakers, according to Culper.

“Our review of trade records suggests substantial declines in CY Q1 2026 shipments,” the report continued, “while mainland operators tell us that there are now ‘very few orders’ in China, presenting ‘a huge blow to Nvidia financially.’”

Nvidia previously defended its relationship with Megaspeed after the New York Times reported in October 2025 that it was under investigation over suspicions that it had helped Chinese customers obtain advanced Nvidia chips.

“We’ve chased down every single concern. And we’ve repeatedly tested and sampled data centers around the world and found no diversion,” Huang told Bloomberg in November 2025.

But one of the most consequential parts of Culper’s report also involved Alice Huang, the Chinese Megaspeed executive who had reportedly engaged in a close relationship with Jensen Huang—the first domino to topple his CEO tenure.

Culper raised questions about her continued influence over Nvidia and her relationship but did not establish any romantic ties.

“Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has not only vouched for Megaspeed, but seems to have quite literally walked alongside Megaspeed at every step, while maintaining an uncomfortably close relationship with Megaspeed’s Alice Huang, a Chinese national,” the report stated. “He was first spotted partying with Alice Huang in June 2024–the same month the Apex/Alibaba pledge was filed. He then dined with Alice Huang in Taiwan in May 2025–just weeks after the news of U.S. trade restrictions.”

Citing a Megaspeed employee, the report added that Jensen Huang visited Megaspeed-linked data centers “every few months” and was always accompanied by representatives from Alibaba. “The Megaspeed employee characterized their relationship with Jensen as ‘very close’, corroborating another former Nvidia employee’s suggestion to us that many Nvidia employees wondered if there was a special relationship.”

Joshua Hong is a News Fellow at Fortune covering data, AI, cybersecurity, energy, and retail.

#5374. Amazon’s Ring tries again with a $250 flying home security drone and a $1,000 patrol robot

by Todd Bishop on Nov 10, 2026 at 5:30 amNovember 10, 2026 at 5:42 am

Amazon’s Ring unveiled a $249.99 flying indoor security drone and a $999.99 mobile patrol robot for businesses, bringing back two ideas that stalled in earlier incarnations.

The Ring Drone Cam and Ring Rover Cam, announced Tuesday, are the first products under the Ring Robotics name, which the company calls “a new category of autonomous, mobile security.” Both devices use a system Ring calls AI Pilot to map a home or business, suggest spots worth checking, and find their own way around obstacles such as furniture and shelving.

The drone stays docked with its camera off until it’s sent out on a schedule, on demand, or automatically when another Ring device is triggered. The Rover patrols stores and offices, using a periscope camera to see over counters and shelving.

The Rover is available for preorder in the U.S. and is scheduled to ship Dec. 16. The Drone Cam is slated for Jan. 27, 2027, but Ring is only taking email sign-ups for now. The fine print notes that the drone hasn’t yet received the required authorization from the Federal Communications Commission.

Scheduled flights and patrols, and reviewing the Rover’s recorded video, require a Ring Protect subscription plan. Ring didn’t say which plans qualify.

Ring says customers wanted to see spots a fixed camera can’t reach, and rooms where they wouldn’t want one mounted.

“The honest answer wasn’t more cameras; it meant reimagining what a security device could be,” said Jamie Siminoff, Ring’s founder and chief inventor, in a statement. “That kind of invention is hard, and it takes time.”

Ring unveiled a flying indoor camera called the Always Home Cam in 2020, also priced at $249.99. The company later opened an invitation list, but the device never went on general sale.

The original drone flew only along paths that owners mapped out with it in advance. Ring says the new one builds a floor plan as the owner carries it through the house, suggests spots to check, and plans its own routes.

The Rover Cam traces back to Astro for Business, a rolling security robot that Amazon launched in November 2023 at a starting price of $2,350. Amazon discontinued it less than a year later, refunding customers and shutting the robots off.

Astro for Business was a spinoff of Amazon’s Astro home robot, an Alexa-powered device on wheels that debuted in 2021 and can patrol the house on its own.

Ring says the new robot was inspired by Astro customers who said roving security was their favorite feature. The Ring team “leveraged the best of Astro” to build it, the company says. Ring is pitching the Rover as “not a home robot that also does security, but a purpose-built security robot.”

The original Astro for the home remains an invite-only product. Amazon has redeployed much of the Astro team to work on a new home robot, CNBC reported Sunday. In March, Amazon acquired Fauna Robotics, a New York humanoid robot startup, saying it would become part of a new Personal Robotics Group. Ring’s announcement doesn’t mention either effort.

The Rover also extends Ring’s push into commercial security, following a $5,000 surveillance trailer for parking lots that it unveiled in January. In security robots, it competes with companies such as Knightscope, which rents its robots through a subscription, and Cobalt AI. At $999.99, the Rover costs less than half what Astro for Business did.

On the security drone front, Indoor Robotics makes a ceiling-docking drone that patrols offices and warehouses, but flying security cameras for the home remain rare.

Siminoff, who launched Ring’s predecessor, Doorbot, in 2012 and sold Ring to Amazon in 2018, left the company in 2023 and returned last year to lead Ring and Amazon’s related home security businesses. Last month, Ring unveiled its first smart lock, a $249 deadbolt with no keyhole and a dial that recharges a dead battery by hand.

#5373. America’s debt problem: why wealthy families should be looking beyond the midterms

Daniel Cooper is a partner and head of Sterlington’s private wealth practice. He advises founders, entrepreneurs and ultra-high-net-worth families on the critical decisions that shape how wealth is protected, transferred and governed across generations. Sterlington advises families on the kind of wealth-structure reviews this piece recommends.

America’s issues with its public finances will outlast the political theatre of any midterm election. The midterms will change the balance of power in Washington, but they will not remove the fiscal pressures facing the country.

For wealthy families, the underlying issue is straightforward, namely that a government carrying historic levels of debt, with rising costs of servicing it, will eventually have to confront the question of how to raise more revenue.

Any administration operating with limited room for additional borrowing and spending will have to consider its options, and private wealth, or taxing the income or private wealth of the rich as it will likely be put, will inevitably be part of that conversation.

Taxation is the obvious starting point. Federal decisions on income, capital gains, estate and gift taxes have a direct bearing on how wealth is held, invested and transferred between generations. The current federal estate and gift tax exemptions of $15m per individual, or $30m for married couples, provide considerable scope for planning. But assuming those thresholds, or the wider tax framework, will remain unchanged indefinitely would be a mistake.

For high-net-worth families, the real vulnerability is not simply whether a tax rate increases but whether the structures they have spent years putting in place will continue to work if the rules change. The time to examine those arrangements is before a legislative change makes the decision urgent.

Nor does diversifying wealth necessarily provide protection against these pressures. Many families spread capital across public equities, private equity, real estate, venture capital and international business interests. Whatever the investment merits of that approach, it does not create immunity from government policy. Different asset classes carry different tax treatments, reporting requirements and regulatory exposures. Changes to capital gains rules, the treatment of investment income or the taxation of particular structures can affect several parts of a portfolio at once.

In other words, diversification can spread investment risk without necessarily spreading tax risk. A portfolio that looks well balanced from an investment perspective may still be exposed to changes in the way governments choose to tax wealth.

State taxation adds another complication. Families with property, businesses or investments across multiple states can face very different obligations depending on where they live and how their affairs are organized, while the interaction between federal and state rules can make even apparently straightforward arrangements surprisingly complex.

For international families, the US system of citizenship-based taxation means American citizens often remain subject to US tax on worldwide income even when living abroad. Non-US families with American assets, business interests or beneficiaries may also find themselves caught by US tax and reporting requirements. Structures that work perfectly well under UK, European or Middle Eastern law can produce a very different result when assessed under the Internal Revenue Code.

The danger during periods of political and fiscal uncertainty is to react to individual headlines rather than consider the family’s overall position.

A more effective approach is to constantly review and adapt, if necessary, the entire wealth structure. Existing arrangements should be tested against a range of possible tax and regulatory scenarios, ranging from the plausible to the Black Swan type.

It also requires advisers to work together. Legal, tax and private wealth specialists need to understand the family’s wider objectives and the implications of decisions across different jurisdictions, as optimizing one part of a family’s affairs is of limited value if it creates an unexpected liability somewhere else.

This is not simply a defensive exercise. Families with well-organized and adaptable structures are better placed to respond to changes in the rules, make decisions calmly rather than under pressure, and choose where to establish businesses or hold assets. Flexibility is particularly valuable when the policy environment is ever changing.

The next two years may tell us more about the balance of power in Washington, but they are unlikely to resolve America’s underlying fiscal challenge. The pressure on government finances will remain, whichever party prevails.

Wealthy families should not wait for Washington to settle the debate before acting. The lesson of America’s fiscal position is not where to invest but when to plan: reviewing estate, trust and ownership structures while there is still time to do so calmly, rather than in the rush that follows a change in the law. The question is not which party wins the next election, but whether a family’s affairs are organized to adapt to whatever comes next.

#5371. Clock Ticking on Zcash’s Sprout Pool: 22,263 ZEC Unmoved Ahead of NU7 Lock

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Daily pool data shows Sprout holders moved more than 300 ZEC out in a September rush, then almost stopped. The last withdrawal was on October 19.

Unless someone acts in the next few days, nearly all of what remains will be unspendable at block 3,543,405.

Most coverage of Zcash's upcoming Sprout freeze quotes the same figure, about 22,000 ZEC. That number is accurate, but it is a single snapshot. It doesn't show whether the people who own those coins are doing anything about the deadline.

We checked the pool every day, and the answer so far is no.

According to ZecStats' daily value-pool records, Sprout has held exactly 22,263.34162335 ZEC since October 19. That is 11 straight days, and more than 12,000 blocks, without a single zatoshi leaving the pool. Our October 25 piece recorded the drop from 22,309 ZEC to 22,263 ZEC. Since then the balance hasn't moved.

ZecStats publishes a daily CSV of every Zcash value pool, using the last block of each UTC day. Its figures follow the valuePools field that a full node returns through the getblockchaininfo call. The archive starts on July 30, 2026, and gives a 92-day picture of the Sprout pool.

Across those 92 days, about 374 ZEC, or 1.65% of the pool, left Sprout. That is an average of roughly 4 ZEC a day. The average hides the real pattern, though: the pool moved on only 15 of the 92 days.

Most of the withdrawals came in a few large transfers in September:

Together with smaller moves on August 31, September 17 and September 19, the 30 days to September 29 saw 310.5 ZEC leave Sprout. That is about 10 ZEC a day.

October was much quieter. Apart from one withdrawal of 46.05 ZEC on October 19, the month's activity was small change:

Since October 19, there has been no movement at all.

At September's pace, about 70 ZEC more would leave before activation. At October's pace, it would be well under 15 ZEC. On the last 11 days' pace, the answer is zero.

The deadline is set in ZIP 259, which defines how the NU7 network upgrade is deployed. It sets the mainnet activation height at 3,543,405.

NU7 does not introduce a new transaction format. Instead, after activation, version 4 transactions become invalid, while versions 5 and 6 remain valid. Sprout's design is the problem. As ZIP 259 puts it: "Because Sprout transfers can only be represented by version 4 transactions, funds remaining in the Sprout pool become unspendable."

The coins would not be destroyed, and NU7 does not change Zcash's supply cap. They would simply be stuck in a pool that no valid transaction can spend from. Today the stranded amount would be 22,263 ZEC, about 0.13% of the roughly 17.01 million ZEC in circulation.

ZIP 259 also skips Zcash's usual three-month gap between the first supporting software release and activation. Operators running unsupported software could stay online and follow a pre-NU7 chain.

As of ZecStats' latest update on October 30 at 13:09 UTC, the chain was at block 3,535,877. That leaves 7,528 blocks until activation.

In October, the network averaged about 1,147 blocks a day, or one roughly every 75.3 seconds. At that rate, block 3,543,405 arrives around 02:00–03:00 UTC on November 6. That is the evening of November 5 in the Americas and the early hours of November 6 in Europe and Africa.

Small changes in block times could move that window by a few hours. Holders who plan to move funds on the final day risk missing the cutoff.

In practice, getting funds out of Sprout means sending a version 4 transaction that moves them into a newer pool before activation. Users need software that can still build Sprout transactions and a synced node or wallet that recognizes their old notes.

The September withdrawals show that some holders are still paying attention. Several were round amounts, such as 99.998 ZEC, which is consistent with someone moving 100 ZEC and paying a fee. The 11-day pause since October 19 suggests something else: most of the remaining 22,263 ZEC may belong to keys that are lost, forgotten or no longer used.

That has been part of the debate about Sprout for years. A pool that has been shrinking slowly since Zcash's early days is now on a fixed timetable. The daily data indicates that most of its remaining balance is not being moved.

Every report that cites "about 22,000 ZEC at risk" is technically correct. The more useful figure for anyone tracking the upgrade is the rate of change, and right now that rate is zero.

The useful thing to watch over the next week is whether the Sprout line in ZecStats' daily data moves again before block 3,543,405. If it doesn't, Zcash will activate NU7 with about 22,263 ZEC permanently locked in its first shielded pool. That would be one of the largest deliberate freezes of user funds by any major blockchain upgrade, and nearly all of it would be coins whose owners did not move them in time.

#5370. From the Lost Generation to Gen Beta: How every generation got its name

Generation Beta had a name before its first members were born. The label for babies born from 2025 through 2039 was already in headlines in late 2024, courtesy of the Australian demographer who also named the generation before it, Gen Alpha.

That is a long way from how this used to work. The Lost Generation got its name secondhand, from a French garage owner, via Gertrude Stein and Ernest Hemingway. A network news anchor named the Greatest Generation more than half a century after it went to war.

There’s no official process for naming a generation; it’s more like a cultural quorum is reached, and a name takes hold, even though it’s never technically fixed. The moniker for tens of millions of people born within a couple of decades of one another can come from a magazine essay, a novel, or a research firm. The only real key to a name sticking is that lots of people start using it.

The labels carry real money. McCrindle, the research firm behind Gen Alpha, projects that cohort will command $5.46 trillion in spending power by 2029. They also shape how managers size up young workers, a habit one Fortune commentary argued hurts Gen Z at work.

Even the people who measure generations are cautious about the boxes. In 2023, Pew Research Center said it would apply generational labels more selectively, warning that the standard definitions “may be too broad and arbitrary to capture differences that exist among narrower cohorts.”

The first widely recognized named generation in Western culture was the Lost Generation, generally dated to births between 1883 and 1900. Its members came of age during World War I, which killed millions of young men, and many of those who survived came home disillusioned with the values they had been raised on.

The origin story may be partly apocryphal. According to Hemingway’s memoir A Moveable Feast, as Britannica recounts it, Stein heard a garage owner in France dismiss the young men of the day as a “génération perdue.” She turned the line on Hemingway: “You are all a lost generation.” He used it as the epigraph to his 1926 novel The Sun Also Rises, and it stuck.

The next named generation, usually dated to births from 1901 to 1927, is called the Greatest Generation. Its members lived through the Great Depression and fought or worked through World War II. The name comes from NBC anchor Tom Brokaw, who described how he came to call World War II veterans the Greatest Generation after covering the 40th anniversary of D-Day in Normandy in 1984. He made it the title of his 1998 bestseller.

The Silent Generation, born from 1928 to 1945, followed. Its name was popularized by a November 1951 Time essay, “The Younger Generation,” which noted, “It has been called the ‘Silent Generation.’” Members of this cadre were generally seen as more conformist, cautious, and quiet than their predecessors, which makes sense given the chill of the early Cold War.

Next came a generation with many members still alive and well today: the Baby Boomers. Born from 1946 through 1964, they numbered about 67 million as of mid-2024, roughly 20% of the U.S. population, according to Pew; the oldest turn 80 this year.

The name needs little decoding. Birthrates veritably exploded after World War II: per History.com, 3.4 million babies were born in the U.S. in 1946, 20% more than in 1945. Annual births topped 4 million every year from 1954 to 1964.

Generation X followed, born from 1965 to 1980. The term had floated around for decades, including in a Robert Capa photo essay after World War II and as the name of Billy Idol’s punk band. It wasn’t cemented until Douglas Coupland’s debut novel, Generation X: Tales for an Accelerated Culture, came out in 1991. The X, fittingly, signaled a generation that resisted definition, like a variable in an equation.

Millennials, born from 1981 to 1996, came of age right around the turn of the millennium. Historians Neil Howe and William Strauss coined the term in their 1991 book Generations, because the cohort would be the first to graduate high school in 2000. “We thought that an upbeat name would be good because of the changing way they were being raised,” Howe told NPR in 2014. The pair built on the idea in their 2000 book Millennials Rising.

For a while the same cohort was also called Generation Y, a label Advertising Age used in a 1993 editorial, but it never really stuck.

Some have argued for a so-called microgeneration couched between Gen X and Millennials. Xennials, a term writer Sarah Stankorb coined in Good magazine in 2014, describes people born roughly from 1977 to 1983, who grew up before computers were common and adapted to them as adults. A similar in-between group, the Zillennials, born roughly 1993 to 1998, straddles Millennials and Gen Z.

Following the Millennials came Gen Z, born from 1997 to 2012, by Pew’s definition. Its name is the logical follow-on to X and Y. Its nickname, Zoomers, is a riff on “boomer” that Merriam-Webster traces to at least 2016, well before pandemic-era video calls. The word had an earlier life, too: a 2003 Fortune story used “zoomers” for empty-nesters with spare money to spend.

With the Latin alphabet used up, Generation Alpha took the first letter of the Greek one. The name comes from social researcher and demographer Mark McCrindle, who popularized it in his 2009 book The ABC of XYZ: Understanding the Global Generations. Alphas, born from 2010 to 2024, are the first cohort born entirely in the 21st century, so the “first” in alpha makes sense.

Next is Generation Beta, the cohort born, or to be born, between 2025 and 2039, by McCrindle’s definition. A memorable book or persuasive article could always give the Betas a title that better fits the zeitgeist. But generations once got their monikers years after their last members were born, and this one was named before its first.

Whether Beta sticks is still up to the rest of us. Generation Y had a name, too.

#5369. PitchBook to give early-stage startups free access, using their data to feed a new tool for VCs

by Todd Bishop on Nov 10, 2026 at 7:23 amNovember 10, 2026 at 7:25 am

PitchBook announced a new program to give early-stage startups free use of its private-market data, if they share their financials and other company details.

The Seattle-based company says the new program, dubbed PitchBook for Startups, will feed PitchBook Origin, a new deal-sourcing product that helps venture capitalists and other investors find startups before they raise their first institutional round.

PitchBook announced both offerings Tuesday morning at Web Summit in Lisbon. Owned by Morningstar since 2016, the company has more than 3,000 employees and sells subscriptions to venture firms, private equity investors and dealmakers.

The launches come as first-time startup financings hit a record. There were an estimated 8,625 such deals in the U.S. through the third quarter, already more than the 8,507 in all of 2021, according to the PitchBook-NVCA Venture Monitor. PitchBook attributes part of the surge to AI, which it says is making it easier to start companies.

The startup program is open to pre-seed and bootstrapped companies that haven’t taken money from a venture firm or other institutional investor, or raised a priced round, the type of funding round that sets a valuation.

Founders can use PitchBook to find investors who are active in their sector and stage, and to compare their valuation and growth against similar companies.

To keep their free access, startups must update their company information every quarter. PitchBook says that information can include financials, team growth and product milestones. Only “select portions” of that data will go into Origin, the company said, without saying which.

Origin covers about 25 million companies, including stealth, pre-funding and bootstrapped companies. About 15 million of them are new to PitchBook. It scores companies on how well they match an investor’s criteria and sends alerts when they show new activity.

“What’s been missing is visibility into the stage before a company raises, when the most important signals are the hardest to see,” said Paul Santarelli, PitchBook’s chief solutions officer, in a statement announcing the products.

PitchBook didn’t disclose pricing for Origin, and the product’s web page currently asks investors to join a waitlist.

#5368. Pete Hegseth’s $1.5 trillion Pentagon budget request is DOA after Democrats swept midterms, but global defense spending could still hit $8 trillion

A wave of Democratic midterm victories may have put the kibosh on the Trump administration’s plans to boost the Pentagon’s budget, but global defense spending is expected to top $8 trillion anyway.

Rep. Adam Smith, the top Democrat on the House Armed Services Committee, argued in a letter to colleagues that the Defense Department’s proposed $1.5 trillion budget for 2027, a more than 40% increase, was too high and would come at the expense of services to the American people.

He called for a smaller military budget as well as a probe into the Pentagon’s dealings with defense contractors.

“We must thoroughly review our national defense strategy and develop a more realistic and sustainable approach that does not require a defense budget in excess of $1 trillion or paid for through draconian cuts to critical domestic programs,” Smith wrote.

Economists and public policy experts say a growing interest in cybersecurity and rearmament amid ongoing geopolitical conflicts has accelerated a cycle of defense spending that slowed after the Cold War and ramped up again after 9/11.

According to asset management firm Carlyle, defense spending has increased to 2.0% of the GDP across the G7 countries of Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the UK, and U.S. That’s the highest share in more than three decades. At the current rate of spending, it could reach 3.8%, or roughly $8 trillion in defense commitments.

The U.S. accounts for about one-third of the world’s defense spending, surging past the $1 trillion mark in fiscal 2026. While it’s by far the biggest spender—providing aid and arms to allies in Europe as well as its own military—other wealthy nations are accounting for a growing share of the world’s defense outlays.

As war continues in the Middle East and Ukraine, countries are shifting how they think about risk. Rather than responding to or preparing for a particular conflict, countries are building up their resources as part of a structural shift, leading to a worldwide rearmament push, particularly in Europe, according to retired Admiral James Stavridis, vice chairman of global affairs at Carlyle and former NATO commander.

“None of this is unique to the United States,” he wrote in a research note published in September. “Europe and Japan are both increasing defense budgets meaningfully, and the underlying logic is the same everywhere: if you cannot count on someone else to defend you, secure your energy, or protect your infrastructure, you build the capability yourself, and you build it now.”

Indeed, European Union defense spending hit €418 billion ($461 billion) in 2025, or about 2.2% of its GDP, and is projected to increase to €454 billion ($500 billion), or 2.4% of GDP) this year, according to data from the Council of the European Union.

Huw van Steenis, former securities analyst and partner at Apollo Global Management, observed that European budgets aren’t just showing up in defense companies, but also in increased investments in infrastructure, spurred by disruptions to subsea cables, as well as the recent outages of hundreds of supermarket fridges as a result of cybersecurity attacks.

These disruptions could contribute to additional spending on security from NATO, on top of a commitment to spend 3.5% of GDP on core defense, van Steenis wrote in a blog post on Friday.

“The bottom line is that some of the next beneficiaries of Europe’s defense buildout may sit in infrastructure, energy and industrial technology rather than in the defense sector itself,” he said.

More broadly, Europe may also be bolstering its defenses as a result of ongoing wars and the pulling away of American military support, according to Linda Bilmes, a Harvard Kennedy School public policy lecturer and author of The Ghost Budget: U.S. War Spending and Fiscal Transparency.

“What is driving this whole enormous bill?” she told Fortune. “In Europe, it’s the combination of the war for four years in Ukraine and Russia, and the unreliability of the United States to support NATO.”

EU member states have sent nearly $83 billion in military support to Ukraine since the beginning of its war with Russia in 2022. That total is likely to increase as the Pentagon reportedly winds down its leadership of the NATO-based Security Assistance Group in Germany, which coordinates military training and supplies to Ukraine, in July.

The divestment is part of a larger strategy from the Trump administration to withdraw global military support as part of its “America First” ethos and protectionist ideology.

At the Shangri-La Dialogue in Singapore on May 30, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth encouraged Asian allies to shift their defense models away from reliance on U.S. aid.

“Our approach asks Pacific nations to do what many are already eager to do: invest seriously in their own defense, contribute more to collective security,” he said.

But Rebecca Patterson, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, warned in a post earlier this year that the global rearmament boom could worsen budget deficits, inflation, and interest rates.

“For the private sector, higher interest rates on government debt translate into higher borrowing costs for companies and households, the latter importantly including mortgages and auto loans,” she said. “All else equal, these costs weigh on economic growth.”

While Europe ramps up its spending, the U.S.’s military budget is about to come under increased review. With Democrats taking the majority in both the House of Representatives and Senate, they will want to make significant changes to the Republicans’ defense spending legislation.

Bilmes believes Democrats will try to shift spending away from the Pentagon and toward the State Department and United Nations dues as a means to enhance its soft power.

“There are a lot more people who are not interested in purely pushing some of the Trump agenda for bigness,” Bilmes said. “I think that there will probably be a significant change in terms of pushing to restore some of the soft power that has been cut.”

Sasha Rogelberg is a reporter and former editorial fellow on the news desk at Fortune, covering retail and the intersection of business and popular culture.

#5367. Allen Family Philanthropies gives $10M to hundreds of small arts groups across Washington state

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 10, 2026 at 7:30 amNovember 9, 2026 at 2:56 pm

Allen Family Philanthropies and Seattle nonprofit ArtsFund awarded $10 million to 745 small arts and culture organizations across Washington state, and renewed the grant program for another $10 million next year.

The latest Community Accelerator Grant awards range from $2,500 to $25,000 and reach organizations in 37 of the state’s 39 counties. The 2027 renewal brings the program’s total to $50 million over five years.

For 2026, the program focused on groups with annual budgets under $1 million, which raised the average award by about 25%, from $10,753 last year to $13,423.

The change followed a sector analysis by Allen Family Philanthropies and SMU DataArts. It found that smaller arts groups lost an average of one staff position between 2023 and 2024, while organizations with budgets over $1 million added an average of five.

“The incredible reach of this program across our state, along with the significant findings from our report, show just how much this type of flexible support is needed to bolster Washington’s rich and diverse arts and culture sector,” said Lara Littlefield, executive director of Allen Family Philanthropies.

Of this year’s grantees, 496 are in Northwest Washington, 132 in Southwest, 67 in Eastern and 50 in Central Washington. Recipients include 12 of the state’s 29 federally recognized tribes, and more than 22% are in rural counties.

A handful of the organizations blend art and technology, including Tacoma’s Fablab Nonprofit ($25,000), Seattle-based Simulated Immersive Experimental Realities ($15,000) and Bellingham Makerspace ($2,500).

The Old Hotel Art Gallery in Othello, in Adams County, has received a $25,000 grant each year since 2024. The gallery used the money to pay staff a living wage, to keep operating until its annual fundraiser, and to renovate its historic building, which now brings in rental income.

Gallery director Samantha Copas said the 2025 award “truly kept our doors open.”

Allen Family Philanthropies, formerly known as the Paul G. Allen Family Foundation, was founded in 1988 by the late Microsoft co-founder and his sister, Jody Allen. Arts and culture is one of its core program areas, along with youth and the environment. Last year the foundation committed nearly $7 million to eight Seattle Center nonprofits, including KEXP and the Museum of Pop Culture, to expand youth access to the arts.

ArtsFund will hold a virtual webinar in the spring for organizations interested in applying for 2027 grants. Details will be posted here.

See the full list of 2026 grant recipients here.

#5366. ‘We are losing ground’: Professors log 55-hour weeks as pay stagnates and states question their workloads

Public universities helped make American higher education a draw for students and researchers worldwide. Now lawmakers and governing boards from Kansas to Utah want proof that the professors who teach there work hard enough.

Faculty say the premise is backward. Professors who spoke with Fortune describe 55-hour weeks, departments that have shrunk by as much as half, and raises that haven’t kept pace with inflation.

“We are losing ground,” said Renita Coleman, a journalism professor at the University of Texas at Austin.

As scrutiny of higher education grows, state legislators, governing boards, and administrators have started questioning how professors spend their time and whether they deliver enough for their salaries and job protections. Some have pushed to limit tenure. Others are demanding a detailed accounting of faculty responsibilities.

Public confidence in American higher education has fallen sharply over the past decade. According to Gallup, 38% of Americans expressed a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in higher education in 2026, down from 57% in 2015. The share expressing very little or no confidence rose from 10% to 25%.

The weakening trust comes amid a convergence of concerns, from rising college costs and questions about the value of degrees to political battles on campuses. Those frustrations have fueled skepticism of tenure, which grants professors permanent faculty status after they meet a university’s standards for teaching, research, and service.

Tenure was designed to safeguard academic freedom. But the American Council of Trustees and Alumni acknowledged in July that the public increasingly sees it as “a mere promise of job security, even for incompetent or unproductive professors.”

Against that backdrop, lawmakers and university governing boards in states including Wisconsin, Utah, Ohio, and Kansas have moved to tighten faculty accountability. They have imposed minimum teaching loads, more rigorous post-tenure reviews, and other requirements to ensure professors do their share.

For Coleman, the assumption that professors ease up once they earn tenure couldn’t be further from reality.

“If they would only follow us around for a while, they would see this is ridiculous,” she said. “The pressure, the way they think, as soon as we get tenure, you’re going to stop working.”

Earning tenure can take half a dozen years, and by then the pace of the job is habit. The idea of slowing down can feel almost foreign, Coleman said.

“By the time we get tenure, we’re so ingrained in this, we can’t stop,” she said.

George Dehner, a history professor and department chair at Wichita State University, said the scrutiny often starts from a basic disconnect about what professors do.

“If you think the faculty are scamming you and don’t really work hard…this idea that faculty are working four or six hours a week teaching classes is a deep misunderstanding of what faculty do,” Dehner said. He and his peers “easily” work 55-hour weeks, he added, though their contracts stipulate 40-hour weeks during the nine-month academic year.

Many universities have long used a rough 40-40-20 model for faculty time: 40% teaching, 40% research, and 20% service to the institution and broader community.

In January, the Kansas Board of Regents, which governs the state’s six public universities, put those expectations in writing. Under its new policy, faculty at the three research universities (the University of Kansas, Kansas State, and Wichita State) must devote 40% to 55% of their workload to teaching, 35% to 45% to research, and 5% to 20% to public service. At the three regional universities, teaching rises to 60% to 75%.

Every faculty member now needs a written work plan, and annual reviews are mandatory. Those who fall short of workload expectations are placed on an improvement plan, and tenured faculty with two consecutive unsatisfactory annual reviews face dismissal, reassignment, or an additional one-year improvement plan.

Tenured faculty will also undergo a comprehensive peer review every five years, down from every seven.

Dehner described the policy as a concession to lawmakers who had pushed to give the regents greater authority to revoke tenure. Rather than protecting faculty, he argued, the new requirements reflect the same suspicion that professors aren’t doing enough.

“It is absolutely not welcome,” Dehner said. “It comes from a space where there’s a deep suspicion that faculty don’t do anything… that’s a bad-faith place to start. This belief that faculty are lazy and are scamming them [is] compounded by the fact that they have no idea what higher education people do.”

Gamal Weheba, an engineering professor at Wichita State, also sees the policy as an attempt to appease legislators rather than a meaningful measure of productivity. Academic work, he argued, can’t be measured by hours spent in a classroom or an office.

“It’s not just an idea of having a time card that I clock in and clock out before I talk to students,” Weheba said. “That can never happen.”

The Kansas Board of Regents did not respond to Fortune’s request for comment. At a January meeting, Regent Matt Crocker said the new policies strengthen accountability for state higher education spending, the University Daily Kansan reported.

“The question I seem to get all the time, especially being here in Topeka, is making sure I’m being a good steward for the state’s funding for higher education, and I think the program and policies help answer that question,” Crocker said.

For faculty, one of the biggest frustrations with the new mandates is that they’re being asked to do more without more colleagues to share the load.

When Coleman started teaching at UT Austin in 2005, her department had roughly 25 full-time tenured faculty members. Today it has about 18, a decline of roughly 28%.

The same pattern shows up in Kansas. Dehner said Wichita State’s history department has shrunk from about 17 faculty members when he joined in 2004 to roughly nine today. In Weheba’s engineering department, the count has fallen from about 14 to eight.

Nationally, about 32% of faculty members held full-time tenured or tenure-track appointments in fall 2023, down from about 53% in 1987, according to data from the American Association of University Professors (AAUP).

The shrinking ranks matter because tenured faculty carry duties well beyond the classroom. They serve on university committees, advise students, help colleagues pursue research funding, and sit on search committees for new university leaders, a particularly time-consuming job amid the revolving door of college presidents.

Professors also face problems that were far less prominent when many of them started: student mental health crises, the rapid adoption of AI, cuts to research funding, and political and social unrest on campus.

“There are more burdens than ever being placed on faculty shoulders, which is putting incredible strain on them individually, but also strain on the overall ecosystem in higher ed,” said Geoff Watson, CEO of NCFDD, which provides faculty development resources.

“When you put all of that together, more is being asked of faculty, and actually they’re being provided less support than they ever have been,” he added.

None of that means professors should get a pass, or that they’re all complaining, Coleman said. Universities have long had ways to deal with faculty who don’t meet expectations, she noted, including pushing some out.

A legislative audit released in Utah in October suggests those mechanisms don’t always work. Auditors examined materials from 666 performance reviews of tenured faculty, and only eight concluded that a professor’s teaching needed improvement.

The auditors highlighted 40 cases in which professors received “satisfactory” ratings despite evidence of poor teaching. Utah Legislative Auditor General Kade Minchey told Fortune his office has also received allegations of harassment and of professors not showing up to class.

The report pinned much of the problem on leadership. Department chairs, who are often responsible for holding faculty accountable, typically rotate through the job and take on its administrative duties on top of their own teaching, research, and service, leaving them little time or incentive to confront colleagues.

“When chairs are faculty first and supervisors second, they may neglect the harder, time-intensive leadership responsibilities that drive accountability,” the report stated.

The audit called on universities to strengthen the supervisory role of department leaders and redefine what chairs do. It also asked the Legislature to consider whether the minimum due process required to remove a tenured professor is excessive.

Minchey stressed that the findings weren’t “an attack on tenure,” but rather “a problem of leadership, and it’s a problem of structure.”

Much of the push for faculty accountability has come from Republican-led legislatures, and the Nov. 3 midterms reshuffled that map. In Texas, Democrat Gina Hinojosa unseated Gov. Greg Abbott. In Wisconsin, which wrote a minimum teaching load into law, Democrats flipped both legislative chambers.

That gives some faculty reason for optimism, but neither result rewrites existing policy, and meaningful change is unlikely to happen overnight. The workload strain, meanwhile, isn’t confined to red states.

In Massachusetts, free community college has helped drive enrollment up more than 43% since 2022, adding roughly 27,000 students, according to the state. The program has opened doors for students and added pressure on the professors who teach them.

Darren Stocker, a criminal justice professor at Cape Cod Community College, typically teaches five classes a semester. Each can have as many as 32 students, and he often makes room for more.

The result is workdays that stretch at least 12 hours, “from sun up to sundown, seven days a week,” he said, as he grades assignments, meets with students, prepares lectures, and handles his other responsibilities.

Pay compounds the long hours. Stocker said Cape Cod housing costs have made it increasingly hard for educators to live near campus.

“It’s very difficult to really live in the area in which you work,” Stocker said. “That’s the reality of it.”

Average pay for full-time faculty rose 2.3% between fall 2024 and fall 2025, but inflation ran 2.7% over the same period, according to the AAUP’s annual report on faculty pay. Adjusted for inflation, faculty salaries remain 9.5% below their fall 2019 levels.

Policy changes could ease some of that pressure. Rebuilding confidence in higher education, and the research capacity it has lost, will take considerably longer.

“There is no more pressing issue for higher education than getting very serious about how we rebuild what’s been lost and hopefully build upon it from there,” Watson said. “But it’s not a short-fuse fix that is going to have to take years to kind of come back.”

Stocker, for one, isn’t looking for a way out.

“I absolutely love my job. I don’t think there’s anything I would ever want to do more than what I do now, and that’s teaching in the classroom,” Stocker said. “I live to see the success of my students.”

Preston Fore is a reporter on Fortune's Success team.
